profile.summary: This is the inverse-folding comparison reported in the HyInv technical report, not a released suite. Ten published inverse-folding models and HyInv design sequences for the same held-out backbones from five panels (CATH4.3 test, CATH4.2 test, TS500, TS50 and RecentPDB), the designs are refolded, and the methods are compared by scTM, the TM-score between the predicted structure of a design and the input backbone, with native sequence recovery and sequence diversity reported beside it. It is useful to someone choosing a sequence-design model for screening libraries, with the caveat that the panels, the baseline settings and the scoring were all chosen and run by the team releasing HyInv.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report: Abstract; Section 5.1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is protein inverse folding: given a backbone, produce amino-acid sequences that fold into it. The comparison asks how structurally consistent a method's designs are, at what sequence diversity. Screening needs many candidates rather than one, so the report states that a model is useful in proportion to the diversity it offers at a given structural quality, and compares methods at comparable diversity rather than at one temperature. Structural consistency is read from refolding: the designed sequence is folded by a structure predictor and the prediction is compared with the input backbone.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Five test panels of single chains are used: CATH4.3 test (1,882 chains), CATH4.2 test (1,120), TS500 (500), TS50 (50) and RecentPDB, which is 121 chains from 111 recent PDB entries covering 26,766 residues at lengths 42 to 978. The panels hold standard chains with complete backbones, and RecentPDB was screened for homology to PDB and CATH entries before 2025. ESMFold2 folds every design on all five panels; RecentPDB is additionally folded by Boltz2 and Protenix2, neither of which is used in training. That gives seven panel and predictor columns. A sixth panel, CATH4.3 validation, is the development panel on which the checkpoint and the sampler setting were chosen before any test panel was generated. Four further application panels (de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, loop and window redesign, and four named enzymes) have panel rules, thresholds and endpoints fixed before designs were generated. Not every backbone in them was chosen by rule: ten of the twelve pocket backbones were chosen by rule and two were single cases chosen earlier, the 8 loop and window backbones were chosen by rule, and the four named enzymes are a fixed list that the report says is homologous to the training data and chosen for display.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix A; Appendix G, Table 10

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each method designs sequences for every backbone in a panel at its own published setting. The designs are folded and scored by scTM, the TM-score of the predicted structure of a design to the native backbone, computed on the C-alpha trace at valid sites, normalised by the native length and clipped at one; higher is better. A failed fold is a gap in the average rather than an imputed value. Panel values average the designs of a chain first and then the chains. Recovery is descriptive and has weight zero in the reward, and diversity is matched rather than ranked. The headline comparison is a paired difference: the macro-average of the per-chain scTM difference between HyInv and a baseline, with a 95 per cent percentile interval from 10,000 resamples with a fixed seed; a starred difference is one whose interval excludes zero, and intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. For sampler and ablation comparisons the report instead reads scTM at a fixed diversity from a least-squares quadratic fit of scTM against diversity over a temperature grid, with no extrapolation.
sections.source_locator: Report: Appendix A; Appendix B

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: HyInv has the highest scTM in all seven panel and predictor columns, with an average of 0.875 against 0.867 for ProteinZero V2 with ESM2 weights and 0.863 for ProteinMPNN. Of the 70 comparisons (ten baselines across the seven columns), all 70 point estimates favour HyInv and 61 have an interval that excludes zero. The report states which nine include zero. The parallel decoders PiFold, CMLM, LM-Design and DPLM-2 3B sample at much lower diversity than HyInv, so their differences are not at matched diversity.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 5.2; Appendix D.2

sections.title: Application panels
sections.body: Beyond the five test panels, the report runs the same default setting on four single-chain design tasks. On 74 de novo backbones in 58 clusters at 30 per cent sequence identity, with 4 designs per backbone, the endpoint is the number of designs per backbone that are both foldable (ESMFold2 scTM at least 0.9) and novel (identity below 0.3 to the nearest UniRef50 sequence and to the nearest sequence of the pretraining library). On 12 ligand-pocket backbones, residues within 4 angstroms of the ligand keep their native identity, 384 designs are made per backbone and cell, and the endpoint is the number of different sequences after clustering at 50 per cent identity among the designs that pass an scTM of at least 0.90 and a site C-alpha RMSD of at most 1.0 angstroms. Loop and window redesign covers 8 backbones chosen by rule plus 4 named enzymes whose catalytic residues are fixed, with 128 designs per backbone and region. The report says the named enzymes are homologous to the training data and were chosen for display.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 6; Appendix G

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: No scoring harness or panel manifest is published, so the panels themselves cannot be rebuilt from the release. What the repository does offer is the design step: the hyinv package installs with pip, and one command designs a given number of sequences for a PDB backbone, with options for fixed positions, the draft and rewrite temperatures, the device and the accelerated inference path. Refolding and the scTM calculation have to be supplied by the user.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation; Usage

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Five test panels of single chains: CATH4.3 test (1,882 chains), CATH4.2 test (1,120), TS500 (500), TS50 (50) and RecentPDB (121 chains from 111 recent PDB entries, 26,766 residues, lengths 42 to 978). CATH4.3 validation (1,529 chains in the store's dataset list) is the development panel. Four application panels add 74 de novo backbones, 12 ligand-pocket backbones, 8 loop and window backbones and 4 named enzymes.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix G, Table 10

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Evaluation only: every panel is a test set and each test panel was evaluated once. Model selection used a separate development panel, CATH4.3 validation, on which the checkpoint and the sampler temperatures were chosen before the test panels were generated. The test panels are the published test splits of CATH4.3, CATH4.2, TS500 and TS50 plus the authors' own RecentPDB panel.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix A

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: scTM is the primary metric, higher is better: the TM-score of the predicted structure of a design to the native backbone on the C-alpha trace at valid sites, normalised by native length and clipped at one. Native sequence recovery (higher is more native-like, but descriptive only) and sequence diversity (mean pairwise normalised Hamming distance between a chain's designs, matched rather than ranked) are reported beside it. pLDDT, scRMSD (lower is better) and a C-alpha lDDT-style score are also reported. The application panels use novel-and-foldable yield per backbone, distinct passing designs per plate, site RMSD and region RMSD.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix B

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Ten released models at their published single-temperature settings: ProteinMPNN, ProteinMPNN with grouped decoding, ProteinMPNN low-noise grouped, ProteinZero V2 with ESM1 weights, ProteinZero V2 with ESM2 weights, PiFold, CMLM, LM-Design 650M, DPLM-2 3B and LigandMPNN. The native sequence refolded is shown as a reference line. ProteinMPNN is the only baseline with a temperature sweep.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix D.1; Appendix D.3

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Three controls, each partial. The RecentPDB panel was screened for homology to PDB and CATH entries before 2025. The reinforcement-learning pool of 50,000 backbones was filtered against the benchmark datasets with a homology mask. The application panels were screened with MMseqs2 against the pretraining library and the benchmark reference set, counting a hit at 30 per cent identity and 80 per cent coverage; the report states this is a coverage rule, so shorter similar fragments remain, and the four named enzymes are homologous to the training data by design. The baselines are released checkpoints whose own training data the report does not screen.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 1; Section 5.1; Appendix G, Homology of the panels

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Paired differences carry 95 per cent percentile intervals from 10,000 resamples of the resampling unit, with one resample shared across all compared rows and a fixed seed; the intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons, and the report flags that a few starred intervals have a lower end within 0.001 of zero. Two independent generate-and-fold runs on the development panel differed by -0.0008 and +0.0016, which the authors read as noise of about 0.0015 in one evaluation, and they say differences between checkpoints below about 0.003 are not resolvable. Scores at equal diversity carry intervals from 1,000 draws in which all curve points are recomputed from one cluster resample.
facts.source_locator: Report: Appendix A

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a protein backbone, given as a single chain, for which a method must design sequences; panel values are macro-averages over chains. In the application panels an example is a de novo backbone, a ligand-pocket backbone, or a backbone with a nominated loop or window.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 1; Appendix A

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported. The panels are drawn from CATH and PDB chains and the four named enzymes are TEM-1 beta-lactamase, subtilisin, lysozyme and PETase, but the report gives no species composition for any panel.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix G

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. Every quantity in the comparison is computed from predicted structures and designed sequences, and the report states that none is an experimental measurement.
facts.source_locator: Report: Appendix B

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: A backbone structure. HyInv reads only the N, C-alpha, C and O backbone atoms of the input PDB, and LigandMPNN, which can read ligand atoms, is run on backbone coordinates only. In the constrained application panels a method is additionally given the positions whose native identity must be kept.
facts.source_locator: Report: Appendix D.1; Appendix G; README.md: HyInv

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: No adaptation to the panels. Every baseline is run from its released weights at the single setting at which it was published and is not tuned to the panels, and HyInv uses one setting throughout, chosen on the development panel. Some baseline cells were regenerated by the authors and used only where the procedure reproduced the released score on RecentPDB.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix D.1

strengths.text: The comparison is made at comparable sequence diversity rather than at one temperature, and the report quantifies how far from equal diversity the comparison is: the largest diversity offset, 0.016, is worth at most 0.0011 scTM at the slope of the development curve.
strengths.source_locator: Report: Appendix A, Scores at equal diversity

strengths.text: Model selection and the test evaluation are separated: the checkpoint and the sampler temperatures were fixed on a development panel before the test panels were generated, and each test panel was evaluated once.
Because the primary structure predictor is also the reinforcement-learning reward, the RecentPDB panel is additionally folded by two predictors that never enter training, Boltz2 and Protenix2.

Regenerated baseline cells are accepted only where the authors' procedure reproduced the released score on RecentPDB, and the per-baseline reproduction difference and fraction of identical sequences are printed.

limitations.text: Every number is author-reported: the team releasing HyInv chose the panels, ran all ten baselines at settings of their choosing, and defined the scoring. Only HyInv has a tuned setting and a temperature sweep on most panels.
Nothing here is an experimental measurement. Designs are judged by a structure predictor, and the primary predictor ESMFold2 is also the reward used to train HyInv.

The margins are small next to the stated run-to-run noise. The average margin over the strongest baseline is +0.008 scTM, while one evaluation carries noise of about 0.0015 and differences below about 0.003 are called unresolvable; 9 of the 70 baseline comparisons have an interval that includes zero.
limitations.source_locator: Report: Section 5.2; Appendix A; Appendix D.2

limitations.text: Two baselines are run outside their declared range or compared off matched diversity: ProteinZero V2 is declared for backbones of up to 100 residues but run on the full panels, and the parallel decoders sit at much lower diversity than HyInv.

review.note: Read the text layer of the HyInv technical report PDF (report dated 2026-10-14) and the hyinv README.md and LICENSE, all from Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results at commit 0dcc533cc9f8f76c90ecbfe944df816b6672328a, on 2026-11-27. No command was executed and no human review is claimed.

run_guide.summary: Install the released HyInv package and design sequences for one backbone; the refolding and scTM scoring used in the report are not released, so they are not covered here.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or later and PyTorch; safetensors and numpy are the only other dependencies.
For the accelerated path, a CUDA build of PyTorch and triton; the authors verified triton 3.3.1 on an H20.
A backbone as a PDB file. mmCIF must be converted to PDB first.
The hyinv package is released under the MIT licence.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results
cd Hyra-results
git checkout --detach 0dcc533cc9f8f76c90ecbfe944df816b6672328a
cd AI4Science/hyinv
steps.explanation: The README does not give a clone command. These lines were added so that the install step below runs against the same commit as the saved README, and the path is the package directory in the repository tree.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.explanation: The first line installs the reference implementation. The second is optional and adds the triton kernels used by the accelerated paths on CUDA GPUs.

steps.title: Design sequences for a backbone
steps.explanation: Writes 128 designed sequences for the backbone in structure.pdb to a FASTA file. The report's default setting is draft temperature 0.6 and rewrite temperature 0.34, which are the defaults of the options listed in the README.

steps.title: Keep chosen positions fixed
steps.explanation: The constrained application panels keep nominated residues at their native identity. This is the command form the README gives for that, with positions numbered by PDB residue number and qualified by chain for multi-chain inputs.

steps.title: Use the accelerated path
steps.shell: python -m hyinv design --pdb structure.pdb --n 128 --fast bf16 --out designs.fasta
steps.explanation: The bf16 setting is the fastest path but a numerically different one: the README states that sequences with the same seed are not identical to the default off path. The report's evaluated sequences all come from the reference sampler.

outputs: A FASTA file of designed sequences, one record per design, with chains separated by a forward slash for multi-chain inputs.
No score: the refolding and scTM calculation of the report are not part of the release.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The commands reproduce the design step only. The panels, the refolding recipe and the scoring code of the comparison are not published, so the reported numbers cannot be reproduced from the release.
Outputs are identical only for the same seed, batch size, device type and PyTorch version, and the README states that CPU and GPU random streams differ.

hyinv-20261106-benchmark-report-comparis.notes: The record is one technical report's comparison, not a released suite: there is no leaderboard, no panel manifest and no scoring code, so results_url and data_url are null in every structured entry. The code_url and code_licence point at the hyinv package in the same repository, which is MIT; the repository root licence is not a recognised SPDX identifier, and no licence is stated for the report PDF itself, so its store_bytes is false. The loop and window redesign panel (8 backbones chosen by rule) and the four named enzymes are described in the Application panels section but have no structured entry, because the report prints their endpoints only in figures. The report's own date, 2026-10-14, is printed on its first page; no release date for the comparison is stated, so released is null throughout. Per-method values beyond those quoted sit in figures and in Tables 6 and 7 of the PDF and were not transcribed.

profile.summary: This is the protein language model evaluation reported in the HyPLM technical report, not a released suite. HyPLM-Flash and 28 public checkpoints from 13 model families (29 models in all) are run through the same evaluation code in BF16 on 32 tasks: zero-shot variant scoring from the masked-language-model head on ProteinGym, masked-residue likelihood on two held-out panels, and linear probes on frozen representations for structure, function, localisation, interaction and fitness. It is useful to someone choosing a protein encoder for embeddings or variant scoring, with the caveat that the developer of one of the models chose the tasks, wrote the adapters and ran every baseline.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report: Section 4; Appendix A

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three capabilities of a protein encoder, each read without fine-tuning the encoder. First, zero-shot variant effect: each substitution is scored by the masked-marginal log-likelihood ratio and the score is correlated with an experimental fitness measurement. Second, how well the model models protein sequence at all, as the negative log-likelihood of masked residues under identical masks. Third, what its frozen representations contain, probed by linear or bilinear heads for secondary structure, residue contacts, fold, enzyme and Gene Ontology annotation, subcellular localisation, metal-ion binding, human protein interaction, and fitness or property regression. Throughput on one GPU is measured beside the accuracy so that models can be placed on an accuracy against speed plot. That plot does not compare like with like on precision: HyPLM-Flash is timed on its INT8 engine and the baselines in their reference implementations, while all accuracy figures are BF16 runs.
sections.source_locator: Report: Sections 3 and 4.1 to 4.3; Figure 1 caption; Appendix A, Probes and Throughput

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks are taken from existing benchmarks rather than built afresh: ProteinGym v1.3 for zero-shot substitutions, TAPE for secondary structure, ProteinNet contacts, remote homology, fluorescence and stability, CASP14 and CASP15 evaluation domains for contacts, the SaProt and DeepFRI splits for enzyme commission and Gene Ontology terms, DGEB for prokaryotic enzyme classification and archaeal retrieval, DeepLoc through PEER for localisation, PEER for human protein interaction, and FLIP and FLIP2 for AAV, GB1, Meltome, amylase and a cross-protein hydrolase split. Each row of the task table prints the number of proteins in the train, validation and test splits, and where a row groups several tasks the sizes are those of the first. Two panels are the authors' own: 479 proteins from their held-out UniRef split, and 887 recently released PDB chains, clustered at 50 per cent identity with MMseqs2 after removing exact matches to the training corpus.
sections.source_locator: Report: Table 4; Section 4.3

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every model is run in BF16 through a thin adapter around its reference implementation, and inputs longer than a model's window are processed in windows with 50 per cent overlap whose residue representations are averaged. For the probes, sequence-level tasks use representations mean-pooled over residues without special tokens and per-residue tasks use the residue representations; for every task and model six layers at relative depths 0.25, 0.5, 0.625, 0.75, 0.875 and 1.0 are evaluated and the layer and the regularisation strength are selected on the validation split, or by 5-fold cross-validation on the training split where a task has none. Regression probes are closed-form ridge regressions, classification probes are L2-regularised logistic regressions fitted with L-BFGS, multi-label tasks fit one output per term and report Fmax, and the contact head is a symmetric bilinear form on 32-dimensional projections trained with AdamW on up to 8,000 ProteinNet proteins. A ProteinGym score is the sum over a variant's substitutions of the log probability of the mutant minus that of the wild type, with each position masked on its own, aggregated by the benchmark's official procedure. Confidence intervals come from 5,000 bootstrap replicates over assays, proteins, queries, sequences or pairs, with identical resamples for paired differences.
sections.source_locator: Report: Appendix A, Models, Probes, Zero-shot scores and likelihood, Statistics

sections.title: Reproduction checks and withheld results
sections.body: The authors state that their runs of eight published ESM-2 and ESM C checkpoints reproduce the ProteinGym leaderboard to within 0.0025. They withhold the zero-shot and likelihood results of xTrimoPGLM because their runs fall 0.07 to 0.09 below the leaderboard and its likelihood is implausibly high, which they attribute to an incompatibility between their adapter and that model's masked-language-model head; its embedding results are kept. Models without a suitable masked-language-model head (ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3) are left out of the zero-shot and likelihood panels. ESM3-open and SaProt are evaluated from sequence alone although their published ProteinGym results also use structure inputs, and E1-600M is run on the query sequence alone although it is trained to use retrieved homologues. Three regression splits (GB1 two-vs-rest and three-vs-rest and the FLIP2 cross-protein hydrolase split) are reported but excluded from the summary statistics, because their validation data come from the training distribution while the test sets are strongly shifted and numerically equivalent runs of the same model differ by up to 0.2.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 4.1; Appendix A, Statistics and Deviations

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: No evaluation harness, task packaging or scoring script is published, so the 32 tasks cannot be rerun from the release. The repository publishes the model and its inference engine: a download script for the weights, a pip install, an encode call that returns residue or mean-pooled representations from a chosen layer, and a logits call that masks a position so that a masked-marginal variant score can be computed. The README states that the INT8 default is within 0.01 of BF16 on zero-shot, structure, function-annotation and likelihood metrics, and recommends BF16 when training regressors on near-identical variants.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 32 tasks, drawn from published benchmarks except for two likelihood panels of the authors' own, the held-out UniRef split and the PDB time split. The task table lists ProteinGym v1.3 substitutions (217 assays), a held-out UniRef panel (479 proteins) and a PDB time split (887 entries); TAPE secondary structure (8,678 train, 2,170 validation, 513 test on CB513, with TS115 and CASP12 grouped in the same row), ProteinNet contacts (25,299 / 224 / 40), CASP14 and CASP15 contact domains (82 and 95), TAPE remote homology (12,312 / 736 / 718); EC in two splits (13,090 / 1,465 / 1,604 for the first), GO-MF, GO-BP and GO-CC (26,225 / 2,904 / 3,350 for the first), DGEB EC (512 train, 128 test), DGEB Arch retrieval (2,343 queries), DeepLoc through PEER (8,743 / 2,190 / 2,745), metal-ion binding (5,068 / 662 / 665), HumanPPI (26,319 / 234 / 180); and FLIP, FLIP2 and TAPE regression splits for AAV (28,626 / 3,181 / 50,776 for two-vs-many), GB1 (381 / 43 / 8,309), Meltome (5,149 / 643 / 1,366), amylase (2,574 / 644 / 488), a cross-protein hydrolase split (11,970 / 2,993 / 9,972), fluorescence and stability (21,446 / 5,362 / 27,217 for the first) and thermostability (5,056 / 639 / 1,336).
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Each probed task keeps the train, validation and test split of its source benchmark, with the sizes printed in the task table. The validation split selects the layer and the regularisation strength; where a task has no validation split (DGEB EC) selection is by 5-fold cross-validation on the training split. The zero-shot tasks have no training split and are scored on all 217 ProteinGym assays. The two likelihood panels are test-only: 479 held-out UniRef proteins and 887 recent PDB entries. Three FLIP and FLIP2 regression splits are deliberately shifted between validation and test and are excluded from the summary statistics for that reason.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4; Appendix A, Probes and Statistics

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: One primary metric per task, as the task table prints them. Spearman correlation for ProteinGym substitutions and for every fitness or property regression (higher is better); negative log-likelihood in nats, with perplexity beside it, for the two likelihood panels (lower is better); three-state accuracy for secondary structure, precision at L/5 over long-range pairs for contacts, fold accuracy for remote homology, Fmax for EC and the three Gene Ontology branches, macro F1 for DGEB EC, MAP@5 for DGEB Arch retrieval, and accuracy for localisation, metal-ion binding and HumanPPI (all higher is better). Contacts are residue pairs whose C-beta atoms, or C-alpha for ProteinNet, are closer than 8 angstroms, and long range means a sequence separation of at least 24. Embedding throughput in residues per second on one H20 is reported beside the accuracy. The speed figures are not a same-precision comparison: HyPLM-Flash is timed on its INT8 engine and the baselines in their reference implementations with the fastest attention kernel each supports, while every accuracy figure is a BF16 run.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4; Table 3; Appendix A, Probes; Figure 1 caption; Section 3; Appendix A, Throughput

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: 28 public checkpoints from 13 model families, from ESM-2 8M to ESM-2 15B, giving 29 models with HyPLM-Flash. The families named in the report are ESM-1b, ESM-2, ESM C, ESM3-open, E1, DPLM, SaProt, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3, AMPLIFY and xTrimoPGLM. For the ProteinGym comparison the report also lists published leaderboard values for the top single-sequence entries, including the supervised predictors VespaG and VESPA.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4; Appendix A, Models; Table 5

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: One task-level control and no control over the baselines' own training data. The PDB likelihood panel holds entries released later than the training data of every model evaluated, clustered at 50 per cent identity with MMseqs2 after exact matches to the authors' training corpus were removed, and the UniRef panel is held out of HyPLM-Flash training. For the probed tasks the report relies on the source benchmarks' own splits and describes no further identity cut-off or time split, and it does not screen any public checkpoint's training data against the task test sets.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4.3; Table 4

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Paired bootstrap confidence intervals, 5,000 replicates, resampling the unit that matches the task: assays for ProteinGym with the official aggregation recomputed in each replicate, proteins for structure and likelihood, queries for retrieval, and sequences or pairs elsewhere; paired differences use identical resamples. The report prints 95 per cent intervals for the zero-shot differences between HyPLM-Flash and each comparable encoder. No seed replicates of the probe fitting are reported, but the report states that on the three excluded regression splits numerically equivalent runs of the same model differ by up to 0.2.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4.1; Appendix A, Statistics

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A protein sequence in most tasks, with the unit of scoring varying by task: an assay of substitutions for ProteinGym (217 assays, scored one variant at a time and correlated within the assay), a protein for the likelihood panels and the sequence-level probes, a residue for secondary structure, a residue pair for contacts, a query for DGEB Arch retrieval, and a protein pair for HumanPPI.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4; Appendix A, Probes

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported as a composition. The report names the source benchmarks rather than the species they cover; the only organism-linked labels it prints are the human cell Meltome split, the human protein interaction task, and DGEB's prokaryotic enzyme classification and archaeal retrieval tasks.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Experimental measurements enter only through the source benchmarks. The zero-shot task correlates model scores with the 217 substitution assays of ProteinGym v1.3, and the regression probes are fitted to FLIP, FLIP2 and TAPE measurements of AAV and GB1 fitness, amylase and hydrolase activity, melting temperature, fluorescence and stability. The report does not describe any assay protocol itself, and the structure, annotation and likelihood tasks involve no assay.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4.1; Table 4

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The amino-acid sequence alone, for every model. Models that can read more are deliberately restricted: E1-600M is run on the query sequence without retrieved homologues, and ESM3-open and SaProt are evaluated from sequence alone although their published ProteinGym results also use structure inputs. Representations may be taken from any of six layer depths, selected on validation data.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4; Appendix A, Deviations

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot and frozen probes only; no encoder is fine-tuned. Zero-shot scores come from the masked-language-model head, and every supervised task fits a linear probe, or a bilinear contact head, on cached frozen representations, with the layer and the regularisation strength chosen on validation data. Features are cached in FP16, or FP32 for the Ankh models. Every accuracy number is from a BF16 run of the model.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4; Appendix A, Probes

strengths.text: Every model is run through one evaluation code path in the same precision, with the same probe family, the same six candidate layer depths and the same selection rule, so differences between models are not differences between published protocols.

The authors check their own pipeline against an external reference: runs of eight published ESM-2 and ESM C checkpoints reproduce the ProteinGym leaderboard to within 0.0025, and the one model they could not reproduce is named and its affected results withheld.
Differences carry paired bootstrap intervals over the natural resampling unit, and the report reads small zero-shot gaps as ties rather than wins.

The likelihood panel uses chains released later than the training data of every model evaluated, with exact matches to the authors' corpus removed, which is a time-based control rather than a random split.

limitations.text: The evaluation is run by the developer of one of the models under test: the authors chose the 32 tasks, wrote the adapters, selected the layers and ran every public checkpoint themselves.

The probed tasks inherit whatever leakage their source splits carry: apart from the two likelihood panels the report describes no identity cut-off or time split of its own, and it does not check any public checkpoint's training data against the test sets.

Models are compared outside the setting they were built for in at least three cases, which the report states but which still limits the comparison: E1-600M is trained with retrieved homologues and is run without them, and ESM3-open and SaProt can read structure but are run from sequence alone.

Three of the regression splits are unreliable by the authors' own account and are dropped from the summary statistics while still being printed in the tables, so a reader comparing per-task values must know which splits the averages exclude.

Neither the evaluation code nor the task packaging is released, and the report publishes per-task values for HyPLM-Flash and twelve other encoders only, so the 29-model comparison cannot be rerun or inspected task by task.

representations cached at six layer depths, or masked-language-model logits

per-task metric on the test split
paired bootstrap difference between models
diagram.caption: Zero-shot tasks read the masked-language-model head directly; the supervised tasks fit a probe on frozen representations, with the layer selected on validation data before the test split is scored.

gaps: No evaluation code, task packaging or result file is released, so nothing here can be rerun by a third party.
Per-task values are printed for HyPLM-Flash and twelve other encoders only, although 29 models were run.

The report prints no accuracy value for the INT8 engine that the release defaults to; every accuracy number is a BF16 run, and the only INT8 statement is the README's claim that the metrics are within 0.01 of BF16.

The task table gives one train, validation and test triple per row, so for the grouped rows (secondary structure, EC, Gene Ontology, AAV, GB1, fluorescence and stability) the sizes of the tasks other than the first are not printed.
The report does not state the species composition of any task.

run_guide.summary: Install the released HyPLM-Flash engine and produce the two kinds of output the evaluation reads: frozen representations for the probes, and masked-position logits for zero-shot variant scoring. The evaluation code itself is not released.
prerequisites: A CUDA GPU (the README recommends Hopper GPUs such as the H20 or H100) and Python 3.10 or later.
2.6 GB of FP32 weights, released as two shards in the repository's GitHub Releases and fetched by the download script; curl is needed.
torch, safetensors, triton and flash-attn, installed by the pip step.
The package is released under the MIT licence.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results
cd Hyra-results
git checkout --detach 0dcc533cc9f8f76c90ecbfe944df816b6672328a
cd AI4Science/hyplm_flash
steps.explanation: The README does not give a clone command. These lines were added so the steps below run against the same commit as the saved README, and the final path is the package directory in the repository tree.

steps.title: Download the weights and install
steps.explanation: The script fetches, merges and verifies the two weight shards; the pip step installs the package and its dependencies. The README notes that a GITHUB_TOKEN is only needed if the API rate limit is reached.

steps.title: Extract frozen representations
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from hyplm import HyPLMEncoder

encoder = HyPLMEncoder.from_pretrained("weights")
sequences = ["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ", "ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY"]

residue = encoder.encode(sequences)
pooled = encoder.encode(sequences, pooling="mean")
layer16 = encoder.encode(sequences, layer=16)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's Python example, wrapped in a shell heredoc so it runs as one command. Mean-pooled vectors are what the report's sequence-level probes read, and the layer argument is how a particular depth is taken; the report selects among six relative depths on validation data.
steps.source_locator: README.md: Usage; Report: Appendix A, Probes

steps.title: Score one substitution zero-shot
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from hyplm import HyPLMEncoder

encoder = HyPLMEncoder.from_pretrained("weights")
sequence = "MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"
logits = encoder.logits(sequence, masks=[2])[0]
log_probs = logits[2].log_softmax(-1)
tokens = encoder.tokenizer.tokens
score = log_probs[tokens.index("V")] - log_probs[tokens.index("T")]
print(score)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's masked-marginal example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It gives the log probability of the mutant minus that of the wild type at a masked position, which is the per-substitution quantity the report sums for a ProteinGym variant.
steps.source_locator: README.md: Usage; Report: Appendix A, Zero-shot scores and likelihood

steps.title: Choose the precision for the task
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from hyplm import HyPLMEncoder

encoder = HyPLMEncoder.from_pretrained("weights", precision="bf16")
print(encoder.encode(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"], pooling="mean")[0].shape)
PY
steps.explanation: INT8 is the default. The README recommends bf16 when fitting regressors on near-identical variants, such as the AAV and GB1 splits of FLIP, because INT8 representations of variants of one protein differ by about 1 per cent. The keyword is the one named in the README's precision table.

outputs: Lists of CPU FP32 tensors in input order, without the leading and trailing special tokens: one [L, 1280] tensor per sequence for residue representations, or one [1280] vector per sequence when mean-pooled.
An [L, 33] logits array from the logits call, from which a masked-marginal substitution score is computed.
No task metric: the probes, the task data and the scoring of the report are not released.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
They cover running the model only. None of the 32 tasks, the probe fitting or the bootstrap statistics is published, so the reported numbers cannot be reproduced from the release.
The report's accuracy numbers are BF16 runs while the release defaults to the INT8 engine; the README states the metrics agree to within 0.01 but prints no per-task INT8 value.
A single sequence may be up to 8,190 residues, and invalid characters raise an error.

hyplm-flash-20261106-benchmark-report-ev.notes: The record is one technical report's evaluation, not a released suite: there is no leaderboard, no evaluation code and no task packaging, so results_url, code_url, data_url and the licence fields are null in every structured entry. The code_licence is left null deliberately: the MIT licence in the repository covers the hyplm_flash model package, not the unreleased evaluation code. One discrepancy a reviewer should check: Section 4.3 describes the likelihood time split as 887 PDB chains released after 2 September 2026, while Table 4 describes the same 887-entry panel as RCSB PDB entries released 9 Sep to 7 Oct 2026; the structured entry quotes the table and does not state a date range. The task table prints one size triple per row and says the sizes are for the first task of a grouped row, so the structured entries name which task each size belongs to and no size is repeated onto a sibling task. GB1 has a structured entry omitted on purpose: the row covers three splits, the report does not say which one the printed sizes belong to, and two of the three are excluded from its own summary statistics. The 29-model comparison is author-run throughout, by the developer of HyPLM-Flash.

profile.summary: This is one review paper's own comparison, not a released suite. It asks how much a graph neural network for protein interaction prediction gains from protein-level node features, and which kind of protein information helps most. Nine protein embedding methods, three each from sequence, structure and function, are used in two ways on two link prediction benchmarks (OGBl-ppa and HuRI): on their own in a protein-only multilayer perceptron, and as node features for six graph neural network configurations, against the same networks with randomly initialised node features. It is useful to someone deciding whether to attach protein language model, inverse folding or knowledge graph embeddings to a PPI link predictor.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Experimental design

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Link prediction on a protein interaction network: given the known edges of an interactome, score candidate protein pairs. The comparison is set up around three questions. Whether adding biologically informative node features to a graph neural network improves it over random features. Which source of node features, sequence, structure or function, works best. And whether combining network topology with protein representations beats using protein representations alone. The third question is answered by an ablation in which the task is reformulated as binary classification over concatenated protein embeddings with a multilayer perceptron and no network at all.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Comparative analysis, research questions; Experimental design

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Two existing benchmarks are reused, chosen to differ in species coverage and in how negatives are made: OGBl-ppa, a multi-species benchmark with randomly sampled negatives under a closed-world assumption, and HuRI, a human dataset with experimentally validated true negatives. The paper reports graph sizes of 576 289 nodes and 30 326 273 edges for the OGBl-ppa interaction graph and 8248 nodes and 51 813 edges for HuRI. Protein identifiers were mapped to UniProt, sequences taken from UniRef50 and then mapped to PDB identifiers through CATH for structures. The function embeddings come from a biomedical knowledge graph built by linking the proteins of the interaction graph to the Gene Ontology classes that describe them, using a STRING release matched to the one OGB uses and a 2020-06-01 Gene Ontology Annotation release, converted to a directed labelled RDF graph; the paper reports 620 555 nodes and 5 989 238 edges for the OGBl-ppa knowledge graph and 52 513 nodes and 321 259 edges for the HuRI one.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Data; Table 4

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each benchmark keeps its own task and evaluation protocol; the paper reproduces the OGBl-ppa leaderboard hyperparameters so that its numbers are comparable with that leaderboard. Two metrics are reported for every cell, Hits@100 and accuracy, both higher is better. On the OGB side, Hits@100 means ranking each positive validation or test edge against 3,000,000 randomly sampled negative edges and counting the fraction ranked in the top 100. Every embedding and network combination is compared against the same network with randomly initialised node features, which is the control that answers the first question. A majority-vote ensemble over the different representations is reported as an eleventh column. The results tables mark the best score per method and per table, bold the cells where a biological embedding beats random features, and give a maximum standard deviation for the table rather than per cell: 0.0711 for OGBl-ppa and 0.0928 for HuRI.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Experimental design; Tables 5 and 6 footnote; OGB page: ogbl-ppa prediction task

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: Function-derived embeddings were strongest. The paper reports gains over the random-feature baselines such as ESM-2 with GraphSAGE on OGBl-ppa and NGNN combined with SEAL on HuRI for sequence features; structural embeddings improved on the baselines in both tasks, with the largest gain for NGNN with a GraphSAGE branch; and knowledge graph embeddings gave the largest improvements overall. Functional representations beat sequence and structure consistently, while no consistent difference appeared between sequence and structure. The majority-vote ensemble often beat individual sequence or structure embeddings but usually lost to the functional ones. The protein-only multilayer perceptron ablation reaches performance close to the simpler graph baselines with knowledge graph features alone, which the authors read as evidence that network structure and protein features are complementary.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results and discussion

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two link prediction benchmarks and the knowledge graphs built over them. OGBl-ppa: interaction graph of 576 289 nodes and 30 326 273 edges, with a knowledge graph of 620 555 nodes and 5 989 238 edges. HuRI: interaction graph of 8248 nodes and 51 813 edges, with a knowledge graph of 52 513 nodes and 321 259 edges. A Gene Ontology graph of 44 266 nodes and 71 515 edges is listed beside them. The paper gives no test-set size for either task.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 4

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Each benchmark's own split is used and the paper does not restate it. For OGBl-ppa the OGB documentation describes a biological throughput split: training edges are associations measured by high-throughput technology or obtained computationally, while validation and test edges are associations that can only be measured by low-throughput laboratory experiments. The negatives differ between the two tasks, which the paper treats as the important difference: OGBl-ppa samples negatives at random under a closed-world assumption, HuRI carries experimentally validated true negatives. No split rule is given for HuRI.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Data; Results and discussion; OGB page: ogbl-ppa dataset splitting

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Hits@100 (Table 5) and accuracy (Table 6), both higher is better, reported for every combination of node feature source and model on both datasets. Hits@100 is the OGB ranking metric: the fraction of positive test edges ranked in the top 100 against 3,000,000 randomly sampled negative edges. No other metric is reported in the two result tables.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Tables 5 and 6 captions; OGB page: ogbl-ppa prediction task

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The same graph neural networks with randomly initialised node features are the reference point, run with the leaderboard hyperparameters for OGBl-ppa. The models are GCN, GraphSAGE, NGNN with a GCN or a GraphSAGE branch, each of those two combined with SEAL, and a multilayer perceptron; a majority-vote ensemble over the representations is reported as well. The protein-only multilayer perceptron with random embeddings is the baseline for the ablation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experimental design; Tables 5 and 6

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None of the study's own. The comparison relies on the two benchmarks' own splits, and the authors name homology-based partitioning as future work rather than something they did. Two further sources of leakage are acknowledged but not controlled: the protein embedding models are pretrained on public sequence, structure and annotation data that overlap these proteins, and the functional embeddings come from a Gene Ontology knowledge graph whose annotation coverage favours well-studied proteins. The paper quantifies the coverage: in OGBl-ppa 10.6 per cent (61 352) of proteins are not annotated, of which 7.8 per cent are also test proteins, while HuRI proteins are fully annotated.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results and discussion; Conclusions

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: A single maximum standard deviation per dataset, given in the footnote of both result tables: 0.0711 for OGBl-ppa and 0.0928 for HuRI. No per-cell standard deviation, no confidence interval and no statistical test between cells is reported, and the number of repeated runs behind those figures is not stated.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Tables 5 and 6 footnote

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a candidate edge between two proteins: a protein pair that the model must score as interacting or not. The nodes carrying the features are individual proteins, each represented by a 1024-dimensional sequence or structure embedding or a 128-dimensional function embedding.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Comparative analysis; Experimental design

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Multi-species for OGBl-ppa and human only for HuRI. The paper's degree figure covers 55 species in OGBl-ppa across eight kingdoms (Pseudomonadati, Bacillati, Fungi, Metazoa, Viridiplantae, Discoba, Amoebozoa and Alveolata), while the OGB documentation describes the dataset's nodes as proteins from 58 different species. HuRI is described as a human-specific dataset.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 5 caption; Data; OGB page: ogbl-ppa graph

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: The labels are experimental interaction evidence carried by the two source benchmarks, not measurements made for this study. For OGBl-ppa the edges are biologically meaningful protein associations from STRING, including physical interactions, co-expression, homology and genomic neighbourhood, and the split separates high-throughput from low-throughput evidence. HuRI supplies experimentally validated true negatives as well as positives. The paper describes no assay protocol itself.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Data; Results and discussion; OGB page: ogbl-ppa graph and splitting

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The interaction network plus one protein-level representation per node. Three sources are allowed, one at a time: sequence, from the protein language models ESM-2, ProtTrans and ProGen2 over UniRef50 sequences; structure, from the inverse folding models ESM-IF1, PiFold and ProstT5 over PDB structures reached through CATH; and function, from the knowledge graph embedding methods TransE, ComplEx and RDF2Vec over a Gene Ontology and STRING knowledge graph. The random-feature baselines read the topology alone, and the ablation reads the embeddings alone.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experimental design; Data

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: The protein embeddings are precomputed once from released models and injected as fixed node features; the graph neural networks are trained on each task, reproducing the OGBl-ppa leaderboard hyperparameters. No protein embedding model is fine-tuned on the interaction task. The ablation trains only a multilayer perceptron on concatenated embeddings.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experimental design

strengths.text: The three sources of protein information are compared under one framework with three representative methods each, and every combination is run against the same network with random node features, so the gain attributable to the features can be read directly.

The two datasets were chosen to differ in a way that matters for interpretation: one is multi-species with randomly sampled negatives, the other single-species with experimentally validated negatives, and the authors use that contrast to explain part of the performance gap.
The confound behind the winning feature type is reported rather than hidden: the authors measure annotation coverage in OGBl-ppa and note that annotation bias favours well-studied proteins.
A protein-only ablation with no network is run alongside the hybrid models, which separates the contribution of the embeddings from the contribution of the topology.

limitations.text: Uncertainty is reported as one maximum standard deviation per dataset with no per-cell figure, and no test is applied between cells. Several of the differences the paper discusses are smaller than those maxima (0.0711 for OGBl-ppa and 0.0928 for HuRI), so individual rankings cannot be separated from run-to-run variation.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Tables 5 and 6 footnote; Results and discussion

limitations.text: There is no control for homology or for pretraining overlap. The embedding models are pretrained on the same public sequence, structure and annotation resources the test proteins come from, and the authors themselves list homology-based partitioning as work still to be done.

The winning feature type depends on annotation availability rather than on the protein itself, which limits how far the conclusion carries: the functional embeddings read Gene Ontology annotations, and the authors say the advantage comes with greater dependence on annotation availability and quality and that broader evaluation on weakly annotated benchmarks is needed.

The text and the tables do not agree on one method. The results text reports a gain for GraphSAGE with DistMult on HuRI, but the knowledge graph columns of Tables 5 and 6 are TransE, ComplEx and RDF2Vec, with no DistMult column.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results and discussion; Tables 5 and 6 column headers

limitations.text: Nothing executable is published with the paper. The code and the dataset sources are listed in supplementary tables rather than in the article, so the comparison cannot be rerun from the text, and the article itself is under a non-commercial licence.

diagram.title: Protein embedding and GNN comparison workflow
steps: interactome: OGBl-ppa or HuRI
protein embedding per node: sequence, structure or function
node features injected into a GNN, or used alone in an MLP
link prediction scored by Hits@100 and accuracy
compared with the same model on random node features
diagram.caption: Each of the nine embedding methods is run both as a standalone protein representation and as node features for six network configurations, always against a random-feature control.

gaps: No test-set size is given for either task: the paper prints graph node and edge counts only.
The number of repeated runs behind the reported maximum standard deviations is not stated, and no per-cell variance is given.
The code and the per-dataset sources and licences are in supplementary tables S1, S4 and S8, which are served through a download gate and were not retrieved, so no code address is recorded here.
The split rule for HuRI is not described in the article, and the OGBl-ppa split had to be read from the OGB documentation rather than from the paper.
Hyperparameters for the embedding methods and the networks are in supplementary tables S3 and S5 to S7, which were not retrieved.

The supplementary material was not retrieved. No command was executed and no human review is claimed.

profile.summary: This is one paper's own benchmark, not a released suite. It scores AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3 and ESMFold on experimental structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank between 2022 and 2024 whose sequences have no close homologue among structures released up to the end of 2021, giving 1666 monomeric and 994 dimeric targets. Monomer predictions are classified from RMSD and LDDT against the experimental structure, dimer predictions from DockQ at the interface. It is useful to someone asking how these three predictors behave on recent targets without usable templates, and the per-structure results are published through the authors' ProModEv portal and a Zenodo deposit.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and methods

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How accurately three structure predictors reproduce an experimental structure from sequence, on targets chosen to be hard for template-based modelling. For monomers the question is global and local agreement with the crystallographic, cryo-electron microscopy or NMR structure. For dimers it is whether the predicted interface matches the experimental one, which is a harder question than getting each chain right. The paper also asks whether the predictors know when they are wrong, by comparing the predicted confidence pLDDT with the measured accuracy class, and whether remaining template similarity explains the failures, by stratifying each class by a template quality score.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, quality assessment sections; Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: All 39,298 protein structures released between 1 January 2022 and 31 December 2024 were downloaded from the PDB and their sequences compared by BLAST with every PDB sequence released up to 31 December 2021, at an e-value cut-off of 0.001. The authors state that these dates were chosen so that the targets are outside the training data of all three predictors. Sequences below 40 per cent identity were kept whatever the coverage, and sequences below 70 per cent query coverage were kept whatever the identity. Entries were then classified as monomer, dimer or higher-order oligomer using PDBe biological assembly annotations plus manual curation, and only monomers and dimers were kept, giving 2799 monomers and 2179 dimers; for dimers an entry was kept even if only one chain lacked a homologous structure. CD-HIT at 90 per cent identity removed redundancy, with the two chains of a dimer concatenated before clustering, and chains shorter than 20 or longer than 2700 residues were dropped. The final set is 1666 monomers and 994 dimers.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Collection of benchmarking datasets and structure selection criteria

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Five structures per sequence were generated with AlphaFold2 v2.2.3 and with the AlphaFold3 server, and one with ESMFold v1.0.3 at default parameters. For monomers the top-ranked AlphaFold model (ranked_0) and the single ESMFold model were aligned with the experimental structure and scored by RMSD and LDDT, with TM-score reported as a further similarity measure. From the two primary metrics each prediction falls into one of three classes: accurate (RMSD at most 3.0 angstroms and LDDT at least 0.7), correct with domain movement (RMSD above 3.0 angstroms but LDDT at least 0.7), and incorrect (RMSD above 3.0 angstroms and LDDT below 0.7). For dimers, ligands were stripped from the experimental files, residue numbering was fixed with the DockQ package's fix_numbering.pl script, DockQ was computed for all five AlphaFold predictions and the best-scoring model kept, and the result was classified by the CAPRI bands: incorrect below 0.23, acceptable 0.23 to 0.49, medium 0.49 to 0.80, high quality 0.80 and above. pLDDT was recorded for every prediction, monomer and dimer, as a per-residue confidence measure on a 0 to 100 scale. Statistics are Spearman correlations and t-tests between metrics.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions; Residue alignment and quality assessment; Quality assessment of predicted dimer structures; Statistical analysis

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: The headline numbers are that AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 correctly predicted 88 per cent of the monomers and 77 per cent of the dimers, while ESMFold reached 76 per cent of the monomers and 41 per cent of the dimers; restricted to X-ray and cryo-electron microscopy structures, accuracy rose to 95 per cent for AlphaFold and 83 per cent for ESMFold on monomers, because most failures involved NMR structures. Confidence tracks accuracy poorly at the failure end: of the 200 incorrect AlphaFold2 monomer predictions, 150 (75 per cent) still had pLDDT at least 70, and of the 191 incorrect AlphaFold3 predictions, 158 (83 per cent) did. Residual template similarity is low across the set: of the 1666 monomers, 652 (39 per cent) have no homologous structure at all (template quality 0), 936 (56 per cent) have template quality between 1 and 40, and 78 (5 per cent) above 40, and the incorrect class is enriched in targets with no homologue.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, monomer sections

sections.title: Where the results live
sections.body: The per-structure benchmarking values are not printed in the article. They are served by ProModEv, a web portal the authors built for the purpose, with sortable tables and in-browser structure comparison, and they are also deposited on Zenodo. The Zenodo record holds nine archives: the experimental monomer and dimer structures (RCSB_Monomers, RCSB_Dimers), the AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3 and ESMFold predictions for both, and a pLDDT graph archive. The record is dated 1 January 2026 and carries a CC BY 4.0 licence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Development of ProModEv; Data availability; Zenodo record 17749805

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two sets drawn from the same pool: 1666 monomeric and 994 dimeric PDB structures released between 1 January 2022 and 31 December 2024. They come from 39,298 structures released in that window, reduced to 2799 monomers and 2179 dimers by the homology and assembly filters and then to the final counts by CD-HIT clustering at 90 per cent identity and the length limits. Among the monomers, the paper prints 1314 (79 per cent) solved by X-ray diffraction, 160 (9.6 per cent) by electron microscopy and 190 (11.4 per cent) by NMR; these sum to 1664, not 1666, so the paper's method breakdown leaves two monomers unaccounted for; the 994 dimers are 795 (80 per cent) homodimers and 199 (20 per cent) heterodimers, with 760 (76.5 per cent) by X-ray diffraction, 219 (22 per cent) by electron microscopy and 15 (1.5 per cent) by NMR.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection; Results, Sequence selection and model generation

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train or validation split: this is an evaluation-only set and all 1666 monomers and 994 dimers are scored. The separation is temporal and by homology rather than by split: targets were released after the training cut-off of all three predictors and were filtered against every PDB sequence released up to 31 December 2021.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Monomers: RMSD (lower is better) and LDDT on a 0 to 1 scale (higher is better) are the two primary metrics, combined into three accuracy classes, with TM-score reported beside them as a topological similarity measure. Dimers: DockQ (higher is better), which combines interface RMSD, ligand RMSD and the fraction of native contacts, classified by the CAPRI bands. pLDDT on a 0 to 100 scale (higher is better) is recorded for every prediction as the predictor's own confidence, not as an accuracy measure.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, quality assessment sections

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three predictors, compared with each other rather than against a baseline method: AlphaFold2 v2.2.3 run locally, AlphaFold3 through its web server, and ESMFold v1.0.3 run locally at default parameters. There is no template-based or physics-based reference method, and no null model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two controls, both stated. A time cut-off: only structures released from 1 January 2022 are used, which the authors say puts them outside the training data of all three predictors. A homology filter: every sequence was BLASTed against all PDB sequences released up to 31 December 2021 at e-value 0.001 and kept only if identity was below 40 per cent or query coverage below 70 per cent; for dimers an entry was kept if one chain met the rule. Residual similarity is then quantified rather than assumed, through a template quality score that is the product of identity and coverage, and reported per accuracy class. The authors note that for dimers an entry could enter with one homologous chain.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection; Results, template quality analysis

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No replicate or interval is reported for any accuracy figure. Sampling variation is handled by selection rather than by averaging: five models per sequence are generated for AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 and the best one is taken (the top-ranked model for monomers, the highest-DockQ model for dimers), while ESMFold produces a single model. The statistics reported are Spearman correlations and t-tests between metrics, not confidence intervals on the class counts.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, quality assessment and Statistical analysis

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a PDB entry whose biological assembly is a monomer or a dimer, predicted from its amino acid sequence and compared with the deposited experimental structure. For dimers the unit of scoring is the interface between the two chains.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection and dimer assessment

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported. The targets are whatever PDB entries pass the release-date, assembly and homology filters; the paper reports their experimental method, oligomeric state and length but gives no species composition.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Sequence selection and model generation

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Experimental structure determination is the reference. The paper gives the monomer targets as solved by X-ray diffraction (1314), electron microscopy (160) and NMR (190), which sum to 1664 of the 1666 monomers; the dimer targets by X-ray diffraction (760), electron microscopy (219) and NMR (15). No binding, activity or other functional assay is involved.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Sequence selection and model generation

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The amino acid sequence, as retrieved from the PDB entry. Each predictor then uses whatever it normally uses internally: AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 build multiple sequence alignments, which the paper notes affects their dimer run time, while ESMFold reads sequence alone. Ligands are not supplied to any predictor, and were removed from the experimental files before interface scoring for that reason.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions; dimer assessment

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot inference from released tools. Nothing is trained or fine-tuned: AlphaFold2 v2.2.3 and ESMFold v1.0.3 were installed from their own repositories and run, ESMFold at default parameters, and AlphaFold3 was used through its public web server.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions

strengths.text: The target selection is independent of the predictors and documented step by step, from 39,298 released structures down to 1666 monomers and 994 dimers, with the date cut-off, the BLAST thresholds, the assembly classification, the CD-HIT clustering and the length limits all stated.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection

strengths.text: Residual template similarity is measured rather than assumed: a template quality score is computed for every target and the accuracy classes are broken down by it, so a reader can see that 39 per cent of monomers have no homologue at all.
Predicted confidence is reported against measured accuracy, which exposes how often a confident prediction is wrong on these targets.

The per-structure results are published rather than summarised only: an interactive portal serves them, and the predicted and experimental structures are deposited on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 as nine archives.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Development of ProModEv; Data availability; Zenodo record 17749805

limitations.text: The accuracy classes rest on thresholds the authors chose themselves (RMSD 3.0 angstroms and LDDT 0.7 for monomers), so the headline percentages move if a reader prefers other cut-offs. The DockQ bands, by contrast, follow the CAPRI standard.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, quality assessment sections

limitations.text: The three predictors are not run under equal conditions. AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 get five models per target and the best is selected, while ESMFold produces one, and AlphaFold3 was run through a web server rather than locally, so its exact version and settings are outside the authors' control.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions; dimer assessment

limitations.text: The homology filter is weaker for dimers than for monomers, because a dimeric entry was kept even when only one of its two chains lacked a homologous structure, so some dimer targets contain a chain with a close template.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection

limitations.text: No uncertainty is attached to the reported percentages, and the comparison between predictors is made on class counts with no interval or test between them.

No evaluation code is released. The portal and the Zenodo deposit hold the structures and the per-structure scores, but the custom shell and Python scripts behind them are not published, and the article itself is under a non-commercial licence.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Statistical analysis; Data availability; licence statement
