profile.summary: FoldBench is a low-homology benchmark for all-atom biomolecular structure prediction: 1522 biological assemblies from the PDB, organised into nine tasks covering protein, RNA and DNA monomers and six interface types (protein-protein, antibody-antigen, protein-ligand, protein-peptide, protein-RNA and protein-DNA). Targets were deposited after the AlphaFold 3 validation cut-off of 13 January 2023 and filtered against a reproduction of the AlphaFold 3 training set, so a single benchmark can be used to compare co-folding models across molecule classes. Interfaces are scored by success rate (DockQ at least 0.23, or ligand RMSD below 2 angstroms with LDDT-PLI above 0.8 for ligands), monomers by LDDT. The targets, the evaluation code and reference results are published under the MIT licence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Methods, Data curation procedure; README: FoldBench Targets, Leaderboard

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an all-atom co-folding model can build the correct structure of a whole biological assembly, and in particular the correct interface between its parts, on targets it is unlikely to have memorised. The nine tasks separate the question by molecule class and interaction type, because the authors treat antibody-antigen interfaces, protein-ligand complexes and nucleic acids as the hard cases. Beyond raw accuracy, the benchmark measures how accuracy depends on similarity to the training set: protein-ligand results are split into an unseen-protein subset and an unseen-ligand subset, and success rate is plotted against ligand similarity to the training data.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, Benchmarking protein-ligand co-folding performance

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The authors first reproduced the AlphaFold 3 training set at its 2021-09-30 cut-off, then took PDB entries deposited after 13 January 2023 and before 1 November 2024. Entries must be non-NMR with resolution better than 4.5 angstroms, fewer than 300 polymer chains and between 10 and 2560 tokens under the AlphaFold 3 tokenisation, and the first bioassembly of each entry is the target. Assemblies are cleaned: water removed, chains with fewer than 4 resolved residues or all-unknown residues removed, protein chains with a C-alpha gap over 10 angstroms removed, and clashing chains dropped by a stated rule. Targets are then split into monomers (one polymer chain, below 40 per cent identity to the training set) and interfaces (chain pairs with any heavy atoms within 5 angstroms), each with its own homology rule: a polymer-polymer interface is dropped if both chains exceed 40 per cent identity to two chains of one training complex, protein-protein interfaces are further filtered with Foldseek-Multimer at TM-score below 0.5, a protein-ligand interface is dropped if the protein exceeds 40 per cent identity and the ligand exceeds 50 per cent Tanimoto similarity to a ligand in the same training complex, and protein-peptide interfaces require the protein below 40 per cent identity. What remains is clustered at 40 per cent identity for proteins and 100 per cent for nucleic acids and peptides, keeping the highest-resolution member, under per-task resolution limits.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Inputs are generated once from the mmCIF of each bioassembly as AlphaFold 3 JSON, with bond information removed, and then converted to each model's own format. Every model predicts with a 5 by 5 sampling strategy, five seeds by five samples, with 10 recycles, and unless stated otherwise the reported result is the structure with the highest ranking score. Scoring uses OpenStructure v2.8 as the main tool, for LDDT, TM-score and GDT-TS on monomers and for DockQ on most protein interfaces; protein-nucleic acid interfaces are scored with the DockQ v2 program because OpenStructure does not support them. An interface counts as a success at DockQ at least 0.23, and DockQ is also binned into incorrect, acceptable, medium and high. Protein-ligand interfaces use binding-site superposed, symmetry-corrected ligand RMSD, with success defined as ligand RMSD below 2 angstroms and LDDT-PLI above 0.8. Antibody CDR H3 loop RMSD is computed separately after Chothia renumbering through AbNum and PyRosetta4. Monomer tasks report LDDT rather than a success rate. Inference ran on NVIDIA H800 80GB GPUs.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model Inference and Evaluation and metrics; README: Leaderboard note

sections.title: Leaderboard and the training cut-off problem
sections.body: The repository keeps a leaderboard with two target sets: the full set of targets released after 2023-01, and a subset released after 2024-01. On the full set AlphaFold 3 leads at 72.93 per cent on protein-protein, 47.90 per cent on antibody-antigen and 64.90 per cent on protein-ligand, with antibody-antigen the weakest task for every model. The readme marks Boltz-2 and RosettaFold3 with an asterisk because their training cut-off is later than FoldBench's reference date of 2023-01-13: the low-homology guarantee holds only against PDB data before that date, so those models may have seen the targets, and the readme says their results are for reference only and should not be compared directly with the valid models. Two further caveats are printed: nucleic acid monomer results are omitted from the 2024-01 set for want of targets, and one model's protein-RNA row is blank because of inference or evaluation errors.
sections.source_locator: README: Leaderboard and its footnotes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository is cloned, a conda environment is created from environment.yml, and scoring runs in two steps. The first, evaluate.py, reads a prediction_reference.csv for the named algorithm and, for each requested target type, merges the target table with the prediction table on PDB identifier and scores every prediction against its ground truth with OpenStructure; for the protein-DNA and protein-RNA interface types it additionally scores with DockQ v2. The second, task_score_summary.py, aggregates those per-target scores into success rates or LDDT per task and writes a summary table. Running on more than the bundled examples needs the target CSV files edited and the referenced ground-truth CIF files downloaded from a link the readme gives, and a model's predictions registered in prediction_reference.csv.
sections.source_locator: README: Getting Started, Evaluation; evaluate.py

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 1522 biological assemblies from the PDB, in nine task sets. The paper's Methods give 334 protein monomers (after removing 7 de novo designed proteins), 14 DNA monomers, 15 RNA monomers, 558 protein-ligand interfaces, 172 antibody-antigen interfaces, 279 general protein-protein interfaces (antibody-antigen excluded), 51 protein-peptide interfaces, 70 protein-RNA interfaces and 330 protein-DNA interfaces. The repository readme lists the same counts except for protein monomers, where it says 330 structures. The protein-ligand set is further split into an unseen-protein subset of 76 targets and an unseen-ligand subset of 482 targets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, final clustering and resolution cut-offs; Results, protein-ligand; README: FoldBench Targets

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Evaluation only: there is no training split, and every target is scored. The separation from training data is by deposition date and by homology to a reproduced AlphaFold 3 training set, with a per-task homology rule, followed by clustering at 40 per cent identity for proteins and 100 per cent for nucleic acids and peptides. The leaderboard reports two nested evaluation sets, targets released after 2023-01 (the full set) and the subset released after 2024-01, and the protein-ligand task is additionally reported on its unseen-protein and unseen-ligand subsets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure; README: Leaderboard

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Interfaces are scored by success rate, higher is better: DockQ at least 0.23 for protein-protein, antibody-antigen, protein-peptide, protein-RNA and protein-DNA, and ligand RMSD below 2 angstroms together with LDDT-PLI above 0.8 for protein-ligand. Monomer tasks report LDDT, higher is better. DockQ is also binned as incorrect below 0.23, acceptable 0.23 to below 0.49, medium 0.49 to below 0.80, high 0.80 and above. Further measures reported beside these are TM-score and GDT-TS for monomers, LDDT-LP for the ligand pocket, and CDR H3 loop RMSD for antibodies, lower being better for the RMSD measures.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation and metrics; README: Leaderboard note

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The paper evaluates five all-atom predictors: AlphaFold 3, Boltz-1, Chai-1, HelixFold 3 and Protenix. The repository leaderboard adds OpenFold 3 (preview) to the same set, and lists Boltz-2 and RosettaFold3 separately as models whose training cut-off is later than the benchmark's reference date. There is no classical docking or template-based reference method.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; README: Leaderboard

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: This is the benchmark's main design feature. Targets must be deposited after 13 January 2023, the AlphaFold 3 validation cut-off, and before 1 November 2024. The authors reproduced the AlphaFold 3 training set at its 2021-09-30 cut-off and filtered against it with a rule per task: monomers below 40 per cent sequence identity; a polymer-polymer interface removed when both chains exceed 40 per cent identity to two chains of one training complex; protein-protein interfaces additionally filtered by Foldseek-Multimer at TM-score below 0.5; a protein-ligand interface removed when the protein exceeds 40 per cent identity and the ligand exceeds 50 per cent Tanimoto similarity to a ligand in the same training complex; protein-peptide interfaces requiring the protein below 40 per cent identity. Remaining similarity is then measured rather than assumed, by reporting accuracy against training-set similarity. The limit is stated plainly in the readme: the guarantee holds against PDB data before 2023-01-13 only, so models with a later training cut-off are flagged and set aside. The readme also says the authors developed an algorithm to identify and prevent overfitting of models on FoldBench, without describing it.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure; Results; README: Leaderboard footnotes

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Sampling variation is handled by generating 25 structures per target for every model (five seeds by five samples, 10 recycles) and reporting the one with the highest ranking score, with best-of-25 comparisons shown separately. Figures carry 95 per cent confidence intervals on mean success rates and mean DockQ scores, and box plots show medians and interquartile ranges. The leaderboard tables in the repository carry no interval.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model Inference; Figure 3 and Figure 4 captions; README: Leaderboard

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is either a single polymer chain (a protein, RNA or DNA monomer) or one interface, a pair of chains whose closest heavy atoms are within 5 angstroms, extracted from a predicted full biological assembly. For the protein-ligand task the example is a protein and ligand interface, with one interface chosen at random per ligand. Each target comes from the first bioassembly of a PDB entry.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported. Targets are PDB biological assemblies selected by date, resolution, size and homology; the paper and the readme report molecule class, chain counts, token counts and oligomeric state but give no species composition.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Overview of the benchmark; Figure 2 caption

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Experimental structure determination, with NMR excluded. Entries must be non-NMR with resolution better than 4.5 angstroms, and the per-task limits are tighter: below 2.0 angstroms for general protein-protein interfaces, below 2.5 angstroms for antibody-antigen, protein-RNA and protein-DNA interfaces, and no further limit for protein-peptide interfaces. No binding or activity assay is involved.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The full specification of the assembly: sequences and chemical components of every entity, generated from the mmCIF of the bioassembly as AlphaFold 3 JSON with bond information removed, then converted to each model's own input format. Each model uses its own multiple sequence alignment and template pipeline, which the paper notes is not uniform: AlphaFold 3 and HelixFold 3 search RNA alignments and templates locally while the other three do not, and the commit and alignment source of each method are listed in a supplementary table.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model Inference

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot inference from released checkpoints. No model is trained or fine-tuned for the benchmark; each is run at a pinned commit with the stated sampling strategy. The repository invites a contributor to submit an algorithm for the maintainers to run, through a packaging guide, rather than submitting scores.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model Inference; README: Integrating a New Model into FoldBench

strengths.text: One target set and one scoring pipeline cover nine tasks across proteins, nucleic acids and ligands, so results for different molecule classes come from the same construction rules rather than from separate task-specific datasets.

The homology filter is explicit and per task, built against a reproduction of the AlphaFold 3 training set, and includes a structural filter (Foldseek-Multimer at TM-score below 0.5) for protein-protein interfaces rather than sequence identity alone.

The benchmark reports how accuracy depends on similarity to training data instead of only reporting a single number, including a ligand-similarity breakdown that the authors read as evidence of memorised binding modes.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Benchmarking protein-ligand co-folding performance

strengths.text: Targets, evaluation code and reference results are released under the MIT licence, with a documented path for a new model to be run by the maintainers and a maintained leaderboard that is updated when new models are evaluated.
strengths.source_locator: README: Updates, License, Integrating a New Model; LICENSE; Paper: Code availability

limitations.text: The low-homology guarantee is dated. It holds only against PDB data before 2023-01-13, so any model trained after that date may have seen the targets; the readme flags Boltz-2 and RosettaFold3 on that ground and says their numbers should not be compared with the valid models.

Some tasks are too small to carry much weight: 14 DNA monomers, 15 RNA monomers and 51 protein-peptide interfaces, and the nucleic acid monomer results are omitted from the 2024-01 set altogether for want of targets.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, final counts; README: Leaderboard footnotes

limitations.text: The models are not run through identical pipelines. The authors had to modify several of them to get predictions at all, remove glycans for Boltz-1, drop modified residues for HelixFold 3, patch an AlphaFold 3 error and work around a Chai-1 token limit, and the alignment and template search differs between methods.

Not every model produces a score for every target, so the denominators differ: the final counts of predictable and assessable targets per task and model are given in a supplementary table, and one leaderboard cell is blank because of inference or evaluation errors.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation and metrics; README: Leaderboard footnotes

limitations.text: The two counts published for the protein monomer task do not agree: the paper's Methods give 334 targets, the repository readme 330 structures. Neither source explains the difference.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, final clustering and resolution cut-offs; README: Monomeric Structures

run_guide.summary: Clone the benchmark, build its conda environment, score a model's predictions per target and aggregate them into success rates and LDDT per task.
prerequisites: conda, to create the environment from the repository's environment.yml.
A model's predicted structures, registered in prediction_reference.csv for that algorithm with its ranking scores and file paths.
The ground-truth CIF files: the bundled examples come with four, and the full referenced set is a separate download the readme links.
The evaluation code is MIT licensed.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/BEAM-Labs/FoldBench.git
cd FoldBench
git checkout --detach 4273f6877d82bd0b2fa476d1b2f34d121cbccc70
steps.explanation: The readme's clone command, with a checkout line added so the steps below run against the same commit as the saved readme and script.

steps.title: Create the evaluation environment
steps.shell:
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate foldbench
steps.explanation: Builds the environment the scoring scripts need, which includes OpenStructure and DockQ.

steps.title: Score each prediction against its ground truth
steps.explanation: The readme's first evaluation step, run here on the bundled Protenix example. Reading evaluate.py, it loads prediction_reference.csv from the algorithm's evaluation directory, and for each target type merges the target CSV with that table on pdb_id and scores it with OpenStructure, adding DockQ v2 scoring for the protein-DNA and protein-RNA interface types.

steps.title: Aggregate the scores into the task table
steps.shell:
python task_score_summary.py \
  --evaluation_dir ./examples/outputs/evaluation \
  --target_dir ./examples/targets \
  --output_path ./examples/summary_table.csv \
  --algorithm_names Protenix \
  --targets interface_protein_ligand interface_protein_dna monomer_protein \
  --metric_type rank
steps.explanation: The readme's second step. It summarises the per-target scores for the named models and task types into the final success rates and LDDT values and writes them to the given path.

outputs: Per-target score files under the algorithm's evaluation directory, as the bundled example's OpenStructure and DockQ v2 JSON files show.
A summary table at the path given to the second step, holding the success rate or LDDT per task for the named models.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
They score predictions only. Generating the predictions needs each model run separately, which the repository supports through per-algorithm containers rather than these steps.
Going beyond the bundled examples needs the target CSV files edited, the referenced ground-truth CIF package downloaded from an external link, and prediction_reference.csv updated by hand.

ucc-research-benchmark-foldbench.notes: Sizes in the structured entries are the paper's Methods counts for the full target set, which the readme repeats except for protein monomers (334 in the paper, 330 in the readme); the disagreement is recorded as a limitation and no attempt is made to reconcile it. The leaderboard's 2024-01 set is a subset with no published per-task count, so none of these sizes applies to it. The protein-ligand subsets (76 unseen-protein, 482 unseen-ligand) are subsets of the 558 and are not given their own structured entry. The data and code licence is the repository's MIT licence, which covers the targets and the evaluation code; the article itself is CC BY-NC-ND, so its saved XML is not redistributable. The released field is null: no source prints a release date for the benchmark, and the readme's update lines are change notices rather than a release date. profile.summary: PepSpecBench is a benchmark for predicting peptide tandem mass spectra: given a modified peptide sequence, a precursor charge and a normalised collision energy, a model must predict the fragment-ion intensity pattern. It harmonises two public spectral libraries, PROSPECT and MassIVE-KB, into matched 500k/50k/50k train, validation and test subsets under one scope (peptide length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6, three PTMs), splits them so that no peptide backbone appears in two partitions, and projects every model's output into one 234-dimensional canonical ion space so that architectures with different native outputs can be compared. It adds a seven-subset cross-species suite of 20k spectra each, evaluated zero-shot, and metadata perturbation probes. Six models were retrained by the authors on these splits.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Sections 3.1 to 3.3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a model reproduces the measured fragment-intensity pattern of a peptide's MS/MS spectrum, and how far that ability survives three stresses. First, fair comparison: all models are scored in one canonical ion space rather than in their own output formats. Second, leakage: whether apparent accuracy depends on seeing the same peptide backbone in training, tested by comparing three split rules under one model and one data source. Third, robustness: whether a model trained on human libraries transfers zero-shot to other species and to a cancer cell line, and whether it uses collision energy and precursor charge in a physically sensible way, probed by perturbing that metadata.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Sections 4.1 to 4.3; Section 5

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Two in-domain sources are combined under one scope: PROSPECT, a curated spectral library with broad PTM coverage and several collision energies per peptide, and MassIVE-KB, a larger community-curated human library. Both are filtered to peptides of length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6 and the UNIMOD 1, 4 and 35 modifications, and reconstructed into 500k train, 50k validation and 50k test spectra each; the appendix names these PROSPECT-Mini and MassIVE-KB-Mini. Because MassIVE-KB mixes heterogeneous sources, a single default normalised collision energy of 25 is applied to all its spectra. The cross-species suite is seven subsets drawn from ProteomeXchange studies, each truncated to 20k spectra after the same filtering, covering human reference and HeLa, yeast, two E. coli subsets, C. elegans and A. thaliana, identified with MaxQuant at 1 per cent false discovery rate.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Table 1; Appendix A, Composition and Collection

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an intensity prediction for an input triplet of modified sequence, precursor charge and normalised collision energy. Because the six baselines have different native output spaces, each has a projection into one shared canonical ion space that enumerates every combination of cleavage position, b or y ion type and fragment charge up to a maximum; with a reference length of 40 and maximum fragment charge 3 this space has 234 dimensions. Prediction and ground truth are both projected, a validity mask is built, and three metrics are computed over the masked positions: spectral angle (SA), where lower is better and the range is 0 to 1, spectral angle similarity (1 minus SA), and Pearson correlation. Results are aggregated as medians with bootstrap confidence intervals. All six baselines were retrained by the authors on the benchmark splits.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 to 3.3

sections.title: The split rule and what it is worth
sections.body: A partition is backbone-disjoint when the sets of unmodified amino-acid sequences in any two partitions are mutually exclusive, which blocks both exact sequence reuse and the same backbone appearing with different modifications. PROSPECT is split by deterministic hashing of the backbone; for MassIVE-KB the official disjoint splits are kept, filtered within each partition, and checked for zero backbone overlap. The benefit is measured rather than asserted: with Prosit and PROSPECT held fixed, a naive random split lowers median SA from 0.1376 to 0.1254 and raises Pearson correlation from 0.8921 to 0.9099, while a modified-sequence split stays close to backbone-disjoint (SA 0.1392, correlation 0.8895). The authors read this as exact backbone reuse being the dominant leakage path, and state in their limitations that backbone disjointness does not remove higher-order sequence homology.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Backbone-Disjoint Split; Section 4.2, Table 3; Section 5

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: The in-domain ranking depends on the source: Prosit Transformer has the best median SA on MassIVE-KB (0.0977 against 0.0995 for Prosit), while Prosit leads on PROSPECT (0.1376 against 0.1419), which the authors attribute to MassIVE-KB holding longer peptides and higher charges. Mid-tier models are less stable: UniSpec beats PredFull on PROSPECT but collapses on MassIVE-KB to SA 0.3369 with near-zero correlation, while PredFull holds at SA 0.1673. The in-domain ranking does not survive transfer: under MassIVE-KB training, PredFull beats both Prosit models on all five out-of-distribution testbeds, and the appendix shows the Prosit models reaching negative median correlation on several subsets. Under PROSPECT training the picture splits again, with Prosit best on C. elegans and A. thaliana and PredFull on E. coli and yeast. The authors note that one apparent out-of-distribution advantage is a Simpson's paradox caused by covariate shift.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 4.1 and 4.3; Tables 2 and 4

sections.title: How to get the data
sections.body: The dataset is published on Hugging Face under the MIT licence, with a dataset DOI. Its configurations mirror the benchmark components: massive_kb and prospect, each in a native representation with the original mass-to-charge and intensity arrays and in the canonical 234-dimensional representation, each with train, validation and test splits; an ood configuration in both representations with a test split only; and a small sample configuration. No evaluation code, model code or leaderboard address is given in the paper.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Data Availability; Hugging Face dataset record

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two in-domain components of 500k train, 50k validation and 50k test spectra each: PROSPECT-Mini, from ProteomeTools, balanced 50 per cent unmodified and 50 per cent modified in every split, and MassIVE-KB-Mini, from the MassIVE-KB v1 human subset at its natural modification rate (unmodified 75.40, 72.83 and 72.09 per cent in train, validation and test). Plus PepSpecBench-OOD, seven subsets of 20k spectra each: human reference, human HeLa, yeast, E. coli reference, E. coli enriched, C. elegans and A. thaliana. All components share the same length, charge and PTM scope.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Appendix A, Composition and Distribution

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Backbone-disjoint train, validation and test splits for both in-domain sources: the unmodified amino-acid backbone sets of any two partitions are mutually exclusive, so neither an exact sequence nor another modified form of it can cross the boundary. PROSPECT is partitioned by deterministic hashing of the backbone; MassIVE-KB keeps its official disjoint splits, scope-filtered within each partition and verified to have zero backbone overlap. The seven cross-species subsets are test-only and used zero-shot. Two weaker rules, a naive random split and a modified-sequence split, are run as a controlled ablation for comparison.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Backbone-Disjoint Split; Section 4.2

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three metrics over the masked positions of the canonical space, the same for every task. Spectral angle (SA) is the primary one: the angular distance between the normalised predicted and observed intensity vectors, in the range 0 to 1, and lower is better. Spectral angle similarity is 1 minus SA, so higher is better. Pearson correlation measures whether relative intensity rankings are preserved, higher being better. All values are reported as medians with bootstrap confidence intervals.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.3; Tables 2 and 4

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Six models, all retrained by the authors on the benchmark splits. Sequence-centric, predicting b and y ion intensities by cleavage position and fragment charge: Prosit (GRU encoder-decoder, about 2.5M parameters), Prosit Transformer (about 86M) and AlphaPeptDeep (modular Transformer, about 1.8M). Full-spectrum or dictionary models projected into the canonical space: PredFull (residual CNN with squeeze-excitation, about 8.2M) and UniSpec (attention-based dictionary model, about 12M). FastSpel, a linear model of about 50K parameters, serves as a lower-bound reference.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The backbone-disjoint split is the benchmark's central control: no unmodified peptide backbone may appear in two partitions, which blocks exact reuse and PTM-variant overlap. Its effect is quantified by the split ablation, and residual similarity is measured in the appendix as the minimum Levenshtein edit distance from each test backbone to the nearest training backbone. The authors state the limit plainly: backbone disjointness does not eliminate higher-order sequence homology, and their own biases note says the backbone split does not eliminate homology-level leakage. Cross-species evaluation is an additional, stronger control, since those subsets come from different organisms and are used zero-shot.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1; Section 4.2; Appendix A, Biases; Appendix B.1; Section 5

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Metric values are medians with bootstrap confidence intervals, reported in the appendix for the in-domain results; the main tables print the medians only. No training replicate or seed variation is reported: each baseline is retrained once per source under the benchmark split.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.3; Tables 2 and 4; Section 4.3

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a single tandem mass spectrum, scored as the intensity vector of its fragment ions. The input is a triplet of modified peptide sequence, precursor charge state and normalised collision energy, and the target is the measured fragment-intensity pattern projected into the 234-dimensional canonical ion space.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human for both in-domain sources, and five species across the cross-species suite: human (a reference proteome subset and a HeLa cancer cell subset), yeast, E. coli (two subsets), C. elegans and A. thaliana. The authors describe the training data as human-centric.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Appendix A, Composition and Biases

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Tandem mass spectrometry. The in-domain labels come from two public spectral libraries, PROSPECT (built on ProteomeTools, with several collision energy settings per peptide) and MassIVE-KB v1, a community-curated library of human measurements. The cross-species spectra come from ProteomeXchange studies and were identified with MaxQuant at a 1 per cent false discovery rate. The authors note that the instrumentation is dominated by the Q Exactive family.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1; Appendix A, Collection and Biases

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Three things and no more: the modified peptide sequence, the precursor charge state and the normalised collision energy. No structure, alignment or spectrum is given at prediction time. The benchmark restricts the scope to peptide length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6 and the UNIMOD 1, 4 and 35 modifications, and a model's output may be in its own native format as long as a projection into the canonical space is defined.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 and 3.2

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training from scratch on the benchmark's own training split: all six baselines are retrained on the benchmark data under the backbone-disjoint splits, separately for each in-domain source, with per-model adaptations and hyperparameters documented in the appendix. The cross-species evaluation is strictly zero-shot, with no fine-tuning or adaptation on the out-of-distribution subsets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 and 3.2

strengths.text: The shared 234-dimensional canonical ion space lets models with different native outputs, from sequence-indexed ion ladders to binned full spectra and fragment dictionaries, be scored on the same footing, and every metric is computed only in that space.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2, Shared Canonical Evaluation Space

strengths.text: The value of the strict split is measured rather than asserted: with the model and data source held fixed, a naive random split is shown to flatter the model by 0.012 median SA, while a modified-sequence split is shown to make little difference.

Out-of-distribution transfer is tested separately for models trained on each in-domain source, which separates architectural robustness from training-source bias and shows that the in-domain ranking does not predict the transfer ranking.

The data are released on Hugging Face under the MIT licence, in both a native representation with the original mass-to-charge and intensity arrays and the canonical representation used for scoring, with a dataset DOI.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Data Availability; Hugging Face dataset record

limitations.text: Every number is produced by the benchmark's authors, who retrained all six baselines themselves rather than using published checkpoints, so the comparison depends on their training recipes and per-model adaptations.

The leakage control stops at exact backbones. The authors state that backbone-disjoint splitting does not eliminate higher-order sequence homology and list that as a remaining bias, so residual similarity between training and test peptides remains.

The scope is deliberately narrow and partly homogenised: three modifications only, one peptide length and charge window, instrumentation dominated by one family, and a single default collision energy of 25 imposed on all MassIVE-KB spectra, which removes real variation from that source.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 and 5; Appendix A, Biases

limitations.text: No evaluation code, projection implementation or leaderboard is published with the paper: only the dataset is released, so a third party cannot reproduce the canonical projections or the reported medians without reimplementing them from the appendix.

Comparisons across the out-of-distribution subsets need care: the authors show that one apparent transfer advantage is a Simpson's paradox created by covariate shift in collision energy and modification state, and that they cannot causally attribute the source effect because the two sources differ in distribution.

profile.summary: PRIME is an evaluation framework for protein language models on a single viral protein: the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor binding domain. Frozen embeddings from five protein language models, with and without domain-specific fine-tuning on 347,432 outbreak RBD sequences, feed a small multi-task network that predicts two deep mutational scanning phenotypes, ACE2 binding affinity and protein expression. The point of the framework is the split: because viral sequences are near-identical, a random split lets mutations at the same residue appear in training and test, so PRIME holds out whole residue positions instead and shows that the random-split numbers are inflated. It is useful to anyone reading reported fitness-prediction accuracy on viral proteins.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Background; Methods, Data collection and curation; Position-stratified validation protocol

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, how well a protein language model's representation of an RBD sequence predicts a measured phenotype: ACE2 binding affinity and expression level from yeast display deep mutational scanning. Second, and the reason the framework exists, how much of that apparent accuracy comes from homology leakage. The same embeddings and the same regression head are evaluated under two split rules, a random split and a position-stratified split that holds out all mutations at a residue position together, and the gap between them is the measurement. The framework also tracks whether domain-specific fine-tuning on outbreak sequences recovers predictive signal, and whether the embeddings separate known viral lineages.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Background; Results, Scaling and fine-tuning overcome the generalization gap

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Three datasets. The outbreak dataset is 347,432 unique SARS-CoV-2 RBD sequences (spike residues 319 to 541) curated from GISAID and the Sequence Read Archive as of 3 February 2023, with duplicates and ambiguous sequences removed; it is used for fine-tuning and for lineage analysis, and is dominated by Omicron (52.70 per cent) and Delta (35.71 per cent). The DMS dataset supplies the labels: 116,257 unique RBD sequences with measured ACE2 binding affinity and 105,525 with quantified expression, from a published yeast display experiment. The betaCov dataset is 75 RBD sequences from diverse Sarbecovirus members, used for cross-species analysis rather than for the regression benchmark.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation; Results, Benchmark data collection

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Frozen embeddings, taken from the last hidden layer or mean-pooled over residues, are fed to a fully connected network of five layers whose hidden size follows the embedding size, with ReLU activations, no dropout and mean squared error loss, predicting binding and expression jointly. Evaluation is 5-fold cross-validation over residue positions: positions are randomly partitioned into five subsets and a sequence joins the training or test side according to whether its mutated positions fall exclusively in that subset. Within each fold the network is reinitialised, trained for 1000 epochs at a learning rate of 1e-5, and scored on the fold's test set; the coefficient of determination and RMSE are computed per fold and averaged. The stratified evaluation was repeated under three fold-assignment seeds (0, 1 and 2) to check that results do not depend on the fold construction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Position-stratified validation protocol and Input features

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: The random split flatters every model. For ESM-C 600M with mean embeddings, a random split gives a coefficient of determination of 0.7711 for binding affinity, while the same base model under the position-stratified split has no predictive signal at all and a negative value of -0.1050. Fine-tuning on the outbreak dataset restores part of it: for the same model the stratified binding figure rises to 0.1823 plus or minus 0.2149 with mean embeddings and 0.2087 plus or minus 0.1451 with sequence-level CLS embeddings. Table 1 reports both splits, both phenotypes, both embedding methods and the fine-tuned and non-fine-tuned conditions for all five models; many of the stratified values are negative. Separately, fine-tuning raised masked language modelling accuracy on RBD sequences from 5.06 per cent to 96.33 per cent for ESM-2 8M, while a BERT model trained from scratch on RBD sequences alone reached 94.09 per cent but failed on rare residues.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Scaling and fine-tuning overcome the generalization gap; Table 1

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository installs as a Python package into a conda environment, with two requirement sets because the authors moved to newer GPUs during revision. Masked language modelling is run by calling the relevant lightning script, and the transfer-learning models take flags for the target phenotype, the learning rate, the number of epochs and the path to a pretrained masked language model checkpoint; the readme ships SLURM examples because the work was done in a SLURM environment. The split comparison lives in its own directory: reading split_comparison.py, it wraps the multi-task fully connected head from the package, sets torch and numpy seeds, trains with Adam under a summed binding and expression mean squared error loss, and uses scikit-learn's KFold and train_test_split to build the two partitions. Its docstring warns that this random split is not the one used originally, so its values do not match the published random-split numbers.
sections.source_locator: README: Installation, Usage; split_comparison.py

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Three. The DMS dataset carries the benchmark labels: 116,257 unique RBD sequences with measured ACE2 binding affinity and 105,525 with quantified expression, from a published yeast display experiment. The outbreak dataset is 347,432 unique SARS-CoV-2 RBD sequences (spike residues 319 to 541) from GISAID and the Sequence Read Archive as of 3 February 2023, used for fine-tuning and lineage analysis; 99.75 per cent of its sequences are 223 amino acids long. The betaCov dataset is 75 Sarbecovirus RBD sequences used for cross-species analysis.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation; Results, Benchmark data collection

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two regimes over the same DMS data, both as 5-fold cross-validation rather than a fixed test set. The position-stratified split partitions residue positions into five subsets and assigns a sequence to training or test according to whether its mutated positions fall exclusively in that subset, so all mutations at a position are held out together. The random split is the comparison condition, in which mutations at the same site can appear on both sides. No per-fold test size is reported. Fold assignment was repeated under three seeds.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Position-stratified validation protocol

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: The coefficient of determination (higher is better, and negative values mean worse than predicting the mean) and RMSE (lower is better), computed per fold and averaged across folds, for each of the two phenotypes. The masked language modelling experiments report residue prediction accuracy instead, and the lineage analysis reports the Adjusted Rand Index against established lineage assignments.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Input features; Table 1; Results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five protein language models across two families, each with and without domain-specific fine-tuning, and each with CLS and mean embeddings: ESM-2 at 8M (6 layers), 150M (30 layers) and 650M (33 layers), and ESM-C at 300M and 600M. A BERT model trained from scratch on RBD sequences with a 320-dimensional embedding space (BERT-RBD) serves as a domain-specific control. The fine-tuned ESM-2 8M model is called ESM-RBD. The repository also lists other transfer-learning heads (BLSTM and GCN, single-task and multi-task) that the benchmark tables do not use.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and scale; README: Models

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The position-stratified split is the control, and it is the point of the paper: all mutations at a given residue position are held out together, so a model cannot see another mutation at the same site during training. The paper is explicit that this measures generalisation to unseen positions rather than to unseen mutants. No sequence identity cut-off, clustering step or time split is applied, and the pretrained models' own training corpora are not screened against the DMS sequences. The 347,432-sequence outbreak set used for fine-tuning is drawn from the same protein as the test data by design.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Background; Methods, Leakage control

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Values are means across the five cross-validation folds with a standard deviation, which Table 1 prints for every cell. The spreads are large next to the differences being discussed: the fine-tuned ESM-C 600M stratified binding figure is 0.1823 plus or minus 0.2149. Fold-construction sensitivity was checked by repeating the stratified evaluation under three independent seeds, and the paper reports that the mutation count distributions stay consistent across seeds and folds. No bootstrap interval or statistical test between models is reported.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Cross-validation and Input features; Results; Table 1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a mutated SARS-CoV-2 RBD sequence, 223 amino acids long for almost all of the outbreak data, with two continuous phenotype labels. The unit that the stratified split holds out is not the sequence but the residue position, so a fold is defined by positions and the sequences follow from them.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation and Position-stratified validation protocol

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: One virus for the benchmark itself: SARS-CoV-2, the receptor binding domain of its spike protein. The cross-species betaCov analysis adds Sarbecovirus members including SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, a pangolin virus and bat coronaviruses, whose RBDs target several mammalian hosts (bat, pangolin, civet, camel and human). The phenotype measurements come from yeast display, so yeast is the measurement host.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation; Results, Benchmark data collection

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Deep mutational scanning by yeast display, from a published study: ACE2 binding affinity for 116,257 sequences and protein expression level for 105,525. No assay was run for this work; the outbreak and betaCov sequences carry no phenotype measurement at all.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, DMS dataset

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The amino acid sequence of the RBD alone. The model sees it as a frozen embedding, either the last hidden layer or a mean over residues, and nothing else: no structure, no alignment and no metadata enters the regression head.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Input features

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Two settings per model, reported side by side. Without fine-tuning, the released checkpoint's embeddings are frozen and only the regression head is trained, which makes it a linear-probe-style evaluation. With fine-tuning, the model is first adapted to RBD sequences by masked language modelling on the outbreak dataset (15 per cent of residues masked, AdamW, learning rate 1e-5, 100 epochs for ESM-RBD 8M and 15 epochs for the scaling tests, effective batch size 512 across eight A100 GPUs), and its embeddings are then frozen for the same head. BERT-RBD is trained from scratch as a control.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Domain-specific fine-tuning and Input features

strengths.text: The leakage effect is isolated properly: the same frozen embeddings and the same regression head are run under both split rules, so the difference between them cannot be attributed to a different model or a different training recipe.

The split rule is the right shape for a viral protein: holding out whole residue positions blocks the specific shortcut that near-identical viral sequences create, where another mutation at the same site is already in training.

Sensitivity to the fold construction is tested rather than assumed: the stratified evaluation is repeated under three independent fold-assignment seeds and the mutation count distributions are shown to stay consistent.
The code is published, including the split comparison as its own directory, and the licence file grants permissive reuse in the wording of the MIT licence.
strengths.source_locator: README: Random vs Position-Stratified Split; LICENSE.md

limitations.text: One protein and two phenotypes. Everything here is the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor binding domain scored for ACE2 binding and expression, so the numbers say nothing directly about other proteins or other fitness measures.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation

limitations.text: Author-reported: the PRIME authors ran every model and also contribute the fine-tuned ESM-RBD models, which are the rows that recover predictive signal under the strict split.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Scaling and fine-tuning overcome the generalization gap

limitations.text: The surviving signal is weak and the spread is wide. The best stratified binding figure quoted in the text is 0.2087 plus or minus 0.1451, and many Table 1 cells are negative, meaning worse than predicting the mean.

The published split comparison does not reproduce the paper's own random-split numbers. The script's docstring states that its random split differs from the one used originally and that the values do not match, so the two sets of random-split figures are not interchangeable.

The underlying sequence data cannot simply be downloaded: the outbreak sequences are identified by a GISAID data set identifier, which requires GISAID access rather than an open file, so a third party cannot rebuild the fine-tuning corpus from the repository alone.

run_guide.summary: Install the PRIME package, fine-tune a protein language model on RBD sequences by masked language modelling, and train the transfer-learning head that predicts a DMS phenotype.
prerequisites: conda, and one of the two requirement sets the repository ships: a newer one for Blackwell-generation GPUs and the original one.
An NVIDIA GPU is recommended, and the readme's examples assume a SLURM cluster with several GPUs.
The DMS phenotype data and the outbreak RBD sequences; the outbreak sequences come from GISAID under a data set identifier rather than an open download.
The licence file grants permissive reuse in the wording of the MIT licence, under a Los Alamos government-contract notice.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit

git clone https://github.com/lanl/prime
cd prime
git checkout --detach d940c51aa0f475b8945789e89761fab0687d5b74

conda create -n blackwell_prime python=3.13.12 -y
conda activate blackwell_prime
pip install -r requirements/blackwell_prime_requirements.txt
pip install -e .

The readme states that the model flag defaults to the smallest available model and that batch size may need adjusting for larger ones; for ESM-C the script is lightning-esmc.py. The directory change follows the repository layout.

steps.title: Compare the two split rules
steps.explanation: The split comparison lives in its own directory. The readme only links that directory and gives no command, so this invocation was read from the script itself, which parses its arguments with argparse and defaults to the ESM2_8M_base embedding file. Reading the script, it trains the multi-task fully connected head on frozen embeddings with a fixed seed and a summed binding and expression mean squared error loss, and builds the partitions with scikit-learn's KFold and train_test_split. profile.summary: This is the public binding free energy benchmark assembled for Ross et al. 2023: 1237 compounds in congeneric series across a wide range of protein targets, released with prepared input structures so that a relative binding free energy method can be scored against measured affinities. It is published alongside a second data set that sets the ceiling for such scoring, a survey of 1867 compounds whose affinities were measured by at least two different assays, which quantifies how well experiment agrees with itself. Someone choosing or developing an affinity prediction method uses the first to measure accuracy and the second to know what accuracy would be good.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Methods, FEP accuracy benchmark; Tables 1 and 2

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The accuracy of a relative binding free energy prediction against measured affinity, for congeneric series of ligands on the same protein. The question is deliberately relative rather than absolute: the authors say absolute binding free energies carry systematic errors that do not matter for deciding which ligand binds more strongly, so the benchmark scores differences between pairs of ligands and the rank ordering within a series. The second data set answers a different question, how much of the remaining error is the experiment's own: it measures how far two assays on the same compounds and the same protein disagree, which bounds what any prediction method could achieve.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Experimental reproducibility survey; Metrics used for analysis

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The prediction benchmark is assembled from published studies: congeneric series were collected from as many earlier free energy studies as possible, plus further data sets with well-resolved structures encountered along the way. A series was included if an X-ray structure of the complex exists for at least one of its ligands, the protein structure has no significant ambiguities, and the affinities were measured as dissociation constants, inhibition constants or half-maximal inhibitory concentrations. Unlike an earlier benchmark, series were not dropped for having few compounds or a narrow affinity range, because the authors wanted coverage of particular chemistries such as macrocycles, charge-changing transformations and buried water displacement. Table 2 lists the 14 constituent data sets and their proteins, totalling 1237 compounds. The structures were then curated by hand: ligand geometries, protonation states of ligand and binding-site residues, flexible regions and in some cases the crystal structure itself were reviewed and changed, with the modifications documented in the supplementary results. The reproducibility survey collected published studies where the same compounds were measured by two assays, grouped as binding against binding (250 compounds), binding against functional (1207) and functional against functional (410), totalling 1867 with duplicates across comparisons, plus unpublished in-house data that is counted in the totals but not released.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Experimental reproducibility survey and FEP accuracy benchmark; Tables 1 and 2

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A relative method produces free energy differences for the edges of a perturbation graph over a series. The authors argue that edgewise errors depend on the graph topology, because graphs are built between similar ligands, so they prefer pairwise errors: after cycle closure correction, a predicted difference is inferred for every pair of ligands in the graph, and the error is taken over all pairs. Both are reported. Correlation metrics are computed on the inferred absolute free energies, not on the differences, because the sign of a difference is arbitrary; the coefficient of determination and Kendall's tau are used. Every aggregate is a weighted average over graphs, weighted by the number of edges for edgewise errors and by the number of compounds for pairwise and correlation metrics, with 95 per cent confidence intervals from bootstrap sampling over graphs or over pairs of assay series. The same weighting is used for the experimental survey, where relative free energies are computed between all pairs of ligands within each assay and compared between the two assays.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Metrics used for analysis; Table 3 footnote

sections.title: The reference result
sections.body: The benchmark's own reference numbers come from FEP+ in the Schrodinger suite (versions 21-3 and 21-4) with the OPLS4 force field and SPC water, run with replica exchange with solute tempering, 12 to 24 lambda windows depending on the perturbation type and 20 ns per window unless stated otherwise. Table 3 puts those results beside the experimental survey: pairwise RMSE 1.25 kcal/mol for FEP+ against 0.91 for the experiment-against-experiment comparison, pairwise mean unsigned error 0.98 against 0.67, coefficient of determination 0.56 against 0.79 and Kendall's tau 0.51 against 0.71, each with a bootstrap interval. Edgewise RMSE and mean unsigned error are reported for FEP+ only (1.17 and 0.91), because an edgewise error has no counterpart in the assay survey.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Simulation details; Table 3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds four things: prepared inputs in two forms, one set up for FEP+ and one generic structure set for any other software; the experimental survey data; the FEP+ 21-4 output files as both Schrodinger files and CSV; and the analysis scripts that produced the published statistics. Scoring is one command: process_fep_benchmark.py takes a directory whose subdirectories hold one output file per system, with the extension given by a flag, and prints the aggregate statistics. Reading the script, it accepts either Schrodinger FMP files or CSV, and requires a Schrodinger installation only for the FMP path. The analysis readme and the script agree that CSV input over-counts ligands with multiple protomers or tautomers, so CSV statistics are approximate while FMP statistics are exact. A second script does the same for the experimental survey.
sections.source_locator: README: Contents; analysis_scripts/README.md; process_fep_benchmark.py usage

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two. The prediction benchmark is 1237 compounds in congeneric series, drawn from 14 named collections: the FEP+ R-group set (199 compounds), FEP+ charge-change (53), OPLS stress set (114), OPLS drug discovery (93), water displacement (76), FEP+ fragments (79), FEP+ macrocycles (34), FEP+ scaffold-hopping (17), Merck sets (264), GPCRs (98), Bayer macrocycles (8), Janssen BACE1 (74), MCS docking (49) and a miscellaneous group (79). The experimental reproducibility survey is 1867 compounds across three comparison types: binding against binding (250), binding against functional (1207) and functional against functional (410); the count includes duplicates because a compound can appear in several assay comparisons, and in-house data contribute to the totals without being released.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Tables 1 and 2

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None. There is no training, validation or test division: the whole collection is an evaluation set, and a method is scored on every congeneric series. The natural unit is the series, and aggregates are weighted averages over series or perturbation graphs rather than over compounds pooled together.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Metrics used for analysis

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Four for predictions, all aggregated as weighted averages with bootstrap 95 per cent intervals. Pairwise RMSE and pairwise mean unsigned error in kcal/mol over every pair of ligands in a graph after cycle closure correction (lower is better) are the preferred error measures; edgewise RMSE and mean unsigned error over the graph's edges (lower is better) are reported beside them but depend on graph topology. The coefficient of determination and Kendall's tau (higher is better) are computed on the inferred absolute free energies, not on the differences. The experimental survey uses the same pairwise error and correlation metrics, so the two sit in one table.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Metrics used for analysis; Table 3

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: One reference method, run by the authors: FEP+ in the Schrodinger suite versions 21-3 and 21-4 with the OPLS4 force field and SPC water. The real reference point for interpreting it is not another method but the experimental reproducibility survey, which is presented as the accuracy ceiling. The paper discusses an earlier benchmark by Hahn et al. for its inclusion rules and alternative crystal structures, but does not run it as a baseline.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Simulation details; Table 3

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Inapplicable as usually meant, and none is described. A physics-based free energy calculation has no training set to leak from, so the benchmark imposes no identity cut-off, time split or held-out family, and the paper does not discuss leakage. For a machine-learning method scored on this collection the position is different and the sources say nothing about it: the series are all taken from published studies, so their structures and affinities are in the public record and may well be in such a model's training data.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, FEP accuracy benchmark

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Every aggregate metric carries a 95 per cent confidence interval from bootstrap sampling over perturbation graphs, or over pairs of experimental series in the survey. The intervals in Table 3 are narrow relative to the gap between prediction and experiment, for example pairwise RMSE 1.25 [1.17, 1.33] for FEP+ against 0.91 [0.83, 1.11] for the assay comparison. Simulation replicates are not reported: each lambda window was run once for 20 ns unless stated otherwise.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 3 footnote; Methods, Simulation details

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: For scoring, a pair of structurally similar ligands bound to the same protein: the quantity predicted is the binding free energy difference between them, and the aggregation unit is a congeneric series with its perturbation graph. For counting, one example is a compound, which is how both tables are totalled.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Metrics used for analysis; Tables 1 and 2

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Inapplicable as a species list. The entities are protein targets and small molecules, and the sources identify the proteins by name (BACE1, CDK2, thrombin, TYK2, the Merck set targets, three GPCRs and so on) rather than by organism. No species composition is stated.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Tables 1 and 2

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Binding and functional affinity assays reported as dissociation constants, inhibition constants or half-maximal inhibitory concentrations; only those three readouts were accepted. Relative free energies are derived from the ratio of two such values, assuming that the ratio of IC50s equals the ratio of inhibition or dissociation constants, which the paper notes holds for many but not all mechanisms and conditions, with temperature taken as 300 K throughout. The survey distinguishes binding assays, which measure dissociation directly, from functional assays, which measure inhibition.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Experimental reproducibility survey

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: A prepared three-dimensional structure of the protein-ligand complex plus the ligand series. Every series has an X-ray structure for at least one ligand, and the release ships the inputs in two forms, prepared for FEP+ and as generic structure files for other software, with metadata on each data set's origin. The structures as released already carry the authors' curation decisions: protonation and tautomeric states, rotamer choices, retained crystallographic waters, and in some cases a changed crystal structure.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, FEP accuracy benchmark and Simulation details; README: Contents

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None: the benchmark is for prediction from structure with no fitting to its data. The reference results come from running a physics-based method at its default settings, with the number of lambda windows set by perturbation type (24 for charge-changing, 16 for scaffold-hopping and macrocyclisation, 12 otherwise) and 20 ns per window unless stated otherwise. The benchmark defines no training split that a learned method could use.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Simulation details

strengths.text: It publishes an accuracy ceiling alongside the benchmark. The same metrics are computed for two assays measuring the same compounds, so a method's error can be read against how far experiment disagrees with itself (pairwise RMSE 0.91 kcal/mol) rather than against zero.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Experimental reproducibility survey; Table 3

strengths.text: The scoring choice is argued and both variants are reported: pairwise errors over all ligand pairs after cycle closure correction, because edgewise errors depend on how the perturbation graph was drawn.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Metrics used for analysis

strengths.text: Inclusion was deliberately broad rather than convenient: small series and series with a narrow affinity range were kept, so that specific chemistries such as macrocycles, charge-changing transformations and buried water displacement are represented.

The release is usable by other software, not only the authors': prepared inputs come in a generic structure form as well as a FEP+ form, the reference outputs ship as CSV as well as Schrodinger files, and the analysis scripts run without a Schrodinger installation. Everything is MIT licensed.
strengths.source_locator: README: Contents; analysis_scripts/README.md, Python dependencies; LICENSE

limitations.text: The structures are curated rather than raw, and the curation was done by the group reporting the reference result: ligand geometries, protonation states, rotamers and in some cases the crystal structure itself were changed. A method scored on these inputs is scored on someone else's modelling decisions.

Part of the reproducibility survey cannot be checked. In-house drug discovery comparisons contribute to the survey totals, but the paper states the raw data has not been published, so the ceiling figure rests partly on data a reader cannot see.

The 1867 figure is not 1867 distinct compounds: the paper says the count includes duplicates because the same compound can appear in several assay comparisons, so it is a count of comparison entries rather than of molecules.

The published statistics are only exactly reproducible with commercial software. Both the analysis readme and the scoring script state that CSV input over-counts ligands with multiple protomers or tautomers, so a user without a Schrodinger installation gets approximate numbers.

Relative free energies are derived from mixed readouts under an assumption the authors flag themselves: that the ratio of two IC50 values equals the ratio of inhibition or dissociation constants, which holds for many but not all mechanisms and assay conditions.

uc-leadopt-20261022-benchmark-fep-public.notes: Two sets, two structured entries, and their sizes must not be mixed: 1237 is the number of compounds in the prediction benchmark (Table 2 total), 1867 is the number of compounds across assay comparisons in the reproducibility survey (Table 1 total), and the survey figure includes duplicates. Neither is a test-set size in the machine-learning sense, since the collection has no splits. The released date 2023-06-26 is the publication timestamp of the repository's v1.0 and v2.0 releases as the GitHub API reports them; the paper states its own results use v1.0. The Boltz-2 supplement's two subsets of this collection (876 complexes and 87 compounds over 4 targets), which the record's attributes describe as separate protocols, come from a source that was not fetched for this page and are not represented in the structured entries; the record's own note that those two subsets must overlap, with the overlap unstated, still stands. Leakage controls are marked inapplicable because the benchmark is built for physics-based prediction with no training set, and the sources say nothing about overlap with a machine-learning model's training data even though every series is from a published study.

profile.summary: Scaffold-Lab evaluates protein backbone generation methods in one pipeline. For the unconditional task a method generates 100 backbones at each evaluated length, ProteinMPNN designs 10 sequences for each backbone, ESMFold refolds them, and the backbones are scored for designability (a self-consistency TM-score above 0.5), novelty (the highest TM-score to any PDB structure), diversity (unique Foldseek clusters over total backbones) and efficiency (average seconds per backbone), with the four combined into a ranking by TOPSIS. Lengths are grouped short (50 and 100), medium (200 to 500) and long (600 to 1000), and each group holds only the methods that could be run at those lengths. It is useful to someone choosing a backbone generator and wanting the designability, diversity and runtime trade-off on one page.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Figure 1 caption; Evaluation metrics; Tables 2 and 3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Four things about a set of generated backbones, plus a description of their physical plausibility. Designability asks whether any sequence folds into the backbone, read from refolding. Novelty asks how far the backbone is from everything already in the PDB. Diversity asks how varied a method's own output is, which matters because a generator that always produces the same fold gives few candidates to choose from. Efficiency is the runtime per backbone. Structural properties (secondary structure content, radius of gyration and MolProbity validity) are described rather than ranked. The first four are combined into a single ranking, because the authors treat the choice of method as a multi-criteria decision rather than a single score.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Designability to Ranking

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: There is no fixed target set: the data are generated by the methods under test. For each method and each evaluated length, 100 backbones are generated, and the lengths are grouped: short covers 50 and 100, medium covers 200, 300, 400 and 500, and long covers 600, 800 and 1000. Which methods appear in a group depends on what could be run there, so the short group holds Genie, FrameFlow, FrameDiff, Chroma and RFdiffusion, the medium group FrameDiff, Chroma and RFdiffusion, and the long group only Chroma and RFdiffusion. Seven methods are evaluated across the two tasks, with release dates from January to November 2023. The reference for novelty is the whole PDB, searched with Foldseek.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Tables 1 and 2; Figure 1 caption; Evaluation metrics, Novelty

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every method goes through the same refolding pipeline: ProteinMPNN designs 10 sequences per backbone, ESMFold predicts each sequence's structure, and the prediction is compared with the generated backbone. A backbone counts as designable when the self-consistency TM-score exceeds 0.5, which the authors prefer to the self-consistency RMSD below 2 angstroms used elsewhere because RMSD becomes less discriminative as proteins get longer; the RMSD criterion is kept for the motif-scaffolding task, where designs are typically under 150 residues. Rather than taking the single best sequence, the headline figure uses a top N strategy with N equal to 3: the mean score of the three best sequences must pass the threshold, on the argument that a backbone accommodating several sequences is more robust. The best-sequence success rate is reported alongside, and success is also plotted against a sweep of thresholds with the area under that curve reported, to avoid depending on one subjective cut-off. Novelty is the highest TM-score to any PDB structure, with a penalty added for backbones that are novel but undesignable. Diversity is unique Foldseek clusters at a TM-score threshold of 0.5 divided by the number of backbones in the group. Efficiency is the mean time per backbone over 100 backbones under identical hardware. The four are combined by TOPSIS, with the relative closeness value reported per length and averaged per group to give a rank.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Material and methods; Evaluation metrics

sections.title: What the ranking found
sections.body: Table 3 reports the four metrics and the TOPSIS closeness per length, with a mean closeness and a rank per group. In the short group FrameFlow ranks first (mean closeness 0.517), ahead of Genie (0.464), Chroma (0.403), FrameDiff (0.365) and RFdiffusion (0.238), although RFdiffusion has the highest designability at length 100 (0.956) and the lowest diversity at length 50 (0.12). In the medium group RFdiffusion ranks first (0.531) ahead of FrameDiff (0.399) and Chroma (0.296). The values show the trade-off the ranking is built to expose: designability falls with length for Chroma and FrameDiff while their diversity rises, and efficiency ranges from 0.11 seconds per backbone for FrameFlow at length 50 to several seconds for Genie and Chroma.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The framework installs from its conda environment file and as a package, and needs a Foldseek PDB database built locally for the novelty and diversity steps. One command runs the unconditional evaluation on whatever backbones are pointed at. Reading config/unconditional.yaml, the defaults are the demo backbone directory, a local ProteinMPNN installation, an output directory, 10 sequences per backbone with a ProteinMPNN batch size of 10, ESMFold as the prediction method, a Foldseek cluster TM-score threshold of 0.5, a seed of 33 and a required Foldseek database path with no default. AlphaFold2 can be used instead of ESMFold through LocalColabFold, configured in the same file. Configuration is through Hydra, so any of these can be overridden on the command line.
sections.source_locator: README: Installation, Usage; config/unconditional.yaml

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: No fixed target set: the evaluated data are generated by the methods under test, 100 backbones per method per evaluated length, each with 10 ProteinMPNN sequences. Nine lengths are evaluated in three groups (50 and 100; 200, 300, 400 and 500; 600, 800 and 1000). The external reference data are the whole PDB, used through Foldseek for the novelty metric. The motif-scaffolding task, outside this record's scope, uses 24 benchmark cases with 100 backbones each.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 1 caption; Table 2; Evaluation metrics, Novelty

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Inapplicable: there is no training, validation or test division, because the benchmark scores freshly generated samples rather than held-out data. The only partition is by sequence length into the short, medium and long groups, and each group holds only the methods that could be run at those lengths, so the method sets differ between groups.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 2; Material and methods

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Four ranked metrics plus descriptive ones. Designability: the fraction of backbones whose mean self-consistency TM-score over the three best sequences exceeds 0.5, higher is better; the best-sequence rate and the area under a threshold sweep are reported beside it. Novelty: pdb-TM, the highest TM-score to any PDB structure, lower is better (more novel), with a penalty term added when the backbone is undesignable. Diversity: unique Foldseek clusters at a TM-score threshold of 0.5 divided by the number of backbones, higher is better. Efficiency: mean seconds per backbone over 100 backbones, lower is better. The TOPSIS closeness value aggregates the four, higher is better. Secondary structure content, radius of gyration and MolProbity validity are reported without ranking. The motif-scaffolding task uses self-consistency RMSD below 2.0 angstroms instead.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics; Table 3 header

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Seven backbone generation methods across the two tasks, with their release dates and categories given: Genie (2023-01, diffusion), FrameDiff (2023-03, diffusion), RFdiffusion (2023-04, diffusion), TDS (2023-06, diffusion), GPDL (2023-10, ESM-based), FrameFlow (2023-10, flow-based) and Chroma (2023-11, diffusion). Of these, Genie and FrameDiff are evaluated on unconditional generation only, TDS and GPDL on the conditional task only, and RFdiffusion, FrameFlow and Chroma on both. The pipeline's own fixed components, ProteinMPNN and ESMFold, were themselves checked against alternatives (ESM-IF1 for sequence design, AlphaFold2 and OmegaFold for prediction).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Material and methods

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None, and the concept barely applies in the usual sense: the backbones are generated rather than held out, so there is no test set to leak. What the benchmark does instead is measure the related quantity directly, as novelty: every generated backbone is searched against the whole PDB with Foldseek and its highest TM-score reported, so a method that reproduces known folds is visible. The authors add a penalty so that a backbone cannot score as novel while being undesignable. There is no control over what the generators themselves were trained on.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Novelty

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Distributions rather than intervals. Each cell rests on 100 backbones and 10 sequences per backbone, and the paper reports the full distributions of self-consistency TM-score and pdb-TM as box plots with medians, plus an area under the threshold sweep so that a result does not hang on one cut-off. T-tests are used where two readings of the same group are compared, for example novelty with and without the designability penalty. No confidence interval is attached to the designability, diversity, efficiency or TOPSIS values in Table 3, and no repeated generation runs are reported.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 2 caption; Table 3

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a generated protein backbone, a single chain of a chosen length, carrying the 10 sequences designed for it and their predicted structures. Aggregation is per method and length group.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Material and methods; Figure 1 caption

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Inapplicable: the backbones are generated de novo and belong to no organism. The only natural data involved is the PDB, used as the reference set for the novelty search, and no species composition is given for it.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Novelty

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. Every metric is computed in silico from generated and predicted structures. The authors state that these are proxies for high-throughput in vitro experiments rather than measurements, and no wet-lab result is part of the benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: For the generator, a target length and nothing else: unconditional generation is sampling a backbone of the requested size. For the scoring pipeline, the generated backbone coordinates, from which ProteinMPNN designs sequences; the configuration exposes a CA_only option, which is off by default. The motif-scaffolding task additionally supplies a motif placement specification.
