facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Released checkpoints run at their own settings, with nothing trained or fine-tuned by the benchmark. The fixed parts of the pipeline, ProteinMPNN for sequence design and ESMFold for refolding, are the same for every method, which is the point of the framework; the paper justifies each choice against an alternative.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Material and methods

strengths.text: Every method is scored through one refolding pipeline with the same sequence designer, the same structure predictor and the same hardware, so differences are not differences between each paper's own protocol.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Material and methods; Evaluation metrics, Efficiency

strengths.text: The designability criterion is examined rather than inherited: the authors explain why they use a TM-score threshold instead of RMSD at long lengths, report both the top-three and best-sequence rates, and publish the area under a sweep of thresholds so a reader is not tied to one cut-off.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Designability; Figure 2 caption

strengths.text: Novelty cannot be gamed by producing unfoldable structures, because the novelty score carries an explicit penalty when the backbone's own designability falls below the threshold.
The framework is published and runnable: MIT licensed, installable from an environment file, with one command per task, a Hydra configuration for the parameters and a Colab notebook for a quick run.
strengths.source_locator: README: Installation, Usage; LICENSE; Paper: Data Availability

limitations.text: The length groups do not hold the same methods, because each method was only run at the lengths it could handle: five methods in the short group, three in the medium, two in the long. A group ranking therefore cannot be read across groups.

Nothing here is measured in a laboratory. Designability means that a structure predictor reproduces the backbone from a designed sequence, which the authors describe as a proxy for in vitro experiments.

The headline ranking depends on choices the authors made and not only on the measurements: the top-three rather than best-sequence rule, the 0.5 TM-score thresholds for designability and for clustering, the novelty penalty weight set to 1, and the TOPSIS aggregation with its weighting.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Designability, Novelty, Diversity and Ranking

limitations.text: The scores depend on two fixed tools whose own behaviour shapes the result. ProteinMPNN is the only sequence designer and ESMFold the only refolding predictor in the reported runs, and the paper's justification for each rests on supplementary comparisons on a subset.

No repeated generation runs and no interval are reported for the ranked metrics, so a reader cannot tell how much of a small gap between two methods is sampling noise. Table 3 prints mean values without preprocessing.

steps: method generates 100 backbones at one length
ProteinMPNN designs 10 sequences per backbone
ESMFold predicts each sequence's structure
self-consistency TM-score over the top 3 sequences gives designability
Foldseek gives pdb-TM for novelty and clusters for diversity
TOPSIS combines designability, novelty, diversity and runtime into a rank
diagram.caption: The generator is the only thing that changes between columns: the sequence designer, the structure predictor, the thresholds and the hardware are fixed.

gaps: Only part of Table 3 is recorded here: the full grid of four metrics by method and length, and the long group's values, were not transcribed.

The distributions in Figure 2, the structural property analysis and the motif-scaffolding results are described in the text but their values sit in figures and supplementary files that were not retrieved.
The mathematical detail of the TOPSIS weighting is in the supplementary materials, which were not retrieved, so the weights behind the published ranking are not recorded.
The dataset and grouping details the paper defers to its supplementary materials were not retrieved.
No information is given about repeated generation runs, so the stability of the ranking is unknown.

profile.summary: BioML-bench measures what an autonomous agent can do with a biomedical machine learning task from end to end. The agent reads a task description, works with the data, writes and runs its own pipeline and produces a submission file; the submission is then scored by that task's own metric and placed against that task's leaderboard, giving a percentile, a medal band and a comparison with human baseline scores. The v0.1-alpha task list holds 24 tasks drawn from four sources: nine from Polaris Hub, six ProteinGym deep mutational scanning tasks, five Open Problems single-cell tasks and four Kaggle competitions. It is built on the MLE-bench scaffold and is agent-agnostic: anything that can read a description and write a submission can be evaluated.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Description and Key Features; experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt (24 rows counted)

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an agent can carry a biomedical prediction problem through every step on its own: understanding the task from prose, looking at the data, choosing a method, implementing it, running it and submitting test-set predictions in the required format. The score is not just the task metric but where that metric places the agent among the people who have already attempted the same task, which is why the grader reports a leaderboard percentile, medal bands and a separate comparison with human baseline scores. Because the task set spans drug properties, protein fitness, single-cell omics and medical imaging, it also measures how far one agent generalises across biomedical domains.
sections.source_locator: README: Description and Key Features; grade.py, grade_submission

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks are repackaged from existing public sources rather than created. The v0.1-alpha list names 24 tasks, counted here from the file: nine with the polarishub prefix (an EGFR potency set, three ADME-Fang endpoints and five Therapeutics Data Commons sets covering CYP2D6 substrate, lipophilicity, Caco-2 permeability, hERG and blood-brain barrier penetration), six with the proteingym-dms prefix (including the SARS-CoV-2 spike binding scan and four Tsuboyama 2023 stability scans, two of them indel sets), five with the manual prefix for Open Problems single-cell tasks (modality prediction, single-cell perturbations, cell-cell communication, spatially variable genes and label projection), and four Kaggle competitions covering pulmonary fibrosis progression, histopathologic cancer detection, brain tumour radiogenomic classification and gastrointestinal tract image segmentation. Each task in the repository carries its own preparation script, configuration and grader, and the data-source layer has separate implementations for Kaggle, Polaris, ProteinGym and manually prepared data.
sections.source_locator: experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt; README: Key Features; repository layout

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Grading reads a submission for a task, computes the task's own metric with that task's grader, then ranks the score against the task leaderboard. Reading grade_helpers.py, rank_score returns the gold, silver and bronze medal flags with their thresholds, whether the score is above the median, the leaderboard percentile from 0 to 100 where higher is better, and the leaderboard size; the direction of the metric is read from the leaderboard rather than assumed. Human comparison is separate: calculate_human_performance_metrics takes the median human score for beats_human and computes a human percentile as the share of humans the agent matches or exceeds, respecting the metric's direction. Aggregation across tasks counts medals and tasks that beat humans and reports the average, best and worst leaderboard percentile over the tasks that produced one.
sections.source_locator: grade.py, grade_submission, aggregate_reports and calculate_human_performance_metrics; grade_helpers.py, rank_score

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Three commands, after installing the package with uv and pulling the prebuilt agent images. prepare downloads and prepares one task's data, run-agent runs a named agent container on a task, and grade scores the resulting submission file and writes a report. The repository ships prebuilt agent images; the only agent the saved sources name is a dummy agent for checking the pipeline, and the readme notes that running a real agent needs an API key file at the repository root. Python 3.11 or later, Docker and uv are the stated prerequisites.
sections.source_locator: README: Quick Start, Prerequisites, Installation, Basic Usage

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 24 tasks in the v0.1-alpha list, counted from the file by source prefix: 9 polarishub tasks (polaris-pkis2-egfr-wt-c-1, three adme-fang endpoints, and tdcommons sets for CYP2D6 substrate, lipophilicity, Caco-2, hERG and blood-brain barrier), 6 proteingym-dms tasks (SPIKE_SARS2_Starr_2020_binding, SBI_STAAM_Tsuboyama_2023_2JVG, PSAE_PICP2_Tsuboyama_2023_1PSE, CBX4_HUMAN_Tsuboyama_2023_2K28, Q8EG35_SHEON_Campbell_2022_indels and CSN4_MOUSE_Tsuboyama_2023_1UFM_indels), 5 manual Open Problems single-cell tasks, and 4 kaggle competitions. Per-task dataset sizes are not stated in the saved sources; each task's data is downloaded by its own preparation script at run time.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Each task keeps the train and test split of its original source, prepared by that task's own preparation script, and the agent sees only the training side while the grader holds the test labels. The saved sources do not state the split rule for any individual task. There is no benchmark-level split: all 24 tasks are evaluation tasks.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Each task is scored by its own metric, whose direction is read from that task's leaderboard rather than fixed. On top of that the grader reports a leaderboard percentile from 0 to 100, higher being better, the leaderboard size, gold, silver and bronze medal flags with their thresholds, whether the score is above the median, and two human comparisons: a boolean for beating the median human and a human percentile from 0 to 100. Aggregation over tasks gives medal counts, a count of tasks beating humans, and the average, best and worst leaderboard percentile.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Two kinds. The human leaderboard of each task is the reference the score is ranked against, with built-in human baseline scores for a separate median comparison. For agents, the repository ships prebuilt agent images, pulled with scripts/pull_prebuilt_images.sh; the only agent named in the saved sources is the dummy agent, which exists to check the pipeline rather than to compete. The saved sources do not say which agents or models produced the published results.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None described in the saved sources, and the design makes leakage likely to matter. Every task is a repackaging of a public competition or public data set, so the data, the published solutions and in several cases the leaderboard itself predate the agents' training cut-offs; the repository holds no identity filter, time split or contamination check, and the readme and grading code do not mention one. The ProteinGym and Open Problems tasks come with their own source splits, which are the only separation in place.
facts.source_locator: README: Description; experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Unreported in the saved sources. The grading code produces one report per submission with no replicate handling, and nothing in the repository defines a number of runs per agent and task, a seed policy or an interval on the aggregate percentiles; the aggregate function simply averages the per-task percentiles. How many runs stand behind a published figure is not stated in anything fetched here.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a whole task: a description, a data set and a submission format, which the agent must turn into test-set predictions in one autonomous run. Below that level the entity differs per task, from a small molecule to a protein variant to a cell to a medical image, but the benchmark's unit of scoring is the task, and a run is graded from a single submission file.

facts.value: Mixed, and not stated as a composition. The task identifiers name human proteins and cell data, a mouse protein (CSN4_MOUSE), a bacterial protein (Q8EG35_SHEON, from Shewanella oneidensis) and the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor binding domain, while the Kaggle and Polaris tasks concern human patients and small molecules. No source fetched here gives a species breakdown.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Whatever each source data set measured, inherited rather than described. The ProteinGym tasks are deep mutational scans, including a binding scan of the SARS-CoV-2 spike and stability scans from Tsuboyama 2023. The Polaris tasks are small-molecule property measurements (potency, metabolic clearance, plasma protein binding, solubility, permeability, hERG inhibition, blood-brain barrier penetration). The single-cell tasks come from Open Problems and the imaging tasks from clinical data. No assay protocol is described in the saved sources.
facts.source_locator: experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The task description in prose plus the prepared task data, inside a container with biomedical libraries already installed, including RDKit and BioPython. The agent writes and runs its own code, so within the container it may use anything available there; what it must produce is a submission file or folder. The saved sources do not state whether network access or external model calls beyond the agent's own API keys are restricted during a run.
facts.source_locator: README: Key Features, Prerequisites

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: The agent trains whatever it decides to train, from scratch, inside the run: there is no fixed model, no frozen representation and no prescribed method. That is the point of the benchmark, which the readme describes as implementing complete solutions from scratch. Nothing in the benchmark is fine-tuned by the maintainers.
facts.source_locator: README: Description

strengths.text: The score is anchored to people rather than to other agents: each submission is ranked against that task's existing leaderboard and separately against human baseline scores, with the metric direction read from the leaderboard rather than assumed.
strengths.source_locator: grade.py, grade_submission and calculate_human_performance_metrics; grade_helpers.py, rank_score

strengths.text: It is agent-agnostic and executable end to end: a submission is just a file or folder, the task set is a plain list of identifiers, and prepare, run-agent and grade are three commands. Everything is MIT licensed.
strengths.source_locator: README: Key Features, Basic Usage; LICENSE; experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt

strengths.text: The task set is genuinely multi-domain rather than one field repeated: the 24 identifiers cover small-molecule properties, protein mutational scans, single-cell omics and medical imaging, each with its own data-source implementation in the repository.
A dummy agent ships with the benchmark, so the pipeline can be checked without spending model calls, and prebuilt agent images are provided to avoid build differences between users.

limitations.text: A percentile is a statement about a particular leaderboard, not only about the agent: it depends on who submitted to that competition and when, and the grader reports the leaderboard size precisely because the denominator varies between tasks.

Contamination is not addressed anywhere in the saved sources. All 24 tasks are public competitions or public data sets with published solutions, and no identity filter, time split or contamination check exists in the repository.
This is a pre-release. The readme labels the version v0.1-alpha and says to expect bugs and incomplete features, which is a caution worth carrying into any comparison based on it.

Nothing in the repository pins how many runs an agent gets, so the published aggregates cannot be read as having a known variance: the grading code averages per-task percentiles with no replicate or interval handling.

Running it costs money and depends on outside services: real agents need API keys for commercial model providers, and each task's data is fetched from its original host (Kaggle, Polaris Hub, ProteinGym or a manual source) at preparation time.

profile.summary: This is one 2020 study's evaluation, not a released suite: the docking server ClusPro was run on all 230 target complexes of Protein Docking Benchmark 5.0 from their unbound component structures, and the top 30 models per target were scored with DockQ. A model counts as good at DockQ 0.23 or above, and success rates are reported in the top 1, 5, 10 and 30 predictions, broken down by target type (enzyme-containing, antibody-antigen and other) and by docking difficulty (rigid, medium, difficult). Three of the 230 targets could not be scored, so the percentages rest on 227. It is useful as a reference point for how far a rigid-body Fourier-transform docking method gets on a standard benchmark, which is what the paper sets out to measure.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Summary; Results, Performance on the protein docking benchmark; Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a rigid-body docking method, given the two unbound component structures of a complex, produces a near-native model of the complex, and whether it ranks that model highly enough to be found. The two questions are kept apart deliberately: success is reported at several cut-offs in the ranked list, because the authors note that docking methods rarely put the best model first and that five or ten models can be passed on for refinement, which is also how the CAPRI experiment has handled submissions. The study's wider aim is to find the limits of the approach, so it also compares cluster-based with energy-based model selection and compares against flexible docking.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary; Results, Performance on the protein docking benchmark

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The target set is not the authors' own: it is Protein Docking Benchmark 5.0, described as a non-redundant and fairly diverse set of complexes in which each entry has the structure of the complex and of one or both unbound components. It holds 40 antibody-antigen, 88 enzyme-containing and 102 other complexes, and classifies them by docking difficulty into 151 rigid-body (easy), 45 medium and 34 difficult targets. The study downloaded the component proteins directly from the benchmark and docked all 230. Table 1 splits the antibody-antigen targets further into 26 with an unbound antibody structure and 12 whose antibody structure comes from the complex.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Quantification and statistical analysis, Protein Docking Benchmark Version 5.0; Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: For each complex the 1000 lowest-energy models were kept and the centres of the 30 largest clusters were scored with DockQ against the native complex. DockQ is a continuous score from 0 to 1 that combines the three CAPRI measures (the fraction of native contacts, interface RMSD and ligand RMSD), with 0.23 or above acceptable, 0.49 or above medium and 0.80 or above high accuracy; the paper treats it as a higher-resolution version of the CAPRI classification. A target counts as solved when an acceptable or better model appears within the chosen cut-off, and rates are given for the top 1, 5, 10 and 30. ClusPro was run per target type with the setting the server recommends for it, the balanced coefficient set for enzymes, antibody mode for antibodies and the others mode for the rest, and those coefficient choices were themselves cross-validated on the earlier benchmark version rather than tuned on BM5.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Quantification and statistical analysis, Evaluating Prediction Accuracy Using DOCKQ and the coefficient validation section

sections.title: What the study found
sections.body: In the top 10 predictions ClusPro produced an acceptable or better model for 51 of the 88 enzyme-containing complexes (57.95 per cent), 19 of the 38 scored antibody-antigen complexes (50 per cent, split in Table 1 into 12 of 26 unbound and 7 of 12 bound-antibody targets) and 27 of the 101 scored other complexes (26.73 per cent), giving 97 of 227 overall (42.73 per cent). Going to the top 30 adds eight enzyme, five antibody and nine other targets, for 119 of 227 (52.42 per cent). Difficulty matters more than type: 51.68 per cent of rigid targets are solved in the top 10 against 31.82 per cent medium and 17.65 per cent difficult, rising to 63.09, 36.36 and 26.47 per cent in the top 30, and every high-accuracy prediction in the antibody and enzyme sets came from the rigid category.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Performance on the protein docking benchmark; Table 1

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Protein Docking Benchmark 5.0: 230 target complexes, of which 40 antibody-antigen, 88 enzyme-containing and 102 other, classified by difficulty into 151 rigid-body, 45 medium and 34 difficult. Three targets could not be scored, two antibody-antigen ones because of their size and one other, so all percentages rest on 227 targets: 88 enzyme, 38 antibody-antigen (26 with an unbound antibody structure and 12 with the antibody structure taken from the complex) and 101 other. The study adds no data of its own; a separate section reviews ClusPro's results in seven CAPRI and CAPRI/CASP rounds, which is a different set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Protein Docking Benchmark Version 5.0; Results; Table 1; Table 2

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No training or test split: every one of the 230 targets is docked and scored. The only partitions are descriptive, by target type and by docking difficulty. Where a parameter choice had to be made, it was made on the previous benchmark version rather than on BM5: five-fold cross-validation on BM4 complexes selected the energy coefficient sets, which were then applied to the 55 BM5 targets that were not in BM4.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Validation of energy weight coefficient sets

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: DockQ, higher is better, on a 0 to 1 scale, with the bands 0.23 or above acceptable, 0.49 or above medium and 0.80 or above high accuracy; a model at 0.23 or above is called a good solution. The reported quantity is a success rate: the percentage of targets with at least one good model within the top 1, 5, 10 or 30 predictions, with the counts of high and medium accuracy models given alongside. DockQ combines the three CAPRI measures, the fraction of native contacts, interface RMSD and ligand RMSD (lower is better for the two RMSD measures), whose own thresholds are also stated.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; The CAPRI Criteria of Prediction Accuracy; Evaluating Prediction Accuracy Using DOCKQ

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The study is about one method, ClusPro, with its PIPER docking engine, so there is no baseline in the usual sense. Three comparisons stand in for one: cluster-based against energy-based model selection within ClusPro, a comparison with flexible docking algorithms, and a review of the historical performance of three servers (ClusPro, HADDOCK and SwarmDock) over seven CAPRI and CAPRI/CASP rounds, where the totals of good predictions are 53, 43 and 33 respectively based on the top 10 models per target.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Summary; Table 2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: One, and only for the parameter choice: the energy coefficient sets were selected by five-fold cross-validation on the earlier BM4 complexes and then applied to the BM5 targets, including the 55 that were not in BM4, so the weights were not fitted on the reported targets. There is no control of the kind a learned method would need: the benchmark is described as non-redundant but no sequence identity cut-off, time split or held-out family is applied for this evaluation, and the docking method is a physics-based scoring function rather than a trained model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Validation of energy weight coefficient sets; Protein Docking Benchmark Version 5.0

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Unreported. The results are counts and percentages of targets with no interval, no repeated run and no statistical test between settings; docking is deterministic given the inputs and settings, and the paper does not discuss variability. The only error-like quantity reported is the number of targets DockQ could not score.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Table 1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a protein-protein complex: the two unbound component structures are the input and the deposited complex is the reference. The unit of scoring within a target is a docked model, the centre of one of the 30 largest clusters, and a target is counted once according to its best model within the cut-off.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Protein Docking Benchmark Version 5.0

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported. The targets are Protein Docking Benchmark 5.0 complexes, grouped by functional type and docking difficulty; no species composition is given anywhere in the paper.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Protein Docking Benchmark Version 5.0

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. The reference is the experimentally determined structure of each complex, taken from the benchmark, and every reported quantity is a geometric comparison with it. No binding or activity measurement is involved.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Protein Docking Benchmark Version 5.0; The CAPRI Criteria of Prediction Accuracy

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The unbound component structures of the complex, downloaded directly from the benchmark, plus the knowledge of which type of complex it is, since the run uses the coefficient set recommended for that type (balanced for enzymes, antibody mode for antibodies, others mode for the rest). For antibodies that mode uses a special parameterisation. No information from the native complex enters the docking.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Evaluating Prediction Accuracy Using DOCKQ, coefficient sets

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: No training. ClusPro is a rigid-body Fourier-transform docking method with fixed energy terms; the only fitted quantities are the weights of those terms, chosen among four published coefficient sets by cross-validation on the earlier benchmark. The paper describes the method as working only with energy expressions that can be written as sums of correlation functions, which is part of the limitation it sets out to measure.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Summary; Validation of energy weight coefficient sets

strengths.text: The target set is an external standard rather than a selection: all 230 complexes of Protein Docking Benchmark 5.0 were docked from their unbound components, with no filtering by the authors.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Performance on the protein docking benchmark

strengths.text: Success is reported at four cut-offs in the ranked list rather than only at the top, which separates the ability to produce a near-native model from the ability to rank it first, and the authors explain why that distinction matters in practice.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Performance on the protein docking benchmark

strengths.text: The breakdown by target type and by docking difficulty, with the number of targets in each cell, lets a reader see that the overall rate is carried by the 151 rigid targets rather than treating it as uniform.

The scoring tool is external and standard: DockQ, which reproduces the CAPRI accuracy classes and is cited as having been used in the official evaluation of a CAPRI round, with its code address given.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Evaluating Prediction Accuracy Using DOCKQ

strengths.text: The per-target results are published with the paper rather than summarised only: the number of acceptable, medium and high accuracy predictions for each BM5 target at each cut-off is given in a supplementary data file.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results; Data and Code Availability

limitations.text: Author-reported, for one method: the group that develops ClusPro ran it, chose the per-type settings and scored the results. The comparisons with other servers come from published CAPRI rounds rather than from runs made here.

Three of the 230 targets are missing from every percentage because DockQ could not score them, two antibody-antigen complexes for their size and one other complex, so the denominator is 227 and the antibody set is 38 rather than 40.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Performance on the protein docking benchmark

limitations.text: The run is not a blind one and not fully method-agnostic: each target type is docked with the coefficient set the authors recommend for that type, so a user who does not know the type of their complex would not reproduce these conditions.
No uncertainty is attached to any figure, so small differences between cells, including between the unbound and bound antibody subsets of 26 and 12 targets, cannot be separated from noise.

This is a 2020 evaluation of a rigid-body method on a benchmark of unbound structures, and the record should not be read against modern co-folding results: the paper itself frames the exercise as finding the limits imposed by the rigid-body assumption.

profile.summary: The CASP16 affinity component was a blind challenge: participants were given protein sequences and ligand SMILES from pharmaceutical discovery projects and asked to predict binding affinities before the measured values were released, then asked again in a second stage with the experimental complex structures in hand. 140 affinity targets were posed across two protein systems, human chymase (17) and autotaxin (123), and 28 groups submitted first-stage predictions. Scoring is a Kendall rank correlation within each system, weighted by the number of affinities submitted. The assessors also computed what a perfect method could achieve given experimental uncertainty, giving a ceiling of about 0.73 against a best achieved value of 0.39, which is the most useful number on this page.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Structure of the Challenge; Results, Affinity Predictions

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a computational method can rank undisclosed drug-like compounds by their measured affinity for a pharmaceutical target, with no sight of the answer. The ranking framing is deliberate: submissions were accepted as absolute dissociation constants, as ratios to a reference ligand, or as plain rankings within a target set, and the scoring is a rank correlation. The second stage asks a different question: whether having the experimental complex structure helps, since in stage 2 the crystal structures were released before the affinity predictions were due. The assessors also measure the challenge's own resolving power, by asking what rank correlation a perfect predictor could reach given the experimental uncertainty of the measurements.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Structure of the Challenge; Results, Affinity Predictions

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The targets come from pharmaceutical discovery projects rather than from a public database: the five protein systems were contributed by Hoffmann-La Roche (chymase, cathepsin G and autotaxin) and Idorsia (the SARS-CoV-2 main protease), with a fifth from the Structural Genomics Consortium, and the data behind them are described in companion papers. Only two systems carried affinity targets: 17 chymase-ligand targets with both structures and affinities, and autotaxin with 93 pairs having both, 96 with structures only and 30 with affinities only, giving 123 autotaxin affinity targets. Each target was posted with a description, the protein sequence, the ligand SMILES with stereochemistry where available, a statement of what to predict and, for structures, a zero-filled template file. Targets for the first four systems were posted on 5 May 2024 with predictions due 21 July; stage 2 ran from 7 to 21 August; the fifth system arrived later and was re-released on 30 August after a SMILES error was found.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, The Challenges and Structure of the Challenge

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each group could submit up to five predictions per target, with Model 1 taken as their preferred one, and the assessment uses Model 1. Accuracy is Kendall's tau computed separately within each protein system and combined as an N-weighted average, where the weights are the numbers of affinities submitted for autotaxin (108) and chymase (14). The ceiling calculation resamples the experimental values under an assumed threefold uncertainty in the measured half-maximal inhibitory concentration and asks what a perfect method would score: 0.54 with a standard deviation of 0.11 for chymase and 0.76 with a standard deviation of 0.02 for autotaxin, which weight to 0.73. The assessors note that the chymase ceiling is lower because its measurements span a 400-fold range against 8700-fold for autotaxin, so the chymase challenge resolves accuracy less well. Baseline predictors are run for context: molecular weight, computed log P, a Gaussian process regressor with a Tanimoto kernel fitted per system on ChEMBL data, AutoDock Vina docking scores for stage 1, and Vina and GNINA scores on the released crystal structures for stage 2.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Structure of the Challenge and Binding Affinity Prediction; Results, Affinity Predictions

sections.title: The disclosure problem and the final target counts
sections.body: During assessment the organisers rechecked whether the affinity data had been published elsewhere and found that it had, for 18 targets: chymase targets L1003 and L1010 in Roche patents, L1013 in another group's publication, and 15 named autotaxin targets in four Roche patents. Those were removed, so the assessed set is 122 affinity targets rather than 140, and a supplementary figure repeats the assessment on all 140 with results the paper says are much the same. For stage 2, structures were available for all 17 chymase targets, of which 14 were used after the removals, and for 93 of the autotaxin affinity targets, of which 89 undisclosed ones with cocrystal structures were usable. Submission counts differ between stages and systems: 21 stage 1 and 24 stage 2 submissions for autotaxin, 28 stage 1 and 27 stage 2 for chymase.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Affinity Predictions, Assessment; Figure 8 and 9 captions

sections.title: What the challenge found
sections.body: Most submissions correlated positively with experiment but quality varied widely. The best group reached an N-weighted Kendall's tau of 0.39, followed by four groups above 0.25; the abstract states the maximum observed tau as 0.42. The best affinity groups are not the best pose groups, and there was no significant correlation between a group's accuracy on autotaxin and on chymase, with one exception. Molecular weight alone correlates with experiment almost as well as the best CASP predictions, while computed log P correlates inversely. Releasing the experimental structures did not shift the distribution of accuracy in stage 2, which the assessors read as the scoring functions being the limiting factor rather than the structures. Against the 0.73 ceiling the best result leaves considerable room, and the assessors estimate the best method's effective uncertainty at about 2 kcal/mol in binding free energy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Affinity Predictions and Comparison With Baseline Affinity Predictors

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 140 affinity targets were posed across two of the five CASP16 protein-ligand systems: 17 for human chymase and 123 for autotaxin. After 18 targets whose affinities had been disclosed elsewhere were removed, the assessed set is 122, and the N-weighted scoring uses 108 autotaxin and 14 chymase affinities. For stage 2, 14 chymase targets and 89 autotaxin targets had usable undisclosed affinities with cocrystal structures. The wider CASP16 protein-ligand challenge also posed 229 pose targets across all five systems, which are outside this record. The autotaxin construct is a hybrid, mostly rat with human binding-site residues and a His tag.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, The Challenges; Results, Affinity Predictions

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Not a split but a time-ordered blind challenge in two stages. Stage 1: affinities predicted from sequence and SMILES before any experimental structure or affinity was public, posted 5 May 2024 and due 21 July 2024 for the first four systems. Stage 2: the experimental complex structures were released and affinity predictions were re-submitted, 7 to 21 August 2024. The last system was shared on 9 August and re-released on 30 August with a 18 September deadline. There is no training set: each group brings its own method and its own training data.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Structure of the Challenge

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Kendall's tau, higher is better, computed within each protein system on the group's Model 1 predictions and combined as an N-weighted average over the two systems, with weights 108 for autotaxin and 14 for chymase. No absolute error metric is used for affinity, because submissions may be rankings rather than values. Alongside the achieved values the assessors report the expected tau of a perfect predictor under threefold experimental uncertainty: 0.54 (standard deviation 0.11) for chymase, 0.76 (0.02) for autotaxin, 0.73 weighted. The pose component, outside this record, uses LDDT-PLI.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Affinity Predictions; Abstract

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five, run by the assessors rather than submitted. For stage 1: ligand molecular weight, the computed octanol-water partition coefficient, both from RDKit, a Gaussian process regressor with a Tanimoto similarity kernel fitted separately per system on ChEMBL data (1110 chymase inhibition values from 0.3 nM to 570 micromolar, 450 autotaxin values from 10 pM to 1.25 millimolar), and AutoDock Vina docking scores. For stage 2, with the crystal structures available: GNINA v1.3 and AutoDock Vina scores after local minimisation. The finding that matters is that molecular weight nearly matches the best submitted predictions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Binding Affinity Prediction; Results, Comparison With Baseline Affinity Predictors

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The design is the control: the data were unpublished pharmaceutical measurements and predictions were due before release. The organisers then checked that assumption and found it broken for 18 targets, whose affinities had appeared in Roche patents or another group's publication, and removed them, reporting the alternative assessment on all 140 in the supplement. The same checking was applied to the pose component, where five main protease targets turned out to have been in the PDB before the deadline and were dropped. A separate analysis uses Foldseek and a chemical overlap score to measure how similar a target's protein and ligand are to anything already in the PDB, so template availability can be related to accuracy. What is not controlled is each group's own training data beyond these disclosures.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Affinity Predictions, Assessment; Methods, Assessing the Existence of Similar Protein-Ligand Structures in the PDB; Methods, The Challenges

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Handled on the experimental side rather than by replicating predictions. The assessors assume about threefold uncertainty in the measured half-maximal inhibitory concentrations, resample under it and report the resulting distribution of the best achievable tau, with standard deviations of 0.11 for chymase and 0.02 for autotaxin. They use the same approach in reverse to estimate the best method's effective uncertainty at about 2 kcal/mol. No interval is attached to any individual group's score, and each group submits once per stage, with Model 1 assessed.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Affinity Predictions

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a protein-ligand pair: a named target system plus one drug-like compound given as a SMILES string, for which an affinity is predicted. Scoring is within a system, because the metric is a rank correlation across that system's compounds, so a single pair has no score of its own.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Structure of the Challenge; Results, Affinity Predictions

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human targets, with one construct caveat. The affinity systems are human chymase and autotaxin, the latter supplied as a hybrid construct that is mostly rat with human binding-site residues and a His tag. The wider pose challenge adds human cathepsin G, human WDR55 and the SARS-CoV-2 main protease.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, The Challenges; Figure 1 caption

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Half-maximal inhibitory concentrations measured in the contributing companies' discovery projects, with the assay details given in companion papers rather than here. The assessors treat them as carrying about threefold uncertainty, and note that the chymase values span a 400-fold range while the autotaxin values span 8700-fold, which is why the two systems differ in how well they can resolve a method's accuracy. The ChEMBL data used for one baseline are also inhibition values.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Affinity Predictions; Methods, The Challenges and Binding Affinity Prediction

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: In stage 1, what the challenge website posted: a description of the data set, the protein sequence, the ligand SMILES with stereochemistry where available, and a statement of what was to be predicted. In stage 2, the experimental coordinates of the protein-ligand complexes as well. Anything else a group brings, including its own training data and templates from the PDB, is unrestricted, which is why the assessors measure template availability separately.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Structure of the Challenge

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Unrestricted and group-specific: each participant uses its own method, trained however it chooses. The paper names examples among the better affinity groups, including graph neural networks trained on PDBbind and a combination of deep docking methods, and the assessors' own baselines include a Gaussian process regressor fitted per target system on ChEMBL data. CASP's convention is one method per group registration, with a laboratory able to register several groups to test several methods.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Affinity Predictions; Methods, Structure of the Challenge

strengths.text: It is genuinely blind on unpublished industrial data: the targets came from company discovery projects and predictions were due before the affinities or structures were released, which is a stronger condition than any retrospective benchmark can offer.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, The Challenges and Structure of the Challenge

strengths.text: The assessors publish the challenge's own ceiling. By resampling the measurements under their experimental uncertainty they show what a perfect method could score (0.73 weighted), which turns a bare correlation into a statement about how much room is left.

Disclosure was audited after the fact and acted on: 18 affinity targets whose values had appeared in patents or a publication were removed, five pose targets found in the PDB were dropped, and the alternative assessment including the disclosed cases is published in the supplement.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Affinity Predictions, Assessment; Methods, The Challenges

strengths.text: Trivial baselines are run alongside the submissions, and the result is informative rather than decorative: ligand molecular weight ranks the compounds almost as well as the best submitted method.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Comparison With Baseline Affinity Predictors

limitations.text: Two protein systems only, and one of them barely resolves accuracy: the chymase measurements span a 400-fold range, which gives a perfect-method ceiling of 0.54, and the assessors warn that coming close to it on chymase does not mean the predictions were good.

The blind condition was partly compromised before assessment: the affinities of 18 of the 140 targets had already been disclosed in patents or a paper, and the organisers only discovered this during the assessment phase.

The denominators move between the figures. 140 targets were posed, 122 assessed, the weighting uses 108 autotaxin and 14 chymase affinities, stage 2 uses 14 chymase and 89 autotaxin, and the number of submissions differs by stage and system, so any quoted tau has to be read with its own target set.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Affinity Predictions; Figure 8 and 9 captions

limitations.text: The abstract and the results section give different maximum values: the abstract says the maximum Kendall's tau was 0.42, while the results state the maximum achieved value as 0.39 and name the best group at 0.39. A reader quoting a headline number should say which.

A group's score does not transfer between systems: the assessors found no significant correlation between accuracy on autotaxin and on chymase, with one exception, so ranking a method from this challenge says little about the next target.

No harness, scoring script or data download is published in the saved source, and the challenge cannot be rerun blind now that the answers are out.

profile.summary: This record is one paper's evaluation built on the POISK dataset, a collection of antibody sequences and binding metadata extracted from patent filings by a large language model pipeline. The evaluation treats structure prediction models as zero-shot binder classifiers: for each antibody and antigen pair the model folds the complex and its interface confidence scores, ipTM and ipSAE, are used to rank patent-supported binders against putative non-binders for the same antigen. The released folding metrics cover six co-folding models with 22,494 rows each. The paper itself is a bioRxiv preprint that this pass could not fetch, so this page is written from the Zenodo release and is deliberately thin on results.
profile.summary_source_locator: Zenodo record 21775623: Overview and Relationship to the folding predictions

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a co-folding model's confidence in the interface it builds can tell a real antibody-antigen pair from a plausible but non-binding one, without any training for that task. The quantity used is not a predicted affinity but a structural confidence score, ipTM or an ipSAE-style score, so the output is a ranking rather than a measurement. The release warns that a score must be read with the chain pair it was computed on: each ipSAE-style score ships beside a column naming that pair, and a value whose pair is not antibody against antigen is not a binding metric.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record: Overview; Relationship to the folding predictions

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The underlying data are extracted from patent text rather than curated from a database. The release is a flat CSV of 93,193 rows and 47 columns, one row per unique record, carrying variable region sequences for the heavy and light chains, the target sequence with its provenance (what the release holds, what the patent's GenBank deposit holds and what the named UniProt entry holds), target metadata including gene symbols, UniProt identifiers and source organisms, experimental binding affinities with assay methods such as surface plasmon resonance and biolayer interferometry, and epitope information including linear ranges and structural contact residues. Extraction was done by a pipeline driven by large language models, with both prompts published verbatim: an extractor prompt run once per patent and an auditor prompt run once per record to re-locate its support in the patent.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record: Dataset Structure and Documentation; Methodology

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The released folding metrics are the evaluation's raw material: one CSV per model for six models, 22,494 rows each, sharing 28 columns whose order differs between files, so a user must align on names rather than position. The metrics include ipTM and ipSAE, and each ipSAE-style score carries the chain pair it was computed on, including a variant that treats the antibody as a single chain. The archives also hold the predicted structures and the predicted aligned error arrays for each model. A caveat the release states plainly is that these predictions were run against dataset version 1.0.1, not against the version 1.1 release they sit beside, so a pairing of metrics to records has to account for the version change, which the release describes as correcting errors found in 1.0.1.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record: Relationship to the folding predictions; Overview; file list

sections.title: What the release says about its own reliability
sections.body: The release is explicit that the labels come from a generative pipeline and may be wrong. It warns that large language model extraction is subject to hallucinations, naming the misassociation of affinity values with antibody variants and errors in residue indexing as the discrepancies to expect. Against that it ships an audit layer with three columns: a verdict in three tiers, where CONFIRMED means every field was explicitly supported by the patent text, PLAUSIBLE means nothing contradicted the record but support was partial, indirect or inferred, and REVIEW means the record appeared incorrect or could not be established and a human should look, which the release says is not an assertion that the row is false; a flags column naming fields with potential mismatches; and a reasoning column explaining how the value was reached. Users are told to verify critical sequences or affinity data against the original patent before any experimental work.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record: Quality Control and Algorithmic Audit; Usage and Limitations

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One release in two parts. The dataset table is 93,193 rows and 47 columns in version 1.1, one row per unique record. The benchmark's folding side is six per-model metric CSVs of 22,494 rows each, with the predicted structures and predicted aligned error arrays archived beside them for af2m, boltz, intellifold, of3, protenix and protenix_v2. The folding predictions were run against version 1.0.1 of the table rather than the 1.1 release.

facts.label: Splits

profile.summary: This is the evaluation published with RhoMax, a method that predicts the maximum absorption wavelength of a microbial rhodopsin from its sequence. The data are the 884 rhodopsin sequences compiled by Inoue et al., which come from 75 wild-type backgrounds with mutants of each. Four train and test splits are drawn over the wild types, 65 wild types for training and 10 for testing in each, with every mutant kept in the same set as its wild type. The error between the predicted and the measured absorption maximum is reported per split, in electronvolts and in nanometres, for RhoMax, for a RhoMax variant trained on structures that include the retinal, and for the earlier Bayesian LASSO sequence model retrained on the same splits. Anyone choosing a wavelength predictor for rhodopsin engineering can read it as a four-way holdout comparison on a small, unevenly distributed data set.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set and Comparison to Previous Methods; Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How closely a model predicts the wavelength at which a microbial rhodopsin absorbs most strongly, given only its sequence. The question matters for optogenetics, where the useful proteins are red-shifted ones: the authors state that the absorption spectrum has to move towards 700 nm, the lower limit of the tissue transparency window, while opsins typically absorb between 480 and 600 nm. The evaluation therefore also exposes how a predictor behaves when the test sequences sit at the red end of the distribution and the training sequences do not, which is what split 4 does.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, RhoMax Performance

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The labels are measured absorption maxima taken from the Inoue et al. data set: 75 wild-type microbial rhodopsin sequences with several mutants each, 884 records in all, each record carrying the sequence, the absorption maximum and the experimental method used to determine it. The distribution is skewed, with most values between 500 and 570 nm, so the authors draw four separate train and test splits instead of one. The splits are made over wild types, 65 for training and 10 for testing, chosen randomly; because most mutants differ from their wild type by one or two mutations, every mutant is placed in the same set as its wild type. The number of mutants per wild type differs, so the train and test set sizes differ between splits, and the authors state that the split protocol does not make the absorption maxima distributions similar between train and test. Inputs are prepared by predicting five structures per sequence with AlphaFold2 through ColabFold without templates, keeping the highest ranked, and cutting out the 24 residues of the retinal binding pocket, whose positions are located with a ClustalW alignment.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set and Protein Structure Generation and Representation

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model takes a sequence and returns one number, the predicted absorption maximum. The error is the absolute difference between the prediction and the measured value, which is also the training loss. Results are reported per split and as the mean over the four splits, as a median and as a mean with a standard deviation, in electronvolts and in nanometres; the authors argue that electronvolts are the better unit because they are linear in energy, and give nanometres as well for comparison with earlier reports. Lower is better. Table 1 holds three columns of this kind: RhoMax trained on structures without the retinal, RhoMax trained on structures with a retinal copied from the closest PDB homologue, and BLASSO. The comparison to BLASSO is made by running the original authors' R code on the same four splits, with the code modified to train in electronvolts. A separate table reports the same four splits for a RhoMax network whose graph attention layers are replaced by plain graph convolutional layers.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Energy Units, Loss Function and Comparison to Previous Methods; Tables 1 and 3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The data sets, source code and a Colab notebook are published in the OpsiGen repository that the paper's data availability statement names. The README gives six local steps: clone the repository, install the requirements, put a FASTA file and a PDB file into the pipeline_auto folder under fixed names, run the pipeline script, then run the predict script. The pipeline script clears and recreates the dists, features and cutted_parts folders and then runs main.py against config.json, which points at the sample FASTA and PDB and at packaged wavelength and sequence files. The predict script passes a configuration folder and a pickled model to run_one_rhodopsin.sh, which submits a Slurm batch job asking for one GPU, so running it as published needs a Slurm cluster. Nothing in the repository read here reproduces the four splits or Table 1.
sections.source_locator: README.md: How to run OpsiGen locally; pipeline_auto/run.sh; pipeline_auto/config.json; predict/run_one_rhodopsin.sh

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One data set, taken from Inoue et al.: 75 wild-type microbial rhodopsin sequences with several mutants each, 884 sequences in total, each with a measured absorption maximum. Most values lie between 500 and 570 nm.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Four random holdouts over wild-type backgrounds. Each split puts 65 wild types in the training set and 10 in the test set, and every mutant goes to the same set as its wild type. Because the number of mutants per wild type varies, the train and test sizes differ between splits, and the paper states the protocol does not make the absorption maxima distributions similar between train and test. No separate validation split is described.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Absolute error between the predicted and the measured absorption maximum, lower is better. It is reported as a median and as a mean with a standard deviation, in electronvolts and in nanometres, per split and as the mean of the four splits. The same quantity is the training loss.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Energy Units and Loss Function; Table 1

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: BLASSO, the Bayesian LASSO sequence regression of Inoue et al., retrained by the RhoMax authors on the same four splits with their R code updated to train in electronvolts. Two further configurations of the method itself are reported alongside: RhoMax trained on structures that include a retinal copied from the closest PDB homologue, and a version with the graph attention layers replaced by plain graph convolutional layers.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Comparison to Previous Methods; Tables 1 and 3

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: One, and it is the main design choice: mutants are never separated from their wild type. Because most mutant sequences differ from their wild type by one or two mutations, each mutant is assigned to the same set as its wild type, so a near-identical sequence cannot sit on both sides of the split. No sequence identity cut-off between different wild types is described.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No repeated training runs or confidence intervals. The spread reported is the standard deviation of the per-sequence errors within each test set, and the four splits themselves show how much the result moves with the partition. The authors attribute the variability across splits to the small size of the data set, and relate the per-split accuracy to the similarity of the train and test distributions measured with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, RhoMax Performance; Table 1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One rhodopsin sequence, wild type or mutant, with its measured absorption maximum. For the model it becomes the 24 residues of the retinal binding pocket of an AlphaFold2 structure, represented as a graph of atoms joined when they are less than 2 Angstrom apart.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Method Summary and Protein Structure Generation and Representation

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Microbial rhodopsins, also called type I rhodopsins, across 75 wild-type backgrounds. The individual species are not listed in the text read here.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Materials and Methods, Data Set

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Spectroscopic measurement of the absorption maximum, reported in nanometres. Each record in the data set names the experimental method used to determine its value.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set and Energy Units

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Sequence only, as the task is defined. Structure is allowed but has to be produced from the sequence: RhoMax folds each sequence with AlphaFold2 through ColabFold without templates and uses a ClustalW alignment to find the binding pocket positions. The BLASSO comparator uses sequence and physicochemical features alone.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Method Summary, Protein Structure Generation and Representation, Comparison to Previous Methods

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training from scratch on each split. RhoMax is a small network of 6,401 parameters trained for 1000 epochs with the Adam optimiser, a learning rate of 0.0001 and L1 and L2 regularisation. BLASSO is likewise retrained on each split rather than used as published.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Network Architecture, Training Details, Comparison to Previous Methods

strengths.text: The split rule is designed against the obvious leakage path for mutational data: mutants stay with their wild type, so a sequence one mutation away from a test case cannot be in the training set.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set

strengths.text: Four separate splits are reported rather than one, which makes the sensitivity of the result to the partition visible, and the authors relate the per-split error to how similar the train and test label distributions are.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set; Results

strengths.text: The comparator is retrained rather than quoted: the authors ran the original BLASSO R code on their own splits, and adapted it so that both methods are trained in the same units.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Comparison to Previous Methods

strengths.text: The data sets, the source code and a Colab notebook are published in one repository, which the paper names in its data availability statement.

limitations.text: The data set is small and skewed: 884 sequences from 75 wild types, most absorbing between 500 and 570 nm. The authors name this as the reason results move between splits and say a larger set would be needed for more consistent results.

The splits are not matched on the label distribution, so a split can be much harder than the others. Split 4 is the example the authors give: its test set is mostly red-shifted rhodopsins while the training set is mostly blue-shifted, and it is the worst split for every method in Table 1.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Set; Results

limitations.text: The comparison was built and run by the authors of the method it favours, and the only external comparator is one earlier model.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods and Results, Comparison to Previous Methods

limitations.text: Inputs depend on predicted structures. Each sequence is folded with AlphaFold2 and the authors report a median C-alpha RMSD of 1.08 Angstrom against the sequences with crystal structures, so pocket geometry carries that error; the retinal-containing variant, built by copying a retinal from a homologue, scored worse.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Protein Structure Generation and Representation; Discussion
