profile.summary: LiPP, the Lipid-Protein Poses benchmark, asks a docking or cofolding tool to place a lipid in its binding site on a protein and scores the pose against the crystal structure. The set holds 331 nonredundant buried, or nonannular, lipid-protein complexes filtered out of BioDolphin version 1.1, all X-ray structures better than 2 Angstrom, covering the eight LIPID MAPS lipid classes and a range of protein functions. Within it, the 36 complexes released after 1 October 2021 form a test set that postdates the training or calibration cutoff of every tool the paper evaluates. Success is a lipid pose whose symmetry-corrected all-atom RMSD is below a cutoff, with a stricter criterion that also requires the pose to pass the PoseBusters physical checks. It is the set to use when choosing a tool for lipid-protein modelling, where small-molecule benchmarks do not apply.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, LiPP Benchmark Set; Materials and Methods, Curation and Comparison of Modeled and Native Structures

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a tool can reproduce the pose of a lipid bound inside a protein pocket. The authors restrict the question to nonannular interactions, meaning lipids held in buried or partly buried pockets as biological ligands, and leave out annular lipids that form a nonspecific shell around a membrane protein. Their reason for building the set is that lipid-protein modelling has no benchmark of its own: the available sets, such as the PoseBusters Benchmark and PDBbind, cover drug-like small molecules, and PDBbind's drug-likeness filter excludes many lipids because of their long aliphatic chains. A second question runs through the evaluation: whether the poses a tool produces are physically plausible at all, which is scored separately from how close they are to the crystal pose.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Materials and Methods, Physically Plausibility; Table 1 footnote

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The starting pool is BioDolphin version 1.1, 127,359 PDB entries each holding one lipid-protein pair. The filters follow the PoseBusters Benchmark recipe: keep X-ray structures better than 2 Angstrom; drop entries with unknown atom types or nonstandard residues, lipids that fail RDKit sanitisation, incomplete entries, and lipids covalently bonded to the protein; drop complexes whose PDB ligand report shows stereochemical errors or atomic clashes; require the minimum lipid to protein distance to lie between 0.2 and 5 Angstrom; and drop entries where the lipid sits within 5 Angstrom of a protein symmetry mate. Redundancy is removed by clustering proteins at 90 per cent sequence identity with DIAMOND and keeping one randomly chosen pair per protein cluster and lipid Chemical Component Dictionary code. The remaining entries were curated by hand against the PDB structures and their papers. What is left is 331 pairs, with 235 unique lipids, lipid molecular weights from 88 to 1,229 Da and protein lengths from 107 to 856 residues. The split is by release date: 36 structures released after 1 October 2021 form the test set and the other 295 the precutoff set. Similarity between the two is assessed with ProteinCartography structure clustering and RDKit atom-pair Tanimoto similarity for the lipids.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Benchmark Set and Curation of the LiPP Test Set; Results, LiPP Benchmark Set; repository test_set.csv

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a modelled complex per benchmark entry, and the five tools evaluated are given different inputs by design. The cofolding tools AlphaFold 3, Chai-1 and RoseTTAFold AA get a protein sequence and a lipid identifier, a SMILES string or a CCD code. The docking tools AutoDock Vina and DiffDock-L get the experimental coordinates of protein and lipid and have to place the lipid; Vina is given pocket positions inferred from the experimental complex while DiffDock-L is run without pocket information. All tools are run with default parameters and no post-prediction refinement, and one top pose per complex is kept, chosen by that tool's own score. Cofolded complexes are superimposed on the experimental structure through the protein coordinates before measurement, which is unnecessary for the docking tools because they were given the experimental protein. The lipid pose error is the symmetry-corrected RMSD computed with spyRMSD. Success is the percentage of complexes under a cutoff, reported from 2 to 3 Angstrom, and the stricter criterion also requires the model to pass every PoseBusters category, which the paper calls PB-valid. Success rates are reported with 95 per cent confidence intervals from the exact binomial distribution, and are broken down by lipid molecular weight and lipid class. A separate analysis asks how well each tool's own confidence score predicts its error, using ipTM for AlphaFold 3 and Chai-1, inter-PAE for RoseTTAFold AA, the confidence score for DiffDock-L and the affinity score for AutoDock Vina.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols, Physically Plausibility, Comparison of Modeled and Native Structures, Evaluation of Scoring Power; Table 2 footnote

sections.title: The PoseBusters comparison columns
sections.body: Tables 2 and 3 put two further columns beside the LiPP results: PoseBusters v1 with 428 complexes and PoseBusters v2 with 308. These are protein and small-molecule sets, not lipid data, and the paper states that the values in those columns were taken from the literature rather than measured here. Several cells are empty because a tool has not been evaluated on PoseBusters, and the AlphaFold 3 column carries a footnote that the published rates used a 2019-09-30 training cutoff. They are context for reading the lipid numbers, not part of the LiPP set.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Tables 2 and 3 and their footnotes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The sets and the reproduction code are in the mcshanlab/LiPP_Benchmark repository. The data folder holds the general set, the test set and a small example set as CSV tables of BioDolphin identifiers with metadata, plus PDB files for each complex and for the protein and lipid split apart. To reproduce the published benchmark a user installs whichever of the five tools they want to test, along with OpenStructure and ProteinCartography, records the paths in config.yaml, and downloads the BioDolphin version 1.1 table into the data folder. Each tool has its own folder under scripts/run_tools with a README: for AlphaFold 3 it is three conda environments, a preprocessing script, a run.sh meant to be submitted to a cluster scheduler, a PyMOL superposition step, an OpenStructure scoring step and a summarising script. The analysis folder holds the evaluation, whose compare.py reads one concatenated table of lipid and protein errors for all methods and produces the success rates and figures.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Dataset availability and Guidance for reproducing the publications; config.yaml; scripts/run_tools/AF3/README.md; scripts/analyze/Evaluation/README.md

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Four tables appear in the benchmark's results. The LiPP benchmark set: 331 nonredundant nonannular lipid-protein crystal structures better than 2 Angstrom, with 235 unique lipids, lipid weights from 88 to 1,229 Da and protein lengths from 107 to 856 residues. The LiPP test set: the 36 of those released after 1 October 2021. The precutoff set: the other 295. Beside them, two small-molecule comparison columns taken from the literature, PoseBusters v1 with 428 complexes and PoseBusters v2 with 308. The repository's general_set.csv has 331 data rows and test_set.csv has 36, counted in this pass.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, LiPP Benchmark Set; Tables 2 and 3; repository CSV files

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: A time split, and no training split. The benchmark is evaluation only: the 331 complexes are divided by PDB release date into the 36-complex test set released after 1 October 2021 and the 295-complex precutoff set, because 1 October 2021 is the day after the latest training or calibration cutoff among the five tools evaluated. The paper reports results on the full 331 and on the 36 separately.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Test Set, Precutoff Set

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Success rate, higher is better, under two criteria. The first is the percentage of complexes whose lipid pose has a symmetry-corrected all-atom RMSD below a cutoff, reported from 2 to 3 Angstrom, with 2 Angstrom used in Table 2. The second, in Table 3, additionally requires the model to pass every PoseBusters category, that is to be PB-valid. Success is also broken down by lipid class and molecular weight. Separately, each tool's own confidence score is compared against its RMSD to judge scoring power, and protein structure error is reported as TM-score and RMSD from OpenStructure.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Comparison of Modeled and Native Structures, Evaluation of Scoring Power, Protein Structure Errors; Table 3 title

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five tools, run by the authors: three cofolding tools, AlphaFold 3 version 3.0.0, Chai-1 version 0.2.0 and RoseTTAFold All-Atom at commit 6c85140; one deep learning docking tool, DiffDock-L version 1.1.3; and one physics-based docking tool, AutoDock Vina version 1.2.3. The paper reports AlphaFold 3 as the best on the full set at 76.1 per cent under the 2 Angstrom criterion, falling to 47.2 per cent on the test set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols; Table 2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two. A redundancy filter at the set level: proteins are clustered at 90 per cent sequence identity with DIAMOND and only one pair is kept per cluster and lipid code, so near-identical complexes do not inflate the set. And a time split for training overlap: the 36-complex test set contains only structures released after the latest training or calibration cutoff of the five tools, which the paper lists per tool in Table 1. The authors also compare the test set and the precutoff set for protein structure and lipid chemical similarity rather than assuming the two are alike.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Benchmark Set, Curation of the LiPP Test Set, Protein Similarity, Lipid Similarity

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95 per cent confidence intervals on every success rate, calculated from the exact binomial distribution and printed in brackets beside each value. Sampling inside the tools is fixed rather than repeated: AlphaFold 3 used a single random seed with five diffusion samples, Chai-1 a single seed with five samples, RoseTTAFold AA one structure per sample, DiffDock-L ten poses and AutoDock Vina nine poses with no fixed random seed. One top pose per complex is carried into the scoring.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 2 footnote; Materials and Methods, per-tool protocols

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One experimental lipid-protein complex structure, that is one lipid bound in one protein pocket, identified by a BioDolphin identifier. A model's lipid pose in that complex is what gets scored.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation; README.md: PDB Structures of the LiPP dataset

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated as such. The entries are PDB crystal structures selected for resolution and quality, and the paper characterises them by protein functional class, including enzymes, immunological receptors, membrane proteins, signalling receptors and lipid transport proteins, rather than by species.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, LiPP Benchmark Set

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: X-ray crystallography. Every entry is an X-ray structure at better than 2 Angstrom resolution, and the lipid pose in that structure is the ground truth; entries whose PDB ligand report showed stereochemical errors or atomic clashes were removed. No binding measurement is used as a label.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Benchmark Set

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: It depends on the tool class, and the paper is explicit that the two classes are not given the same information. Cofolding tools receive the protein sequence and a lipid SMILES string or CCD code only. Docking tools receive the experimental protein and lipid coordinates; AutoDock Vina is additionally given a pocket inferred from the experimental complex, DiffDock-L is not. RoseTTAFold AA additionally used multiple sequence alignments of up to 1024 sequences and up to four structural templates under its default configuration.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols; RoseTTAFold AA

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Out of the box, with no fine-tuning. Every tool was run at its released version with default parameters and settings, and no refinement was applied to its output. The authors note that a curated lipid-protein set could be used for fine-tuning docking force fields or cofolding weights, but that is proposed as future use and not done here.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols; Introduction

strengths.text: The time split is tied to documented training cutoffs: Table 1 lists the training or calibration cutoff of each of the five tools, and the test set contains only structures released after the latest of them.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Test Set

strengths.text: Physical plausibility is scored separately from pose accuracy. A pose only counts under the stricter criterion if it passes every PoseBusters category, which stops a numerically close but chemically impossible pose from counting as a success.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Physically Plausibility and Comparison of Modeled and Native Structures

strengths.text: The sets, the per-tool run scripts and the analysis code are published in one repository, with the exact tool versions, commits and default settings written down in the paper.
Every success rate carries a 95 per cent confidence interval, which matters on the 36-complex test set where the intervals are wide.

limitations.text: The unseen-data subset is small. Thirty-six complexes give confidence intervals tens of points wide, so test-set rankings between tools of similar strength are not settled by it.

The two tool classes are not given the same inputs, so the comparison across them is not apples to apples. Docking tools start from the experimental protein and lipid coordinates and AutoDock Vina is also handed a pocket inferred from the experimental complex, while cofolding tools get only a sequence and a lipid identifier. The authors state the two represent distinct modelling regimes rather than directly equivalent methods.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols

limitations.text: Coverage is deliberately narrow. The set keeps only buried, nonannular lipids in high-resolution X-ray structures, so annular lipids are excluded by design and large or flexible classes, glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids among them, are underrepresented because quality filtering removes them. The authors say LiPP prioritises structural quality over full coverage and that results should be read in that light.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, LiPP Benchmark Set

limitations.text: Reproducing the benchmark needs the BioDolphin version 1.1 table downloaded from a separate project site, the five prediction tools installed locally, AlphaFold 3 parameters obtained from Google DeepMind for non-commercial use, and a cluster scheduler for the per-tool run scripts. No licence is stated for the LiPP repository in the metadata read here.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, AlphaFold 3; README.md: Prerequisites; scripts/run_tools/AF3/README.md

prerequisites: Whichever of the five tools is being tested, installed locally: AlphaFold 3, Chai-1, DiffDock-L, AutoDock Vina or RoseTTAFold All-Atom, plus OpenStructure and ProteinCartography for the analyses.
AlphaFold 3 model parameters, which the paper states were provided by Google DeepMind for non-commercial use.
BioDolphin_vr1.1.csv, downloaded from the BioDolphin project download page and placed in the data folder.
A cluster scheduler: the per-tool run scripts are meant to be submitted through Slurm or an equivalent.
Conda, for the environment files in each tool's environments folder.
No licence is stated for this repository in the metadata read here, so the terms of reuse are unknown.

steps.title: Get the benchmark and the code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/mcshanlab/LiPP_Benchmark
cd LiPP_Benchmark
git checkout --detach 59400a542c8cc4379fd636405a69cbd4b438b660
steps.explanation: The repository the paper names holds both the sets and the reproduction scripts. The checkout line was added here to pin the commit these files were read at.

steps.title: Point the configuration at the installed tools
steps.explanation: Step 2 of the README's prerequisites. config.yaml is where the conda environment directory and the paths to AlphaFold 3, its image, database and parameters, AutoDock Vina and RoseTTAFold All-Atom are set, along with the LiPP CSV and structure paths. The editor command is written here; the README states the requirement, not a command.

steps.title: Add the BioDolphin table
steps.explanation: Step 3 of the README's prerequisites, which asks for the BioDolphin version 1.1 table from the project download page to be placed under the data folder. The copy command is written here from that instruction.

steps.title: Run one tool over the set, here AlphaFold 3
steps.shell:
cd scripts/run_tools/AF3
conda env create -f environments/af3_env.yml
conda env create -f environments/af3_pymol_env.yml
conda env create -f environments/af3_spy_env.yml
conda activate af3
python preprocess.py
./run.sh
conda activate af3_pymol
python run_pymol.py
./run_opensturcture.sh
conda activate af3_spy
python summarize.py
steps.explanation: The six steps of the AlphaFold 3 README in order: create the three conda environments, prepare the inputs, submit the run, superimpose the predicted proteins with PyMOL, score the protein predictions with OpenStructure, then summarise. The run.sh step is meant to go through a cluster scheduler, so it is submitted rather than run directly on a workstation. The script name run_opensturcture.sh is spelled as the repository spells it.

steps.title: Compute the success rates
steps.explanation: The evaluation step. Its README states that compare.py expects a unique_rmsd.csv in the same directory holding the concatenated lipid and protein errors for all methods, and that running it reproduces the published comparison of AlphaFold 3, Chai-1, AutoDock Vina, RoseTTAFold AA and DiffDock-L. The directory change is written here to reach the folder.

outputs: Per-complex lipid and protein errors from the per-tool summarise step, and from compare.py the success rates, visualisations and a results report comparing the five methods, as its README describes them.
limitations: These commands were read from the paper and the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The run step for each tool is written for a cluster scheduler, and the tools themselves have to be installed and licensed separately.
PoseBusters validity and the Tanimoto and ProteinCartography similarity analyses live in other folders under scripts/analyze that were not opened here.

compare.py expects unique_rmsd.csv in its own directory and also reads ../PDB_Classifications/pdb_metadata.csv, and it writes unique_new_rmsd.csv for the subset released after the cutoff date; the saved files do not name any other input table.

lit-structure-20261011-lipp-benchmark-li.notes: Numbers worth a human look. The abstract of the paper says LiPP is 'a curated data set of 311 nonredundant nonannular lipid-protein complex structures', while the Materials and Methods ('contains 331 lipid-protein pairs'), the Results, the headers of Tables 2 and 3 (N = 331) and the arithmetic 36 plus 295 all say 331. The repository's general_set.csv has 331 data rows, counted in this pass, and its README describes a pdb_structures_complex folder of native complex structures without giving a count, so 331 is used throughout this page and the abstract's 311 looks like an error in the source. The PoseBusters v1 and v2 columns are small-molecule results taken from other publications, not lipid data measured here; they are kept as structured entries because the store holds protocols for them, with their own set sizes of 428 and 308 and a note in the dataset field. Table 3 leaves the PoseBusters v1 column empty for every tool and prints one PoseBusters v2 value, 58 per cent for AutoDock Vina, with the other four tools shown as not evaluated. No licence is stated for the mcshanlab/LiPP_Benchmark repository in the GitHub metadata read here, so the data and code licence fields are null; the paper itself is CC BY 4.0. The record's existing source is the Europe PMC fullTextXML address, which has been failing with HTTP 500 for this run; the same full text was taken from NCBI E-utilities.

profile.summary: This is a runtime measurement published with TorchCraft, not a scored benchmark of design quality. It reports how long one TorchCraft design takes at sequence lengths of 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 residues, on an Ascend 910B NPU with 64 GB with and without the fused attention operator, and on an A100 GPU with 80 GB with and without cuequivariance kernels. Runtime is given in minutes per design, obtained by halving the wall-clock time of a run at batch size 2, and the GPU numbers are the mean of three independent runs. Twenty cells are printed in Supplementary Table S9. Anyone planning capacity for a design campaign can use it to see how the cost scales with length and what the two optional acceleration paths are worth.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Supplementary Table S9; Appendix A.3.4 and A.3.5

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Wall-clock time per design, as a function of sequence length and of two optional kernel paths. The purpose is stated in the implementation appendix: TorchCraft optimises sequence logits through a frozen all-atom predictor, which is memory and compute heavy, and the authors describe the optimisations they applied, including a fused attention operator on the Ascend NPU and optional cuequivariance equivariant kernels on the GPU. Table S9 is where those optimisations are quantified. Nothing in this panel scores the designs themselves: it is a timing table.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.3.4 and A.3.5; Supplementary Table S9

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: There is no dataset and no target panel. The table has five length columns, 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 amino acids, and four rows: NPU with fused attention, NPU without it, GPU with cuequivariance and GPU without it. The NPU rows are an Ascend 910B with 64 GB, the GPU rows an A100 with 80 GB. Batch size 2 is described as the recommended setting, and a cell's value is the total wall-clock time of a batch-size-2 run divided by 2. One cell is an exception: NPU without fused attention at 500 residues was run at batch size 1 because batch size 2 ran out of memory. The design task behind the timings is not stated anywhere in the table or its caption; only the sequence lengths are given.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Supplementary Table S9 and its caption and footnote

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The quantity reported is minutes per design, and lower is better. It is derived, not timed directly per design: a batch of two designs is run and the total wall-clock time is divided by two. On the GPU each configuration was run three times and the mean is printed; the caption does not say the NPU rows were repeated. No spread, standard deviation or interval is given for any cell. There is no submission process, no scoring criterion and no comparison with another method's runtime: the four rows are four configurations of the same implementation on two hardware platforms. The authors summarise the effect qualitatively, saying fused attention reduced runtime at several of the larger sequence settings and that its effect depended on length and batch size.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Supplementary Table S9 caption; Appendix A.3.4

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: No timing harness is published, but the design code the timings were taken from is. The TorchX repository the paper names holds the GPU tree on its main branch and an Ascend NPU tree on a separate branch, which is the division the table's two platforms follow. A user installs the base torchx environment first, then runs one of the TorchCraft task scripts for monomer, VHH or minibinder design and times it. The cuequivariance arm of the table corresponds to an optional install and a configuration change the README describes: install the pinned CUDA 12 requirements file, then set the triangle multiplicative and triangle attention options to cuequivariance in the TorchCraft base configuration, where the default is torch. The NPU fused attention arm belongs to the NPU branch, which the README lists as carrying the optional CANN fused attention extra.

Conda or a virtual environment for the torchx base environment, which compiles C++ extensions and builds the CCD chemical data.

torchcraft-20261115-benchmark-runtime.notes: This record is a timing table, not a scored benchmark: all twenty cells come from Supplementary Table S9 of arXiv:2609.19770v1. The structured sizes are null on purpose. A cell is not a count of examples but a wall-clock timing, taken from a batch-size-2 run and halved, with the GPU cells averaged over three runs; the 500 aa cell of the NPU row without fused attention is the one exception, run at batch size 1 after batch size 2 ran out of memory, and the store should not treat its value as comparable with the rest of that row. The paper names no licence for itself, so the paper source carries none and its bytes are not stored; the code repository is Apache-2.0, which both its README and its LICENSE file state. The record's second existing source, the TorchX project site at torchx-cpl.github.io, was not fetched in this pass. Four other records in this batch quote the same paper.

profile.summary: This is the evaluation framework published with MochiBind, a study of whether antibody-antigen affinity predictors generalise to antigens they have never seen. The data are the four antigen systems of the AlphaBind dataset, PP489, PEM, VHH72 and TRA, each a large pool of antibody variants with measured affinities. The task is posed pairwise: given two antibodies against the same antigen, say which binds more strongly. Antigens are rotated so that each in turn is the held-out test antigen while two train and one validates, which means the test antigen is absent from training entirely. Scoring is pairwise accuracy over 200,000 sampled test pairs per antigen, plus retrieval accuracy and precision at K after a global ranking is derived with TrueSkill. Anyone comparing sequence-based and structure-based affinity predictors for candidate ranking can use it as a cross-antigen generalisation test.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup; Table 2

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a predictor can rank antibodies against an antigen it was never trained on. The authors' stated reason for building the framework is that studies in this area differ in dataset curation, splitting and metrics, so models cannot be compared, and that most published models are evaluated in-sample. Two things are measured. Pairwise accuracy asks whether the stronger of two antibodies is identified correctly. Retrieval accuracy and precision at K ask whether the strong binders can be pulled out of a large pool, which is what an in silico screening campaign actually needs. The authors argue that ranking and retrieval are more robust than absolute regression when affinity measurements are noisy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, Retrieval performance and Pairwise accuracy

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The data come from the AlphaBind dataset, which holds four antigen systems: AAB-PP489, a humanoid scFv against human TIGIT; Pembrolizumab-scFv against PD-1; VHH72, a camelid single-chain antibody against the SARS-CoV-1 RBD with cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2; and Trastuzumab-scFv against human HER2. The paper states that each system contains approximately 30,000 antibody variants generated and validated with AlphaSeq. For this benchmark the pools are cut down by stratified sampling to keep the affinity distribution: 5,000 antibodies are drawn from the fine-tuning set and 5,000 from the evaluation set for PP489, PEM and VHH72, giving 10,000 variants each, while 5,000 are drawn for TRA. The four antigens have almost no sequence similarity to one another: Needleman-Wunsch global alignment with BLOSUM62 gives off-diagonal normalised scores between minus 0.053 and 0.034. Pairs are then sampled, 200,000 per antigen, and the training pairs are restricted to those whose relative affinity difference exceeds 10 per cent while the test pairs carry no such threshold. The published sampling script differs from the paper here: as shipped it samples up to 500,000 pairs per antigen with the threshold set to 0 and writes sampled_pairs_500k_0th.pkl, so the released sampler is not the configuration the paper describes, and the 10 per cent value survives in it only as a function default. The script also adds a condition the paper does not mention: a pair is only eligible if both antibody sequences have the same length.
sections.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing and Pairwise data generation; Introduction; data/sample_alphabind_pairs.py

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model is given two antibodies against the same antigen and must say which binds more strongly. The split is a rotation over antigens: in each configuration two antigens supply 400,000 training pairs, one supplies 200,000 validation pairs used to pick the checkpoint, and the fourth supplies 200,000 test pairs with no affinity-difference threshold, and the rotation is repeated so that every antigen is the test antigen once. Pairwise accuracy is the share of test pairs ordered correctly, and Table 2 reports it per held-out antigen for each method. Significance against each baseline is tested with a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test on the 200,000 test pairs, with all p values below 0.0001. For retrieval, pairwise predictions are turned into a global ranking with the TrueSkill algorithm, then retrieval accuracy and retrieval precision at K are computed; in the precision figure an antibody with log Kd below 2, Kd in nanomolar, counts as a good binder. Complex-wise baselines are handled on their own terms: Boltz-2 and GeoDock supply structure-derived confidence scores used as proxies rather than trained affinity predictions, and Graphinity is reported after fine-tuning on the training split because the published model, trained on single-point mutations, did not perform well on this data.
sections.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup and Pairwise setup; Results; Table 2 and Figure 2 captions

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The code is published as a reproducibility release. The repository holds MochiBind checkpoints for each of the four antigen systems, the sampled AlphaBind CSV files and the preprocessed pair pickles, the model and training code, and notebooks for pairwise accuracy and for the Graphinity, GeoDock and Boltz-2 retrieval comparisons. The README gives a conda environment and a requirements install, an embedding generation step and a training entry point at model_src/main_mean.py, and notes that full training expects precomputed ESM mean embeddings in a data_processed_esm_mean directory. The release terms matter: the repository is CC BY-NC 4.0 and the README states it is a non-commercial research release, published for academic reproducibility, with pull requests not accepted so that the code stays as it was used in the paper. The underlying AlphaBind data are MIT licensed, which the README states and links.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Release statement, Repository structure, Directory description, Installation and First Run, License

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One dataset, AlphaBind, with four antigen systems: PP489, PEM, VHH72 and TRA. The paper states each system holds approximately 30,000 antibody variants measured with AlphaSeq. The benchmark uses stratified subsamples of those pools: 10,000 variants each for PP489, PEM and VHH72, made of 5,000 from the fine-tuning set and 5,000 from the evaluation set, and 5,000 for TRA. From those pools 200,000 pairs are sampled per antigen.
facts.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing and Pairwise data generation

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: A cross-antigen rotation with no antigen overlap. In each configuration two antigens give 400,000 training pairs, one gives 200,000 validation pairs for checkpoint selection, and one gives 200,000 test pairs; the rotation repeats so each of the four antigens is the held-out test antigen once. Training and validation pairs are restricted to relative affinity differences above 10 per cent; test pairs have no threshold, so they include near-ties.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Retrieval performance; STAR Methods, Pairwise data generation and Cross-antigen evaluation setup

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Pairwise accuracy is the headline for the comparison in Table 2: the percentage of test pairs in which the stronger binder is identified correctly, higher is better, with significance against each baseline from a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test. Two retrieval metrics complement it, both higher is better: retrieval accuracy, the share of the K highest-ranked candidates that are among the true top binders, and retrieval precision, the share of good binders captured among the recommendations relative to the good binders available. The authors argue for ranking and retrieval over absolute regression metrics such as mean absolute error or correlation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Retrieval performance and Pairwise accuracy; Introduction

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three: Graphinity, an equivariant graph neural network on structural inputs, reported after fine-tuning on the training split because the released model, trained on single-point mutations, did not perform well here; and two structure-derived proxy scorers, Boltz-2, used through its ipLDDT score, and GeoDock. MochiBind, the authors' own sequence-only pairwise model built on ESM-2 embeddings, is the method under test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results; Table 2; STAR Methods, Key resources table

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split itself is the control, and it is the point of the benchmark: the training, validation and test sets cover distinct antigen systems with no overlap, so the test antigen is unseen. Two further things support it. The four antigens have near-zero global sequence similarity to one another, measured by Needleman-Wunsch alignment with BLOSUM62 and normalised, between minus 0.053 and 0.034. And within an antigen the variants come from one seed framework with varied multi-point mutations, which the authors say forces models to learn binding determinants rather than memorising identities. Nothing is said about overlap between the AlphaBind antibodies and the training data of the pretrained ESM-2 model or of the structure-based baselines.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, Retrieval performance

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Significance testing rather than replicates. Each baseline is compared with MochiBind by a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test on the 200,000 test pairs, with all p values below 0.0001 and the chi-squared statistics in Table S1. The paper reports no repeated training runs, seeds or confidence intervals on the accuracies. A sensitivity analysis is given instead: accuracy is stratified by the relative affinity gap within a pair, and it rises as the gap widens, with a large share of test pairs falling in the 0 to 10 per cent band that training excludes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Pairwise accuracy; Figure 5 caption

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A pair of antibody variants against the same antigen, with the measured affinities of both. For the complex-wise baselines the scored unit is one antibody-antigen complex, which is then used to order the pair, and for retrieval the unit is one antibody in a ranked pool.
facts.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Pairwise setup

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human targets with antibodies of mixed origin. The four antigen systems are human TIGIT, human PD-1, human HER2 and the receptor binding domain of SARS-CoV-1 with cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2. The antibody frameworks include a humanoid scFv, two humanised mouse antibodies formatted as scFv, and a camelid single-chain antibody.
facts.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: AlphaSeq affinity measurements. The paper states that each antigen system's approximately 30,000 variants were generated and validated using AlphaSeq, and the labels are measured binding affinities reported as log Kd. The authors treat those labels as noisy, which is their stated reason for a pairwise rather than a regression formulation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing; Results

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Either sequence or structure, which is the comparison the benchmark exists to make. MochiBind reads the antibody and antigen sequences only, through a pretrained protein language model; Graphinity reads structural graphs; Boltz-2 and GeoDock take complexes and return interface confidence scores. The published sampling code adds one restriction on the pairs themselves: both antibody sequences in a pair must be of the same length.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; STAR Methods, Pairwise setup; data/sample_alphabind_pairs.py

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Supervised training on the two training antigens for the pairwise models, and zero-shot use for the proxy scorers. MochiBind is trained on the 400,000 training pairs with the validation antigen used to select a checkpoint. Graphinity is fine-tuned on the same training split, and the paper reports its accuracy before and after fine-tuning in a supplementary table. Boltz-2 and GeoDock are used as published, supplying structure-derived confidence scores with no affinity training.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Retrieval performance; STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup

strengths.text: The split answers the question the paper poses: every antigen is held out in turn and the test antigen appears in neither training nor validation, so the reported accuracy is a cross-antigen number rather than an in-sample one.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup

strengths.text: Training and test pairs are filtered differently on purpose. Training keeps only pairs whose affinities differ by more than 10 per cent, while test pairs are unfiltered, so the evaluation includes the near-ties that a real screen has to cope with.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Pairwise data generation

strengths.text: Differences between methods are tested rather than asserted, with a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test on the 200,000 test pairs for each baseline comparison and the statistics reported in a supplementary table.

Per-antigen heterogeneity is reported instead of being averaged away: the affinity distributions differ markedly between antigens, and the authors show that retrieval precision depends on that composition.

limitations.text: Four antigens is a narrow base for a generalisation claim. Each rotation has two training antigens, one validation antigen and one test antigen, so a reported accuracy rests on a single held-out system and the authors themselves name dataset scarcity as the limiting factor.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup; Limitations of the study

limitations.text: The benchmark was built and run by the authors of the method it favours, MochiBind, and the structure-based comparators are not matched to it: Boltz-2 and GeoDock supply confidence scores that were never trained to predict affinity, and Graphinity had to be fine-tuned before it performed.

Pairs are not drawn from the whole pool. The published sampling script only forms a pair when both antibody sequences have the same length, which is a restriction the paper does not state, so the test pairs do not cover insertion or deletion variants.

The code release is non-commercial and frozen. The repository is CC BY-NC 4.0, the README describes it as a non-commercial research release for academic reproducibility, and pull requests are not accepted so that the code stays exactly as used in the paper.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Release statement, License, Pull requests; LICENSE

lit-interactions-20261011-mochibind-benc.notes: Two numbers in the source disagree and a reviewer should know which this page uses. The introduction and the STAR Methods say each AlphaBind antigen system holds approximately 30,000 antibody variants, while the results section says each unique antigen is associated with 5,000 to 10,000 variants. The second figure matches what the benchmark uses: stratified subsamples of 10,000 variants for PP489, PEM and VHH72 and 5,000 for TRA. The structured size of 200,000 is neither of those: it is the number of sampled antibody pairs in the held-out test set for that antigen, which is the set Table 2's accuracy is computed on, and the test pairs carry no affinity-difference threshold. The published pair sampling script also requires both antibodies in a pair to have the same sequence length, a restriction the paper does not state. Retrieval accuracy and precision appear only in figures, so only the pairwise accuracies are available as numbers. The paper is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and the code repository CC BY-NC 4.0, so no source bytes are stored; the AlphaBind data the code ships are MIT, which the README states and links.

profile.summary: This is the frozen benchmark packet published with RFD4-Proteina on Hugging Face: a set of result tables, not a runnable suite. It scores design methods on four target sets, 24 protein-binding targets, 77 small-molecule targets, 37 Atomic Motif Enzyme tasks and 3 DNA-binding targets, each model, protocol and target having 200 original attempts. Every attempt is judged by one common AlphaFold 3 evaluation with a pass criterion written per benchmark, and the headline number is efficiency: the mean over targets of structurally distinct passers per unit of GPU time, counting both generation and the AlphaFold 3 evaluation. The packet publishes a summary table of 52 rows, a per-target source table, a methods supplement with the criteria and timing rules, and a provenance file with digests. A reader comparing design methods on cost as well as hit rate can use it; it reports computational passers, which the packet says do not establish experimental activity.
profile.summary_source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing, Common AF3 scoring; provenance.json; README.md: Measured design efficiency

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Not just whether a design method succeeds, but what each success costs. Two things are reported for every model, protocol and target: a rate, which is the share of 200 original attempts that pass the common AlphaFold 3 criterion, and an efficiency, which divides structurally distinct passers by the GPU time spent generating them plus the GPU time of the shared evaluation. The packet is explicit about what a pass is not: passers are computational, structural clusters are algorithmic rather than experimentally distinct proteins, and the whole release reuses existing evaluation outputs rather than running anything new.
sections.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing, Common AF3 scoring; README.md: Measured design efficiency

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Four target sets and a fixed number of attempts, with no train or test split: the sets are evaluation panels. The counts are printed in the criteria table, 24 protein-protein interface targets, 77 small-molecule targets, 37 Atomic Motif Enzyme targets and 3 DNA targets, and each model, protocol and target combination has 200 original attempts including native failures and unmatched required motifs, with no replacement of rejected originals. What goes into the release is a frozen selection rather than everything that was ever run: the cohorts come from an evidence freeze file, antibody, HalluDesign, full-pipeline BindCraft and Genie3 search arms are excluded, and the provenance file describes the scope as frozen project benchmark runs rather than a new evaluation of every model revision. Each model's recipe, including steps, checkpoints, sequence designers and input handling, is written out in a table in the methods supplement, which also says that the executed receipts rather than the current upstream README identify what each cohort actually ran.
sections.source_locator: METHODS.md: Supplement methods, Common accounting and timing, Model recipes and adaptations, Common AF3 scoring; provenance.json

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: One shared AlphaFold 3 evaluation decides every pass, with a criterion written per benchmark. Protein binders need binder pTM at least 80 on the native 0 to 100 scale, a minimum interface PAE of at most 1.5 Angstrom and a target-backbone-aligned binder backbone RMSD of at most 2.5 Angstrom, with CA-only RMSD for Genie3, and a target mutation at a hotspot or within 5 Angstrom of binder heavy atoms fails. Small-molecule binders need interface PAE at most 1.5 Angstrom, chain-of-interest ipTM at least 80 out of 100, protein backbone RMSD at most 1.5 Angstrom and ligand RMSD at most 5 Angstrom after protein-backbone alignment; a second, older DISCO criterion on the same 77 targets uses a 2 Angstrom backbone RMSD and a 2 Angstrom ligand centroid displacement with no PAE or ipTM cutoff, and the packet notes the two are not nested. Atomic Motif Enzyme tasks need backbone RMSD at most 2 Angstrom, motif all-atom RMSD at most 1.5 Angstrom and interface PAE below 1.5 Angstrom. DNA targets need interface PAE at most 1.5 Angstrom and a DNA-aligned binder backbone RMSD at most 8 Angstrom. From those verdicts, the ordinary rate is passing originals over 200 and the clustered rate is distinct clusters among passing originals over 200, with clusters computed inside each model, protocol and target by Foldseek at a TM threshold of 0.5 and never pooled. Efficiency is the arithmetic mean across targets of successes divided by generation plus AlphaFold 3 GPU seconds, which the provenance file expresses per GPU-hour and the methods supplement also reports in per-10-GPU-minute units; failed originals and the time they consumed stay in the denominator.
sections.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common AF3 scoring; provenance.json

sections.title: How the timings were taken
sections.body: The timing rules matter as much as the criteria, because efficiency is half the result. Generation time is the complete stored warm generation cost, including required sequence design and intrinsic folding or search, excluding setup, loading, warmup and compilation where those were measured separately, and it is not a diffusion-only timer. Batched costs are amortised across the batch, and the packet says batch shares are not individually measured latency and that the measured batch size is not a claim about maximal throughput. Component columns for MPNN and native folding are already inside the generation figure and must not be added again; a zero means the component did not run or used no GPU and a blank means it was not separately measured. Three exceptions are named rather than hidden: ODesign keeps an approved original-generation timing proxy, Complexa's fixed-small-molecule costs are batched remeasurements rather than batch-1 wall time, and the historical RFD4 protein-binding all-atom arm uses an approved backbone timing proxy and has no measured AlphaFold 3 cost. A configuration with a missing AlphaFold 3 cost drops out of inclusive efficiency comparisons but keeps its successes in rate comparisons.
sections.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing

sections.title: What the tables contain
sections.body: The packet is four files. summary.csv holds one row per panel, model, protocol and dataset, with columns for the criterion, the pass and clustered percentages, successes and unique clusters per 10 GPU-minutes, the number of targets, the number of attempts and a timing note; counting its rows in this pass gives 52, the number the provenance file also states, alongside 2,488 per-target criterion rows in the companion source data. provenance.json records the source release label, the paper commit and path, the metric definition and the SHA-256 digests of the two CSV files. METHODS.md carries the criteria, the timing rules and the per-model recipes. The model card's own efficiency table prints a four-row headline comparison in per-GPU-hour units, with a warning above it that the numbers were measured on the previous release pair in the October 9 2026 frozen benchmark, predate the current checkpoints and have not been remeasured.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Four target sets, with the counts printed in the criteria table: 24 protein-protein interface targets, 77 small-molecule targets, 37 Atomic Motif Enzyme targets and 3 DNA targets. The small-molecule set is scored twice, under the current sm_binder criterion and under the original DISCO criterion, on the same 77 targets. Each model, protocol and target has 200 original attempts, so a panel's attempt count in summary.csv is 200 times its targets, for example 7,400 for the 37 AME targets.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Inapplicable. These are evaluation-only target sets with no train, validation or test partition. The divisions that exist are by panel, by protocol, one-shot or native pipeline, and by conditioning mode, for example fixed and unfixed DNA inputs.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three, all higher is better. The ordinary rate is passing originals over 200. The clustered rate is distinct clusters among passing originals over 200, with clusters computed within each model, protocol and target using Foldseek at TM threshold 0.5, alignment type 1 and minimum sequence identity 0, never pooled across targets or models. Efficiency, the headline, is the arithmetic mean across targets of successes divided by generation plus AlphaFold 3 GPU time; the provenance file writes it per GPU-hour and summary.csv carries it in per-10-GPU-minute columns for both successes and unique clusters.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Thirteen other design methods, each with its executed recipe written out in the methods supplement: RFdiffusion3, BoltzGen, Proteina-Complexa, DISCO, Genie3, BindCraft and BindCraft2 as single-backbone runs, Protein-Hunter, ESMFold2 inversion, RFdiffusion, RFdiffusion2, ODesign and AlphaProtein-novo. RFD4-Proteina itself appears in several arms, with low, medium and high thinking schedules and a search pipeline. The model card's headline table names the best comparator per benchmark: Proteina-Complexa for protein binders, BoltzGen for small molecules, AlphaProtein-novo Codesign for Atomic Motif Enzyme and BoltzGen with fixed DNA for DNA binders.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None in the train and test sense, because the packet evaluates released models on fixed target sets and trains nothing. Two things stand in its place. The evaluation is common: every arm is judged by the same reused AlphaFold 3 outputs and the same criterion, and no arm may select its outputs using that evaluation. And the clustering that produces the distinct-passer counts is kept inside each model, protocol and target so that clusters are not pooled between arms.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None reported. The packet prints no confidence intervals, standard errors or seed repeats; its sample is the fixed 200 original attempts per model, protocol and target, and the efficiency figure is an arithmetic mean across targets rather than a pooled total. For the DNA panel that mean is over three targets. The packet instead documents the conditions that make rows unequal: timing exceptions, differing conditioning between arms, and the caution that the conditioning panels show observed differences rather than isolated causal effects.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One original design attempt against one target, under one model and protocol. Attempts are counted whether or not they produced a usable output, since native failures and unmatched required motifs are included and rejected originals are not replaced. Results are aggregated to one row per panel, model, protocol and dataset in summary.csv.

facts.value: Not stated. The packet names its targets by panel and dataset label, such as the Atomic Motif Enzyme set from M-CSA and the protein, small-molecule and DNA target sets, and gives no species for them in the files read here.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. Every criterion is computational and is defined by the packet itself, from reused AlphaFold 3 outputs. The model card states plainly that computational passers do not establish experimental activity, and the methods supplement that structural clusters are algorithmic, not experimental successes.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Whatever each method's native conditioning takes, and this differs between arms by design, which is why the packet warns about it. Protein targets are templated from propagated coordinate-conditioning information using stored coordinates, DNA alignment includes the target DNA in both conditioning modes, and the datasets column separates fixed from unfixed ligand and DNA inputs and all-atom from backbone protein conditioning. Per-model input handling, down to hotspot projection and bond-type treatment, is listed in the recipe table.

strengths.text: The accounting rules are written down in unusual detail: what generation time includes and excludes, that component columns are already inside it, what a zero and a blank mean, and that batch shares are amortised rather than measured latencies.

The pass criteria are explicit numerical thresholds per benchmark, and where two criteria exist for the same 77 small-molecule targets the packet states that they are not nested and keeps their verdicts separate.

profile.summary: This is the in silico ligand-conditioned pocket design comparison published with TorchCraft. Ten chemically diverse small molecules, ALE, ATP, CHD, CMP, DLU, FAD, IAI, OQO, SAM and TRP, each serve as the ligand a design must build a pocket for. For each method and each ligand 500 designs are generated under that method's own default settings, and the two methods compared are BoltzDesign and TorchCraft. The paper states the 160-residue length and the absence of a supplied native scaffold for the TorchCraft designs. The designs are assessed in two ways: score distributions from AutoDock Vina and affinity predictions from Boltz-2, printed in Figure 5c and 5d, and separately a TorchScore pass rate for TorchCraft, where a design passes when its pLDDT exceeds 70 and its ipTM exceeds 0.7. Nothing here is measured experimentally.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 2.5 and Figures 5c and 5d; Appendix A.4.3.4; Supplementary Figures S8 and S9

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a design method can produce a protein that forms a plausible pocket around a specified small molecule, across a chemically varied panel. The ligands span nucleotides, cofactors, metabolites and drug-like compounds, so the panel also asks how the answer changes with ligand chemistry; the paper reports that score distributions varied across ligands and methods. Three different computational views are used rather than one: a physics-based docking score, a learned affinity prediction, and a predictor confidence pass rate.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.5; Supplementary Figures S8 and S9 captions

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: No dataset and no split. The panel is the ten ligands named in Supplementary Figure S8, chosen for chemical diversity. For each method and each ligand, 500 designs are generated with that method's default settings. For TorchCraft the paper adds that the designs are 160-residue proteins generated without a supplied native scaffold; Appendix A.4.3.4, which covers both methods, gives neither a length nor a scaffold condition for BoltzDesign. Raw outputs are evaluated without post hoc sequence redesign or score-based preselection. The design procedure that produced them is described in the appendix as a staged schedule in which the ligand is added and the interface objective is weighted up gradually, separating fold formation from pocket optimisation, but the benchmark itself is defined by the ligand panel, the design count and the three scores.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.5; Appendix A.1.3 and A.4.3.4; Supplementary Figure S8 caption

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Two methods are compared, BoltzDesign and TorchCraft, and both are evaluated without sequence redesign in the arms that are compared directly. The score distributions of the resulting designs are assessed with AutoDock Vina and Boltz-2 and shown in Figures 5c and 5d. For TorchCraft alone, a TorchScore pass rate is also reported in Supplementary Figure S9: a design passes when TorchScore pLDDT exceeds 70 and TorchScore ipTM exceeds 0.7. A further TorchCraft variant is reported separately, in which ligand-interface residues are fixed, all other positions are redesigned eight times with LigandMPNN, the redesigned sequences are refolded with TorchFold, the structure with the highest pTM is kept, and that is then scored with AutoDock Vina and Boltz-2.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.3.4; Section 2.5; Supplementary Figure S9 caption

sections.title: What TorchScore is
sections.body: The scorer every pass rate in this panel depends on is worth stating plainly, because it is not an independent evaluator. TorchScore is a score-only loading of the same TorchFold implementation used for design: given input coordinates it skips the diffusion structure module and runs the confidence pathway, returning pLDDT, pTM and ipTM. No separate scoring network is trained, and in this study it used the pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, the same checkpoint the designs were optimised against. Sequences rebuilt with FlowPacker are scored from those coordinates and are not refolded from sequence.

profile.summary: This is the in silico cyclic peptide design comparison published with TorchCraft. Eight target systems, listed with PDB entries, crops, hotspots and a peptide length range of 12 to 18 residues in Supplementary Table S6, are designed against by BoltzGen, RFpeptides and TorchCraft, with 100 designs per method per target in the head-to-tail cyclisation setting; TorchCraft is also run in a disulfide-linked setting. A design passes only if its predicted structure forms the intended cycle without chain breaks and its TorchScore pLDDT exceeds 70 and ipTM exceeds 0.5. Figure 4c prints the pass rates per target. The question it answers is which design method produces cyclic peptides that satisfy both the cyclisation geometry and a confidence threshold.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 2.4 and Figure 4c; Appendix A.4.3.3; Supplementary Table S6

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things at once, which is what makes this panel different from the others: whether the predicted peptide is actually cyclic and intact, and whether the predictor is confident about the complex. The authors evaluate two cyclisation parameterisations, head-to-tail, which uses cyclic relative positional encoding so the termini are adjacent in sequence space, and disulfide-linked, which keeps linear encoding and fixes the two cysteine positions that define the linkage. Predicted structures are classified by whether they satisfy the intended cyclisation and the backbone-integrity criteria, with the breakdown of cyclised, intact but not cyclised and backbone-broken predictions reported in a supplementary figure.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.4; Supplementary Figure S6 caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: A target panel, not a dataset, and no split. Supplementary Table S6 lists eight target systems with a PDB entry, the target chains and residue crop, hotspot residues and a peptide length of 12 to 18 residues for each: MDM2, MCL-1, GABARAP, PD-L1, KEAP1, RagA:RagC, IL-23R and albumin, counted from its rows. In the head-to-tail benchmark each method generates 100 designs per target with its default settings. TorchCraft is additionally evaluated in the disulfide-linked setting, where all positions except the two cysteines may be redesigned in the polished variant.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.3.3; Supplementary Table S6

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: For BoltzGen and RFpeptides the full peptide sequence of each generated structure is redesigned eight times with ProteinMPNN without fixing residues, each redesign is rebuilt with FlowPacker and scored with TorchScore, and the redesign with the highest pLDDT plus 100 times ipTM becomes that original design's score. TorchCraft head-to-tail outputs are scored raw and, optionally, after redesigning all peptide positions eight times with the same rebuild and selection procedure. In the disulfide-linked setting raw outputs are scored directly, or all positions except the two cysteines are redesigned eight times and then rebuilt and selected in the same way. The pass criterion has three parts that must all hold: the intended cycle must be formed, the backbone must have no chain breaks, and TorchScore pLDDT must exceed 70 with ipTM above 0.5. Rosetta interface scores for the same panel are reported separately as an orthogonal assessment.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.3.3; Supplementary Figure S7 caption

profile.summary: This is the in silico minibinder comparison published with TorchCraft. Twelve protein targets, each with a fixed crop and length-specific hotspot residues listed in Supplementary Table S4, are given to three design methods, TorchCraft, BoltzGen and RFdiffusion, at binder lengths of 75, 120, 160 and 200 residues, with 100 designs per method per length per target. Every design ends up scored by TorchScore, a score-only loading of the same AlphaFold 3 weights TorchCraft designs against, and counts as a pass when both its pTM and its ipTM exceed 0.7. Figure 2f prints the resulting pass rates aggregated over the four lengths. It is a comparison of computational pass rates between design methods on one target panel, not a measurement of binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 2.2 and Figure 2f; Appendix A.4.3.1; Supplementary Table S4

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a design method produces minibinders that a structure predictor is confident about, across a spread of targets and binder lengths. The quantity is a pass rate: the share of a method's designs for a target that clear a confidence threshold. The authors are explicit that this is predictor-derived rather than experimental, and they add Rosetta interface-score distributions in a supplementary figure for that reason. The length sweep is part of the question: pass rates are reported per target and per binder length before being aggregated, and the paper says they varied by both.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.2; Figure 2f caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: There is no dataset to download and no split. The panel is twelve target proteins, each listed in Supplementary Table S4 with a PDB entry, the target chain and residue crop used, and hotspot residues given separately for the 75, 120 and 160 or 200 residue settings: IL-7Ralpha, InsulinR, PD-L1, TrkA, CD3D, EGFRc, EGFRn, FGFR2, IGF1R, PDGFRbeta, Tie2 and VirB8, counted from the rows of that table. For each method, each length and each target, 100 designs are generated with that method's default settings, so each cell of the comparison rests on 100 original designs.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The two comparator methods and TorchCraft are not scored on identical pipelines, and the paper describes the difference. profile.summary: This is the in silico VHH, or nanobody, design comparison published with TorchCraft. Fifteen protein targets, each with a PDB entry, a crop and hotspot residues in Supplementary Table S5, are designed against by four methods, TorchCraft, RFantibody, BoltzGen and Germinal, over five nanobody frameworks, with 100 designs per method per framework per target and CDR lengths fixed at 8 residues for HCDR1 and HCDR2 and 9 to 21 for HCDR3. A design passes only if it clears two thresholds: a TorchScore ipTM above 0.7 and an ESM2-150M sequence perplexity below 6.31, the second standing in as an expression proxy. Figure 3i prints the pass rates per target and Supplementary Figure S5 splits them by framework.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a method can design nanobody CDR loops, on a fixed framework, that a structure predictor is confident bind the target and that a protein language model considers likely to express. The second part is unusual and deliberate: the pass criterion pairs a structural confidence threshold with a sequence perplexity threshold the authors calibrated against expression data. The framework-stratified figure asks a further question, how much the result depends on which of the five scaffolds is used, with the same target panel and criterion.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: No dataset and no split: a target panel. Supplementary Table S5 lists fifteen targets with a PDB entry, the target chain and residue crop and hotspot residues for each: IL13, HNMT, 1433E, BHRF1, EFNA1, CCL2, IL20, CSF1, MZB1, LIF, XIAP, RSPO1, FCGR3B, UNG and DAF, counted from its rows. Its caption fixes the CDR lengths for all designs at HCDR1 of 8 residues, HCDR2 of 8 and HCDR3 of 9 to 21. Five nanobody frameworks are used, named in Appendix A.5.2.1 as 7EOW (caplacizumab), 8Z8V (ozoralizumab), 5JDS (envafolimab), 7XL0 (vobarilizumab) and 8COH (gefurulimab), the same five identifiers that label the per-framework panels of Supplementary Figures S3 and S5. For each method, each framework and each target, 100 designs are generated with that method's default settings. The expression proxy threshold was built separately: public nanobody expression measurements were combined with accumulated TorchCraft expression data, designs expressing at least 0.08 mg were labelled high expression, and ESM2-150M perplexity was swept as a one-dimensional classifier with the threshold chosen to maximise the Matthews correlation coefficient.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The four methods are handled differently before scoring, and the paper sets out how. For BoltzGen and RFantibody the full designed sequence is redesigned eight times with AbMPNN without fixing residues; for Germinal the original pipeline is followed, fixing CDR residues that contact the interface and applying AbMPNN only outside the CDRs. Each redesigned sequence is rebuilt to all-atom side chains with FlowPacker, the eight rebuilt models are scored with TorchScore, and the one with the highest ipTM becomes that original design's score. TorchCraft is reported raw, scored directly without redesign, and in an MPNN-polished setting where its interface CDR residues are fixed and the rest redesigned eight times with AbMPNN before the same rebuild and selection. The pass criterion is both thresholds together: TorchScore ipTM above 0.7 and ESM2-150M perplexity below 6.31. Rosetta interface-score distributions are reported separately as an additional assessment.

profile.summary: This benchmark pairs a deep mutational scan of the MET kinase domain with predictions from a large set of computational methods, so that the methods can be judged on whether they track a drug-dependent fitness landscape. The measurements cover 5,434 MET missense variants under twelve conditions, a DMSO vehicle control and eleven kinase inhibitors, which is 65,208 rows. Three published tables carry the same rows: mutational effects with predictions made in the 287-residue kinase domain context, the same with predictions made in the 1,390-residue full-length context, and protein-ligand affinity and binding free energy change. Counting the prediction columns across the three tables gives 57. Five further kinase scans, for CDK4, CDK6, EGFR, FGFR and SRC, are published beside them for the same comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening and Repository layout; MET_muteff_kinase_domain.csv header and rows; PMC abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a mutational-effect or affinity predictor responds to which drug is present. The scan gives, for each variant, a fitness score in each of twelve conditions, so a model that produces one number per variant regardless of the inhibitor can be seen to do so. The accompanying preprint's abstract states the question as how well these methods generalise beyond their training sets, and reports that current models produce largely ligand-invariant predictions despite experimentally distinct inhibitor-dependent landscapes, that ligand-aware geometric models such as LigandMPNN and LASErMPNN partially recover resistance-associated hotspots, and that affinity predictors underestimate mutation-induced changes in binding affinity. The repository supports a second question too, since the same variants are scored with predictions made in the kinase domain alone and in the full-length protein.
sections.source_locator: PMC abstract; README.md: Repository layout

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The experimental half is a deep mutational scan of the MET kinase domain read out under a vehicle control and eleven inhibitors, named in the README as A458, Cabo, Camp, Crizo, Gle, Glu, Mere, NVP, Savo, Tepo and Tiv. Each published table has one row per variant and condition: counting the main table in this pass gives 65,208 data rows, 5,434 distinct variants and twelve conditions, each condition carrying all 5,434 variants. Variants are numbered in kinase-domain coordinates from 1 to 287, with 1058 to be added for MET numbering, and every row is a missense variant. Alongside the measured score each row carries the same variant's score in DMSO, binary sensitised and resisted calls, and distances from the residue to the drug taken from a per-condition cofolded structure, with a flag for residues within 5 Angstrom of the drug. The structural side is published too: wild-type cofolds for the twelve conditions from three prediction methods. A clean folder holds the experiment on its own with no model predictions, including a 36-row table of kinase and inhibitor pairs with sequences, SMILES and the scanned position range. Five other kinase scans, CDK4, CDK6, EGFR, FGFR and SRC, are published as one CSV each and the README states they are not split.
sections.source_locator: README.md: opening, Repository layout, Annotation columns; MET_muteff_kinase_domain.csv; clean/kinase_drug_pairs.csv

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The repository is a paired dataset rather than a scoring harness: it publishes the measured target beside each method's prediction and leaves the comparison to the user. The README names the measured DMS score in a condition, the mean column, as the target, and the per-variant predictions sit in the same row, so a correlation or a ranking can be computed per condition or across conditions. Counting the non-annotation columns gives 23 prediction columns in the kinase-domain table, 18 in the full-length table and 16 in the affinity table, 57 in all, which is the figure the README's opening sentence gives as the number of computational methods. Two derived views are published rather than computed by the reader: a difference-score folder that takes the change in fitness score across inhibitor conditions, and a difference-tail folder for identifying candidate sensitising and resistance mutations. Three notebooks are published, for the difference scores, for statistical analysis of the fitness scores and for the figures. What is not in the files read here is a metric definition, a threshold, or a reference result: no aggregate score, no leaderboard and no fixed evaluation split.
