profile.summary: This benchmark asks a method to look at a protein homodimer interface and say whether it is physiological or a crystallographic contact, scoring each entry so that a higher score means more likely physiological. The entries are 1,671 curated homodimer interfaces, 840 physiological and 831 non-physiological, taken from the community-wide study of Schweke and colleagues published in 2023. This package is not the original study: it turns that benchmark into an OpenEBench experiment, with gold-standard labels, four homology-aware five-fold cross-validation splits, the scores of 14 reference methods, validation and scoring scripts, and a static page that scores a submitted CSV in the browser and ranks it against those methods. Anyone with an interface classifier can run it against a published leaderboard without reimplementing the comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Original work and Benchmark task; Zenodo record description

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a scoring function can tell a biologically real homodimer interface from one that only exists because of crystal packing. A submission is a ranking of the benchmark entries, higher meaning more likely physiological, so the main metrics are threshold-free, and threshold-based metrics are reported alongside. The package's own contribution is comparability: it fixes the labels, the folds and the metric code, so a new method's numbers can be put beside the 14 reference methods rather than computed under its own conventions.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Benchmark task, How to submit your own predictions; Zenodo record description

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The entries come from the original community study's curated annotation: 1,677 entries less the six flagged for deletion, leaving 1,671, of which 840 are physiological and 831 are not. The Zenodo record states that these labels are the curated annotation and that they differ for 16 entries from the original 2023 publication, which reported 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces. The reference scores are the ones the 13 research groups submitted to the original benchmark repository, plus a random-forest consensus whose scores are the leave-one-out probabilities provided there. The splits are the package's own work and are documented as such: they are not the folds of the original study. Four strategies are offered, all built so that homologous interfaces stay in one fold, because 1000 of the 1671 entries, 60 per cent, share a CATH superfamily with at least one other entry and a random split would put near-identical interfaces on both sides. Strategy 1 groups by CATH superfamily with a UniProt gene fallback, 853 groups. Strategy 2 clusters chain sequences with MMseqs2 at 25 per cent identity and 50 per cent one-sided coverage, 1076 clusters. Strategy 2b is a BLASTClust clustering at the same nominal parameters, 1045 clusters, which the document calls the most defensible sequence-identity split. Strategy 3, the recommended default and the one the published leaderboard uses, takes the connected components of the union of Strategies 1 and 2b, 688 components with a largest component of 132 entries. All four are verified to have no group spanning more than one fold.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record description; README.md: Example of results; CV_SPLITTING_STRATEGIES.md

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a CSV with one row per entry and a score where higher means more likely physiological. It is then validated and scored. The validation step checks the submitted identifiers against the public reference list and reports how many are missing or unexpected; read in the code, it requires the columns entry_id and raw_score and marks a submission as an error when coverage is not above 0.5. The scoring step computes AUROC, through the Mann-Whitney rank formulation, and AUCPR as average precision, plus accuracy at a threshold, balanced accuracy, F1 and the Matthews correlation coefficient. The threshold matters and the code is explicit about it: a published decision threshold is used when one is passed, and otherwise the script derives the optimal threshold by Youden's J from the same scored population and flags the value as data-driven rather than published. For the cross-validated leaderboard the README states that the thresholds for balanced accuracy, F1 and MCC are learned on the training folds only, and results are reported as a mean and standard deviation over the five folds. A consolidation step turns the per-participant assessments into one leaderboard. The numbers are also reproducible in two ways: the README reports that its demo submission's AUROC computed with the bundle's cross-validation script agrees with the figure the in-browser page produces.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Example of results and How to submit; workflow/validate.py; workflow/compute_metrics.py; workflow/run_pipeline.sh

sections.title: Reading the reference table
sections.body: The README's table of the 14 reference methods carries two caveats that change how it should be read, and both are the package's own. First, the top row is not like the others: the random-forest consensus is a trained classifier rather than a single fixed score, its scores are leave-one-out probabilities taken unchanged from the original benchmark repository, and because leave-one-out does not remove homologous entries from the training set its AUROC should be read as an upper estimate relative to the other methods. Second, the methods did not all score the same entries. The n column ranges from 1,123 to 1,671, a method with fewer entries is evaluated on its own subset, and the README points at QSQE, whose AUCPR exceeds its AUROC, as an example of what that does to a value. Beside the current results the repository also keeps analyses computed before a correction, in a superseded folder, for transparency.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Example of results, Random-forest consensus note, What is in this repository

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Two ways. The quick way is the interactive page, which scores a submitted CSV in the browser, lets the user pick a cross-validation strategy with Strategy 3 as the recommended default, and ranks the result against the 14 reference methods; the README states no file is uploaded anywhere. The local way is the bundle's pipeline script, which is the plain-Python equivalent of the Nextflow description: for every participant directory it runs the validation script against the public reference dataset, then the metrics script against the gold-standard directory, and finally the consolidation script, which writes a data model export and a leaderboard image. One detail to watch, read from the splitting document rather than the README: the cross-validation scripts read cv_fold_assignment.csv, which is Strategy 1, kept for backward compatibility, so using the recommended Strategy 3 locally means pointing the gold-standard directory at a copy of the Strategy 3 fold file under that name.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One set of 1,671 curated homodimer interface entries, 840 physiological and 831 non-physiological. It is the 1,677 entries of the benchmark authors' curated annotation without the six flagged for deletion. The package also ships the gold-standard labels, four fold assignment files, the 14 reference methods' score sets, a demo prediction file of 1,610 entries and a prediction template.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Benchmark task, Example of a new submission, What is in this repository; Zenodo record description

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Four homology-aware five-fold cross-validation splits, defined by this package rather than taken from the original study. Strategy 1 groups by CATH superfamily with a UniProt gene fallback, 853 groups, largest 42 entries. Strategy 2 is an MMseqs2 clustering at 25 per cent identity and 50 per cent one-sided coverage, 1076 clusters, largest 25. Strategy 2b is the BLASTClust clustering at matched nominal parameters, 1045 clusters; the document's prose says the largest holds 27 entries while its own summary table row for 2b says 26, and the document does not resolve the difference. Strategy 3, the recommendation and the basis of the published table, is the connected components of the union of 1 and 2b, 688 components, largest 132. All four are verified to place every group inside a single fold. The scripts, however, read the Strategy 1 file by default.
facts.source_locator: CV_SPLITTING_STRATEGIES.md; README.md: Example of results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC and AUCPR, both threshold-free and higher is better, with AUROC the ranking metric of the published leaderboard. Beside them the scoring script computes accuracy at a threshold, balanced accuracy, F1 and the Matthews correlation coefficient, also higher is better. The threshold is a published one if supplied, otherwise Youden's J computed on the same scored population and flagged as data-driven; in the cross-validated table the thresholds are learned on the training folds only. Values are reported as a mean and standard deviation across the five folds.
facts.source_locator: workflow/compute_metrics.py docstring; README.md: Example of results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Fourteen reference methods, 13 research groups' submitted scores plus a random-forest consensus on the top 221 features. In the README's Strategy 3 table they are, in AUROC order, the random forest consensus, DeepRank-GNN, Rosetta InterfaceAnalyzer, IES normalised, DLScore-BC, QSQE, Voronota, NIPacking, ISPRED4, MaSIF, GOAP, CP/COCOMAPS, shape_hydro_tails and ProbaConsensus with the ScanNet F_Network, counted from the rows of that table.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Example of results; Zenodo record description

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Homology-aware folds, and this is the package's main addition. The splitting document states that 1000 of the 1671 entries, 60 per cent, share a CATH superfamily with at least one other entry, so a random five-fold split would put near-identical or homologous interfaces in both the training and held-out folds and inflate any cross-validated estimate. Every strategy therefore keeps a homology group inside one fold, and all four are verified to have no group spanning folds. The documented exception is the random-forest consensus row, whose leave-one-out probabilities come from the original repository and do not remove homologues from the training set, which is why the package says its AUROC is an upper estimate.
facts.source_locator: CV_SPLITTING_STRATEGIES.md: why a plain random split is unsafe; README.md: Random-forest consensus note

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: A standard deviation across the five cross-validation folds, printed beside every value in the reference table and in the demo submission's result. No bootstrap or confidence interval is reported, and no repeated resampling of the folds themselves.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Example of results and Example of a new submission

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One protein homodimer interface, identified by an entry_id, with a binary gold-standard label, physiological or non-physiological.

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated. The entries are protein homodimer structures from the original community-wide study, identified by entry identifier, and no species information appears in the files read here.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None as such: the labels are curated annotations of whether an interface is physiological, not a measurement. The Zenodo record describes them as the curated annotation of the benchmark authors, differing for 16 entries from the original publication.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Not restricted by the package. A submission is only a table of entry identifiers and scores, so any input a method uses is permitted; the reference methods range from interface energy functions and geometric descriptors to graph neural networks. The original benchmark's structures are distributed by the community repository the package derives from, and this package ships the labels and folds rather than the structures.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Either, and the package distinguishes them. Thirteen of the reference methods are single fixed scores used as submitted, while the random-forest consensus is a trained classifier whose leave-one-out probabilities are used unchanged and are not retrained within the folds. A new submission is a score file, so a method may be trained however its authors wish; what the folds control is the threshold fitting, which in the published table happens on training folds only.

strengths.text: The splits are designed against the leakage this dataset actually has, with the figure stated: 60 per cent of entries share a CATH superfamily with another entry, so homologous interfaces are kept in one fold, and no group spans folds in any of the four strategies.

The package says what it did and did not inherit: the folds are its own proposal and explicitly not the folds of the original study, and the reference scores are the ones the groups submitted to the original repository.

The two caveats a reader needs are printed next to the table rather than buried: that the consensus row is a trained classifier whose AUROC is an upper estimate, and that methods scored between 1,123 and 1,671 entries so rows are not strictly comparable.

Submission is cheap and checkable: a two-column CSV scored in the browser with no upload, and the same numbers reproducible locally with the bundle's scripts, which the README demonstrates by matching its demo result to the in-browser value.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Interactive page and Example of a new submission; workflow/run_pipeline.sh

limitations.text: Rows of the leaderboard are not strictly comparable. Methods scored different numbers of entries, from 1,123 to 1,671, and a method with fewer is evaluated on its own subset, which the README illustrates with QSQE's AUCPR exceeding its AUROC on 1,123 entries.

The top row has an advantage the others do not. The random-forest consensus is a trained classifier whose leave-one-out probabilities come from the original repository, and leave-one-out does not remove homologous entries from its training set, so the package itself says its AUROC is an upper estimate relative to the other methods.

The labels are a curated annotation that differs from the published study. The Zenodo record states that this annotation differs for 16 entries from Schweke et al. 2023, which reported 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces against the 840 and 831 used here, and that six entries flagged for deletion were removed.
The licence is non-commercial. The package is released under CC BY-NC 4.0, both in its licence file and in the Zenodo record, although the source benchmark it derives from is CC BY 4.0.

intake-385-20261124-benchmark-elixir-pro.notes: Numbers and names worth a reviewer's eye. The 1,671 entries are the curated annotation's 1,677 less six flagged for deletion, and the Zenodo record states this annotation differs for 16 entries from the original 2023 publication, which had 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological against 840 and 831 here. The n column of the reference table is not the benchmark size: methods scored between 1,123 and 1,671 entries and each is evaluated on its own subset, so the structured size records the benchmark's 1,671 and the size unit records that range. The structured split is Strategy 3 because that is what the published table and the page's default recommendation use; the repository's own cross-validation scripts read the Strategy 1 fold file for backward compatibility, which a local reproduction has to change deliberately. Two inconsistencies were found by reading the code: the README asks a submitter for columns entry_id and score while workflow/validate.py requires entry_id and raw_score, and compute_metrics.py derives its decision threshold from the scored population by Youden's J whenever no published threshold is passed, flagging it as data-driven. The Zenodo record for this version says 1.0.0 while the README's citation block says 1.2.0 for the concept DOI. The released date is the Zenodo publication date of this version, not a last-modified timestamp. Everything in the package is CC BY-NC 4.0, so no repository bytes are stored; the Zenodo API response is stored as the brief allows.
